questions.question: What do you know about the Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah?
questions.answer: Muhammad Ali Jinnah (1876–1948) was born in Karachi and trained as a barrister at Lincoln’s Inn, London. He became the foremost leader of the All-India Muslim League and led the Pakistan Movement until the establishment of Pakistan on 14 August 1947. Because of his tireless struggle for the Muslims of the sub-continent he is called Quaid-e-Azam, meaning “the Great Leader”. He became the first Governor-General of Pakistan and presided over its first Constituent Assembly, whose inaugural session he addressed on 11 August 1947. He died on 11 September 1948 and is remembered as the architect of Pakistan and a constitutionalist who believed in the rule of law, democracy and the equality of all citizens.
questions.explanation: This pre-reading question draws on prior knowledge, so the wording of students’ answers will vary. The facts given here are the standard biographical ones; the reading text confirms that he addressed the first Constituent Assembly on 11 August 1947 and that the Assembly was presided over by him (Exercise 5, row 1).

questions.question: What was his main contribution?
questions.answer: His main contribution was the creation of Pakistan. Through constitutional agitation, negotiations and the political mobilisation of the Muslims of the sub-continent under the All-India Muslim League, he secured a separate homeland where Muslims could live according to their own faith and culture. After independence he guided the new state as its first Governor-General and, in his address of 11 August 1947, laid down the principles of a democratic, tolerant and welfare-oriented Pakistan based on law and order, equality of citizenship, and justice and fair play.
questions.explanation: The answer combines the historical record with the reading text, which calls the 11 August 1947 speech “one of the most consequential assertions in the history of South Asia” and says that it testifies to the Quaid’s vision of Pakistan.

questions.question: What was his vision for Pakistan?
questions.answer: The Quaid’s vision was of a democratic, sovereign and welfare-oriented state in which all citizens are equal, whatever their community, colour, caste or creed. He wanted Pakistan to be a country governed by law and order, where the life, property and religious beliefs of every citizen are protected; where bribery, corruption, black-marketing, nepotism and jobbery are crushed; where the well-being of the masses and the poor is the first concern; and where the state has nothing to do with a citizen’s religion, because “you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques or to any other places of worship in this State of Pakistan”.
questions.explanation: The vision is stated throughout the reading text: sovereignty of the legislature, the first duty of government to maintain law and order, freedom of worship, non-discrimination, and justice and fair play as guiding principles.

questions.question: Share some famous quotes of the Quaid-e-Azam.
questions.answer: Some famous quotes of the Quaid-e-Azam are: (1) “Unity, Faith and Discipline.” (2) “You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques or to any other places of worship in this State of Pakistan.” (3) “All men are equal in the eyes of God.” (4) “No power can hold another nation in subjection.” (5) “Think a hundred times before you take a decision, but once that decision is taken, stand by it as one man.” (6) “My guiding principle will be justice and complete impartiality.”
questions.explanation: Quotes 2, 3, 4 and 6 are taken directly from the reading text; 1 and 5 are among his most widely quoted sayings. Students may offer other authentic quotations, so this answer is not exclusive.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “unprecedented” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Unprecedented means never known, seen or experienced before; having no earlier example. In the text the Quaid speaks of “this unprecedented cyclonic revolution” — a political upheaval of a kind that had never happened before in the sub-continent.
questions.explanation: Context clue: the word is used with “cyclonic revolution” and with “unknown, unparalleled” in the following sentence, all of which point to something entirely new and without precedent.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “sovereign” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Sovereign means supreme in authority and completely independent; not subject to any outside power. The text speaks of “two independent Sovereign Dominions” and tells the Assembly, “you are now a sovereign legislative body and you have got all the powers.”
questions.explanation: The context pairs “sovereign” with “independent” and with “all the powers”, which shows that it means self-governing and supreme.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “monster” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: A monster here means a huge, ugly and destructive evil that has grown out of control. The Quaid calls black-marketing “this monster which today is a colossal crime against society”, so the word is used figuratively for a monstrous social evil, not for a literal beast.
questions.explanation: The words around it — “colossal crime against society” and “they ought to be very severely punished” — show that “monster” refers to the evil practice of black-marketing.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “starvation” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Starvation means extreme and prolonged hunger, or suffering and death caused by lack of food. The Quaid says that black-marketers “undermine the entire system of control and regulation of food-stuffs and essential commodities, and cause wholesale starvation”, that is, hunger on a mass scale.
questions.explanation: Context clue: “food-stuffs and essential commodities” plus “wholesale” shows that starvation is the mass hunger that results when food is hoarded and sold illegally.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “colossal” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Colossal means extremely large, enormous or gigantic. In the text black-marketing is called “a colossal crime against society”, meaning a crime of enormous size and seriousness.
questions.explanation: The word intensifies “crime against society”; the parallel phrase “a plan which is titanic” in the same passage confirms that colossal belongs to the same family of words meaning huge.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “nepotism” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Nepotism means the unfair practice of favouring one’s relatives or friends, especially by giving them jobs or undue advantages because of the relationship rather than merit. The Quaid calls it “this great evil — the evil of nepotism and jobbery”, something he will never tolerate.
questions.explanation: Context clue: nepotism is grouped with “jobbery” and with “any influence directly or indirectly brought to bear”, which shows that it is the misuse of influence for one’s own people.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “onerous” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Onerous means burdensome; involving a heavy load of work, difficulty or responsibility. The Quaid describes constitution-making as “the very onerous and responsible task of framing our future constitution of Pakistan”.
questions.explanation: The word is explained by its companion adjective “responsible” and by the magnitude of the task named after it, so it means heavy and demanding rather than easy.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “titanic” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Titanic means of enormous size, strength or power; gigantic. The Quaid describes the plan of creating two independent sovereign dominions as “a plan which is titanic, unknown, unparalleled”, that is, a plan of immense scale.
questions.explanation: The adjectives “unknown” and “unparalleled” that follow titanic show that it means exceptionally great in scale, derived from the Titans of Greek mythology.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “gravest” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Gravest is the superlative of grave and means most serious, most solemn or most weighty. The Assembly’s new powers place on its members “the gravest responsibility as to how you should take your decisions”, that is, the most serious responsibility of all.
questions.explanation: Context clue: “responsibility” collocates with “grave” in the sense of solemn and serious; the superlative shows that no responsibility could be more serious.

questions.question: Deduce the meaning of the word “relentlessly” from the context of the text.
questions.answer: Relentlessly means without stopping, weakening or showing mercy; persistently and with unremitting severity. The Quaid says of the evil of nepotism and jobbery, “This evil must be crushed relentlessly”, meaning it must be stamped out with continuous, unforgiving effort.
questions.explanation: The verb “crushed” supplies the idea of force, and the adverb adds the idea of never easing off; the whole clause therefore means relentless, non-stop suppression.

questions.question: Match the phrase “put down” (Column A, No. 1) with its meaning in Column B. Column B: (A) grant of something for (B) be certain to (C) to end fight to make peace (D) to cause something to happen (E) stop holding something (F) to deal or face great problem (G) have an effect of something (H) with full force (I) encourage to do an expected task (J) read or examine thoroughly. The first one has been done as an example.
questions.answer:
1. put down — E — stop holding something (printed example).
Note: in the speech (“We must put that down with an iron hand”) the phrase means “suppress”, but the printed table assigns the literal sense E to the example, so E is retained.
questions.explanation: The book gives this row as the worked example: Column A No. 1 is matched with Column B letter E. The literal meaning of the phrasal verb “put down” is to set something down or stop holding it.

questions.question: Match the phrase “bring about” (Column A, No. 2) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 2. bring about — D — to cause something to happen.
questions.explanation: “Bring about” is a phrasal verb meaning to make something happen. In the text the “cyclonic revolution” brought about “the plan of creating two independent Sovereign Dominions”.

questions.question: Match the phrase “go through” (Column A, No. 3) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 3. go through — J — read or examine thoroughly.
questions.explanation: To “go through” a document, report or list is to read or examine it carefully from beginning to end; this matches meaning J.

questions.question: Match the phrase “conferred upon” (Column A, No. 4) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 4. conferred upon — A — grant of something for [sic]. (The sense is “granted to”: the honour was conferred upon the speaker.)
questions.explanation: “Confer something on/upon someone” means to grant or bestow it. The Quaid thanks the Assembly “for the honour you have conferred upon me”. Column B prints “for” where “to” is meant; marked [sic].

questions.question: Match the phrase “bound to” (Column A, No. 5) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 5. bound to — B — be certain to.
questions.explanation: “Bound to” expresses certainty: “you are bound to succeed” means you are certain to succeed. Hence meaning B.

questions.question: Match the phrase “with an iron hand” (Column A, No. 6) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 6. with an iron hand — H — with full force.
questions.explanation: “With an iron hand” (or iron fist) means with great severity and force, without leniency; it matches meaning H.

questions.question: Match the phrase “to tackle the monster” (Column A, No. 7) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 7. to tackle the monster — F — to deal or face great problem.
questions.explanation: To tackle something is to deal with it boldly; the “monster” is black-marketing, a huge problem, so the phrase means to deal with or face a great problem (F).

questions.question: Match the phrase “bring to bear” (Column A, No. 8) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 8. bring to bear — G — have an effect of something.
questions.explanation: “Bring something to bear on” means to apply it so that it has an effect: the Quaid speaks of influence “directly or indirectly brought to bear upon me”. This matches meaning G.

questions.question: Match the phrase “to bury the hatchet” (Column A, No. 9) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 9. to bury the hatchet — C — to end fight to make peace.
questions.explanation: “Bury the hatchet” is an idiom meaning to stop quarrelling and make peace. The Quaid asks the members to work “forgetting the past, burying the hatchet”, which matches C.

questions.question: Match the phrase “to lead someone to” (Column A, No. 10) with its meaning in Column B (A–J).
questions.answer: 10. to lead someone to — I — encourage to do an expected task.
questions.explanation: “Lead someone to do something” means to guide, induce or encourage that person to do it; this is meaning I.

questions.question: The Quaid-e-Azam was speaking to the Constituent Assembly at ________.
questions.answer: The Quaid-e-Azam was speaking to the Constituent Assembly at national level: (a) national level.
questions.explanation: The Constituent Assembly was the first federal legislature of the whole country — “the inaugural session of Pakistan’s first Constituent Assembly” — so the level was national, not regional, global or provincial.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) national level   (b) regional level   (c) global level   (d) provincial level

questions.question: The main function of the Constituent Assembly was to ________.
questions.answer: The main function of the Constituent Assembly was to make constitution: (c) make constitution.
questions.explanation: The text names two functions; the first is “the very onerous and responsible task of framing our future constitution of Pakistan”, i.e. making the constitution.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) make country as example   (b) honour assembly members   (c) make constitution   (d) practice constitution

questions.question: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, ‘cyclonic revolution’ meant a wave of ________.
questions.answer: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, ‘cyclonic revolution’ meant a wave of revolt: (b) revolt.
questions.explanation: A cyclonic revolution is a violent, sweeping upheaval; the text says it “brought about the plan of creating two independent Sovereign Dominions”, an upsurge against the old order. Among the options, “revolt” alone carries that sense of forceful upheaval.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) discrimination   (b) revolt   (c) elections   (d) legislation

questions.question: The main task of the Govt. according to the Quaid-e-Azam is to ________.
questions.answer: The main task of the Govt. according to the Quaid-e-Azam is to make law and order: (d) make law and order.
questions.explanation: The text states plainly: “The first duty of a government is to maintain law and order so that the life, property and religious beliefs of its subjects are fully protected by the State.”
questions.optionsRaw: (a) make constitution for provinces   (b) stop black marketing   (c) curb bribery   (d) make law and order

questions.question: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, the poisonous thing is ________.
questions.answer: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, the poisonous thing is corruption: (a) corruption.
questions.explanation: He says: “one of the biggest curses from which India is suffering is bribery and corruption. That really is a poison.” Bribery and corruption is therefore the “poison”; black-marketing is called “another curse”.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) corruption   (b) black-marketing   (c) nepotism   (d) law and order situation

questions.question: The colossal crime monster as stated in the text is ________.
questions.answer: The colossal crime monster as stated in the text is black marketing: (b) black marketing.
questions.explanation: The paragraph on black-marketing ends: “you have to tackle this monster which today is a colossal crime against society in our distressed conditions.” The monster is thus black-marketing.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) break the law   (b) black marketing   (c) favouritism   (d) bribery

questions.question: On 11 August 1947, Quaid-e-Azam was speaking to ________.
questions.answer: On 11 August 1947, Quaid-e-Azam was speaking to first legislative body: (b) first legislative body.
questions.explanation: The opening line places the speech at “the inaugural session of Pakistan’s first Constituent Assembly”, and the Quaid tells the members, “you are now a sovereign legislative body”. It was therefore the first legislative body of the new state.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) already function assembly   (b) first legislative body   (c) whole nation   (d) members of the provincial body

questions.question: The first legislative body was bestowed with ________.
questions.answer: The first legislative body was bestowed with full powers: (a) full powers.
questions.explanation: The Quaid says: “remember that you are now a sovereign legislative body and you have got all the powers.” “All the powers” corresponds to “full powers”.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) full powers   (b) limited powers   (c) only make legislative powers   (d) only powers to curb bribery

questions.question: The thing that was already prevailing in the continent after partition was ________.
questions.answer: The thing that was already prevailing in the continent after partition was bribery: (a) bribery.
questions.explanation: The Quaid says bribery and corruption was a curse “from which India is suffering” already — an existing, prevailing evil — whereas black-marketing is presented as a crime of the “distressed conditions” after partition. (Nepotism is described as an inherited legacy, but bribery is the evil the text explicitly says was already being suffered.)
questions.optionsRaw: (a) bribery   (b) foodstuff   (c) nepotism   (d) starvation

questions.question: The guided principles of the Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah are ________.
questions.answer: The guided principles of the Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah are justice & fair play: (b) justice & fair play.
questions.explanation: In his closing lines he says: “I shall always be guided by the principles of justice and fair-play without any political language, prejudice or ill-will.”
questions.optionsRaw: (a) support & cooperation   (b) justice & fair play   (c) prejudice & honour   (d) angularities of majority & minority

questions.question: Why was the Quaid feeling honoured while addressing the first Constituent Assembly?
questions.answer: The Quaid felt honoured because the first Constituent Assembly of Pakistan had invited him to address its inaugural session and had thereby conferred an honour on him. He begins: “I cordially thank you, with the utmost sincerity, for the honour you have conferred upon me.” The honour was twofold: he was addressing, as its president, the first sovereign legislative body of the newly independent state, and he was speaking on an occasion of historic importance for the whole of South Asia.
questions.explanation: The answer is grounded in the opening paragraph of the speech, which calls the address “one of the most consequential assertions in the history of South Asia” and records his thanks for the honour conferred on him.

questions.question: Which is the greatest curse according to the Quaid-e-Azam?
questions.answer: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, the greatest curse is bribery and corruption. He says: “one of the biggest curses from which India is suffering is bribery and corruption. That really is a poison. We must put that down with an iron hand.” He calls black-marketing “another curse” and nepotism and jobbery “this great evil”, but bribery and corruption is the curse he singles out first and most strongly, calling it a poison.
questions.explanation: The superlative in the question corresponds to “one of the biggest curses” and to the metaphor “poison” applied to bribery and corruption.

questions.question: What was the Quaid’s vision about religious freedom?
questions.answer: The Quaid’s vision was one of complete religious freedom and absolute non-discrimination. He declared: “You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques or to any other places of worship in this State of Pakistan.” Religion, caste or creed, he said, “has nothing to do with the business of the State”; there would be “no discrimination, no distinction between one community and another”, and all citizens would be “equal citizens of one State” with equal rights, privileges and obligations.
questions.explanation: These lines occur in the paragraph beginning “No power can hold another nation in subjection” and form the core of his statement on minorities’ rights.

questions.question: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, what lesson should we learn?
questions.answer: According to the Quaid-e-Azam, the lesson is that “no power can hold another nation in subjection” and that freedom must therefore be valued and preserved. He draws this lesson from the end of colonial rule and immediately applies it: “You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques…” The lesson is that a nation which has won freedom must respect the freedom of every community within it and treat all its citizens equally.
questions.explanation: The sentence “No power can hold another nation in subjection. Therefore, we must learn a lesson from this” gives the lesson explicitly; the following sentences show how it applies to religious freedom.

questions.question: How far the key ideas of the Quaid’s speech are applicable to the present scenario?
questions.answer: The key ideas remain highly applicable today. (1) Equality of citizenship: the Quaid’s insistence that no community, colour, caste or creed has precedence is exactly what a plural Pakistan needs to counter sectarian and ethnic prejudice. (2) Rule of law and protection of life, property and worship: the first duty he assigned to government is still the first duty of any state facing crime and terrorism. (3) Crusade against bribery, corruption, black-marketing and nepotism: these evils are still the biggest obstacles to development and to fair distribution of resources. (4) Welfare of the masses and the poor: his instruction to “concentrate on the well-being of the people, and especially of the masses and the poor” is the essence of modern inclusive development. (5) Justice and fair play “without any political language, prejudice or ill-will”: an independent, impartial judiciary and merit-based appointments are still the foundation of good governance. His ideas are therefore not dated; they are a practical charter for reform.
questions.explanation: This is an evaluative question, so the argument and examples may vary. The five points above are each anchored in a specific passage of the speech, which makes the answer textual rather than merely personal.

questions.question: How can we make Pakistan prosperous in the light of the Quaid’s vision?
questions.answer: In the light of the Quaid’s vision, Pakistan can become prosperous if its people and rulers act on five principles. First, work in cooperation: “If you will work in co-operation, forgetting the past, burying the hatchet, you are bound to succeed.” Second, put citizenship above community: “every one of you, no matter to what community, colour, caste or creed he/she belongs is first, second and last a citizen of this State with equal rights, privileges and obligations.” Third, concentrate on “the well-being of the people, and especially of the masses and the poor”, so that growth benefits ordinary citizens. Fourth, establish law and order and crush bribery, corruption, black-marketing, nepotism and jobbery with an iron hand, because no economy can flourish where merit is ignored and food and essential commodities are hoarded. Fifth, let “justice and complete impartiality” guide every decision, so that investors, workers and citizens alike trust the system. Together these produce the social harmony, public trust and hard work on which lasting prosperity depends.
questions.explanation: The answer follows the order of the speech: cooperation and equal citizenship, welfare of the poor, law and order and the three evils, and finally justice and fair play. Quotations are from the text.

questions.question: “I shall always be guided by the principles of justice and fair play without any political language, prejudice and ill-will.” Elaborate these words.
questions.answer: With these words the Quaid-e-Azam sums up the creed by which he meant to govern. “Justice” means giving every person and every community exactly what is due to them under the law, without favour; “fair play” means observing the rules honestly and giving everyone an equal chance, even an opponent. “Without any political language” means that decisions would not be dressed up in slogans or shaped by party advantage; “without prejudice” means without preconceived hostility towards any person, sect or region; “without ill-will” means without malice or the desire to take revenge. He adds that his principle would be “justice and complete impartiality”, and he links this directly to his hope that “with your support and co-operation, I can look forward to Pakistan becoming one of the greatest Nations of the world.” In short, he is promising a government of laws and merit, not of favouritism and slogans — the same standard he demands when he condemns nepotism, jobbery and corruption.
questions.explanation: The answer unpacks each phrase of the quotation and connects it to the related passages of the speech (condemnation of nepotism and jobbery; justice and complete impartiality; Pakistan becoming one of the greatest nations).

questions.question: Read the statement and write whether it is a fact or an opinion: “The Quaid-e-Azam was president of the first Constituent Assembly.” (The first one has been done as an example.)
questions.answer: Fact (printed example). The Quaid-e-Azam presided over the first Constituent Assembly of Pakistan, which is a verifiable historical fact and is confirmed by the opening line of the text, where he makes a “Presidential address” to the Assembly.
questions.explanation: A fact is a statement that can be checked against evidence; the text itself calls the speech a “Presidential address”, so the statement is verifiable and true.

questions.question: Read the statement and write whether it is a fact or an opinion: “Hope that with your support we will make this Constituent Assembly as an example.”
questions.answer: Opinion. It expresses the speaker’s hope and expectation about what the Assembly may become in the future (“I sincerely hope that with your support and your co-operation we shall make this Constituent Assembly an example to the world”).
questions.explanation: A hope about the future cannot be verified as true or false at the time of speaking; it is the speaker’s personal expectation, so it is an opinion.

questions.question: Read the statement and write whether it is a fact or an opinion: “The first duty of Government is to maintain law and order.”
questions.answer: Opinion. It is the Quaid’s judgment about what a government ought to do first (“The first duty of a government is to maintain law and order…”), not a measurable event.
questions.explanation: The sentence is normative — it prescribes a priority rather than recording something that can be observed and verified. Reasonable people may rank other duties first, which marks it as an opinion.

questions.question: Read the statement and write whether it is a fact or an opinion: “All kinds of inhabitants are living in the sub-continent.”
questions.answer: Fact. It states an observable demographic reality: the sub-continent is inhabited by people of many communities, religions, castes and creeds.
questions.explanation: The statement can be verified by observation and census records, and the text itself refers to “This mighty sub-continent with all kinds of inhabitants”, so it is a fact.

questions.question: Read the statement and write whether it is a fact or an opinion: “Nepotism and jobbery are social evils.”
questions.answer: Opinion. Calling nepotism and jobbery “social evils” is a moral and social judgement about them, not a neutral description of an event.
questions.explanation: The statement evaluates the practices rather than merely reporting them; different people might describe them differently, so it is an opinion. (That the practices exist is a fact; that they are evils is a value judgement.)

questions.question: Read the statement and write whether it is a fact or an opinion: “The mighty revolution that has taken place is unprecedented.”
questions.answer: Opinion. The revolution did take place, but describing it as “mighty” and “unprecedented” is the speaker’s evaluation of its scale and uniqueness.
questions.explanation: Words such as “mighty” and “unprecedented” express a judgement about the event; whether it was unprecedented is a matter of interpretation, so the statement as a whole is an opinion.

questions.question: Do you think some of the ideas in this historic speech are not included? Work individually and search out the missed points of above speech using various sources and share these with the class.
questions.answer: Yes. The book itself says that what is printed is “an excerpt”, so several important ideas of the full address are not included. Points a student may find and report: (1) economic policy — the need for industrial development, fair wages, and improvement of agriculture; (2) education and human resource development, including technical training; (3) defence and foreign policy, and the unresolved question of Kashmir; (4) the structure of the federal constitution, provincial autonomy and relations between the centre and the provinces; (5) the rights of labour and the duty of employers, and land reforms for the tiller; (6) the role of women in national life; (7) reform of the civil service and strict accountability of public servants; (8) detailed safeguards for minorities in addition to the general principle of equal citizenship; (9) water, energy and communications as the infrastructure of progress; (10) the duty of citizens to obey the law and pay taxes honestly. A student may add the Quaid’s warnings about provincialism, his call for self-reliance, and his emphasis on character-building.
questions.explanation: This is an open-ended research task, so the list will vary with the sources consulted. The points above are the standard themes of the complete 11 August 1947 address that lie outside the excerpt printed in the textbook; the teacher’s note asks students to use libraries, reference books and the internet, and to present their findings.

questions.question: Now, practice the clustering individually on the following topics and check your work in pairs. (a) Social Media
questions.answer:
Centre: SOCIAL MEDIA

Branch 1 — Platforms: Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, YouTube, X (Twitter), TikTok, LinkedIn.
Branch 2 — Uses: chatting and calls, news and updates, online classes, business marketing, entertainment, freelancing.
Branch 3 — Benefits: instant connectivity, fast access to information, online learning, work from home, cheap advertising.
Branch 4 — Drawbacks: fake news, addiction, cyberbullying, loss of privacy, wasted time, weak face-to-face skills.
Branch 5 — Effects on students: distraction from study, shortened attention span, comparison and low self-esteem, but also educational videos and study groups.
Branch 6 — Safety and privacy: strong passwords, two-step verification, not sharing personal data, reporting abuse, thinking before posting.
Branch 7 — Etiquette: verify before sharing, respect others’ opinions, avoid abusive language, give credit to sources.
Branch 8 — Balance: fixed screen time, no phones during study or meals, outdoor games and reading as alternatives.
questions.explanation: A cluster (mind map) starts with the central word and radiates outward to related sub-topics, which then become body paragraphs. The branches here move from platforms to uses, benefits, drawbacks, effects, safety, etiquette and balance; other branchings are equally acceptable.

questions.question: Now, practice the clustering individually on the following topics and check your work in pairs. (b) Culture
questions.answer:
Centre: CULTURE

Branch 1 — Elements: language, dress, food, music, literature, festivals, rituals, values.
Branch 2 — Regional variety in Pakistan: Sindhi, Punjabi, Balochi, Pashto, Kashmiri and Urdu traditions.
Branch 3 — Symbols and arts: Ajrak and Sindhi cap, embroidery, pottery, truck art, calligraphy, folk dance.
Branch 4 — Heritage: Mohenjo-daro, Makli, Bhit Shah, Shah Jahan Mosque, Lahore Fort; Sufi poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai.
Branch 5 — Transmission: family, school, mother tongue, festivals, media, shrines and fairs.
Branch 6 — Threats: globalisation, westernisation, neglect of mother tongues, imitation of foreign dress and festivals, commercialisation.
Branch 7 — Preservation: museums and archives, heritage laws, mother-tongue education, folk festivals, documentation of crafts, tourism.
Branch 8 — Value: identity, tolerance, hospitality, national unity, pride and economic opportunity through cultural tourism.
questions.explanation: The diagram in the book uses a central oval with six radiating ovals, each carrying key words. This cluster follows that pattern and adds arrows from each branch to supporting details; students’ own clusters may differ in shape and content.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Read the sample essay again and underline the topic sentence and concluding sentence in each paragraph of the essay. After completing this work, share it with your partner.
questions.answer:
Paragraph 1 — Introduction. Topic sentence: “Facebook has become increasingly popular these days.” Concluding sentence: “Facebook has considerably facilitated the learner and the teacher world-wide.”
Paragraph 2 — Body paragraph 1. Topic sentence: “One of the key benefits of using Facebook in teaching and learning is its capacity for online community building.” Concluding sentence: “Thus, Facebook can provide a valuable mode of social interaction for students.”
Paragraph 3 — Body paragraph 2. Topic sentence: “Contrarily, the issue with Facebook concerns safety and privacy.” Concluding sentence: “Therefore, at secondary level teaching and learning, the students should be supported to learn how to protect their profiles and data, and use social networking sites safely.”
Paragraph 4 — Conclusion. Topic (restatement) sentence: “To sum up, it can be said that using Facebook at a tertiary level has positive and negative aspects.” Final statement: “However, if Facebook is going to be effectively and safely used in tertiary teaching and learning, the students and the teachers need careful guidance.”
questions.explanation: A topic sentence announces the paragraph’s main idea, usually at the beginning; a concluding sentence rounds it off, often with “Thus”, “Therefore” or “To sum up”. The introduction states the broad topic and the central argument, the two body paragraphs each develop one side (benefits, then risks), and the conclusion restates the argument and ends with a recommendation.

questions.question: Work in pairs. One of you should write an essay on any of the following topics. Follow the points discussed above for writing the essay. Topic 1: Importance of Culture
questions.answer:
IMPORTANCE OF CULTURE

Outline: Introduction (definition of culture; central argument that culture is both memory and compass) — Body 1 (culture gives identity) — Body 2 (culture builds social harmony and tolerance) — Body 3 (culture has economic and educational value) — Body 4 (culture is threatened by globalisation and must be preserved) — Conclusion (culture must be lived, not merely exhibited).

Culture is the total way of life of a people: their language, beliefs, dress, food, music, festivals, arts and values. It is the invisible thread that ties one generation to the next and tells a society who it is. In a country like Pakistan, where many languages and traditions live side by side, the importance of culture is not an academic question but a social necessity, because culture gives identity, sustains harmony and carries the wisdom of the past into the future.

First, culture gives individuals and communities a sense of identity. A Sindhi who wears the Ajrak, a Baloch who sings a folk song, or an Urdu-speaking child who learns a couplet of Iqbal is drawing on a heritage that tells him where he comes from. The Sufi poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, the crafts of Multan and the festivals of the northern valleys are not mere decorations; they are the memory of a nation. A society without culture is like a tree without roots — it may grow for a while, but it cannot stand against a storm.

Second, culture builds social harmony. Festivals such as Eid, the Urs at Bhit Shah and the Christmas and Diwali celebrations of minority communities bring people together across lines of faith and class. The tradition of hospitality, the shared languages of Sindh and the customs of the village encourage tolerance and fellow-feeling. The Quaid-e-Azam told the first Constituent Assembly that all citizens are equal “no matter to what community, colour, caste or creed” they belong; a living culture, with its habits of courtesy and coexistence, is the soil in which that principle grows.

Third, culture has economic and educational value. Heritage sites such as Mohenjo-daro and Makli, handicrafts, embroidery, pottery and truck art attract tourists and create employment for artisans. Mother-tongue-based education, which is itself a cultural right, helps children learn to read faster and with greater confidence before they move on to other languages. Cultural industries — music, film, publishing, design — are a growing source of income for young people.

Yet culture is under threat. Globalisation spreads one commercial model of dress, food and entertainment across the world, and young people may come to regard their own languages and customs as backward. The answer is not to reject everything modern but to balance: adopt useful technology and ideas while preserving the language, festivals, crafts and courtesy that make us who we are. Schools, families, museums and the media all have a part to play.

In conclusion, culture is both the memory of a nation and its compass. It gives identity, teaches tolerance, supports livelihoods and carries values from one generation to the next. Pakistan can modernise without losing itself if it honours its languages, celebrates its festivals, protects its heritage and teaches its children to be proud of their roots.
questions.explanation: This is a model essay following the book’s structure: introduction with a general statement and central argument, three to four body paragraphs each with a topic sentence and supporting detail, and a conclusion that restates the argument with a final statement. Other answers on this topic are acceptable.

questions.question: Work in pairs. One of you should write an essay on any of the following topics. Follow the points discussed above for writing the essay. Topic 2: Preservation of Heritage Sites
questions.answer:
PRESERVATION OF HERITAGE SITES

Outline: Introduction (definition and examples of heritage sites; central argument that preservation is a national duty) — Body 1 (heritage sites are evidence of our history and identity) — Body 2 (they have educational and economic value through tourism) — Body 3 (threats: neglect, encroachment, vandalism, careless restoration, climate) — Body 4 (measures: legislation, documentation, community involvement, funding, controlled tourism) — Conclusion (a nation that preserves its past secures its future).

Developed body paragraph (values): Heritage sites are the physical evidence of a nation’s history, and once destroyed they cannot be recreated. Mohenjo-daro tells us about the Indus Valley Civilisation, Makli preserves the art of Sindh’s dynasties, and the Shah Jahan Mosque in Thatta shows the craftsmanship of the Mughal age. These places teach students more vividly than any textbook, and they earn foreign exchange through tourism while providing work to guides, artisans and local traders. To lose them is to lose both a classroom and a livelihood.

Developed body paragraph (threats and measures): The dangers are familiar: encroachment, illegal construction around protected sites, vandalism, theft of antiquities and “restoration” carried out with cement and paint by untrained hands. The remedies are equally clear. Strong legislation with real penalties, a complete digital record of every monument, community ownership so that local people guard what gives them income, and a well-funded department of archaeology are all necessary. Tourism must be regulated so that visitors support rather than damage the sites.

(Conclusion) In short, heritage sites are the memory of the nation written in stone. Preserving them is not nostalgia; it is an investment in education, tourism and national pride.
questions.explanation: Model answer with a full outline and two developed body paragraphs plus a conclusion; the other paragraphs are left as points for the student to expand. Other treatments of the topic are acceptable.

questions.question: Work in pairs. One of you should write an essay on any of the following topics. Follow the points discussed above for writing the essay. Topic 3: Proper Conservation of Water
questions.answer:
PROPER CONSERVATION OF WATER

Outline: Introduction (water as a finite resource; Pakistan’s water stress; central argument that conservation is a shared duty) — Body 1 (why water is scarce: rising population, agriculture’s large share of use, waste and leakage, climate change) — Body 2 (conservation at home, in agriculture and in industry) — Body 3 (rainwater harvesting, dams and recharge of aquifers) — Body 4 (awareness, pricing and regulation) — Conclusion (small habits and sound policy together can avert a crisis).

Developed body paragraph (the problem): Pakistan is an agricultural country that depends on the Indus and its tributaries, yet it stores very little of the water that flows down to the sea each year. A rapidly growing population, the heavy demand of canal irrigation, leaking municipal pipes and the careless washing of cars and streets all put pressure on a supply that nature does not increase. Climate change makes the glaciers that feed the rivers unpredictable. A country that wastes water is, in effect, throwing away its food and its future.

Developed body paragraph (solutions): Conservation must work at three levels. At home, we can repair leaking taps, take shorter showers, use buckets instead of hoses and reuse washing water for plants. In agriculture, drip and sprinkler irrigation, laser levelling of fields and lining of canals can save a large part of the water now lost. In industry and cities, recycling and metering encourage careful use. On a larger scale, rainwater harvesting, small dams and the recharge of underground aquifers store water for dry seasons. Above all, schools and mosques must teach that water is an amanah, a trust, not a free and endless commodity.

(Conclusion) Proper conservation of water is neither a luxury nor a technical puzzle alone; it is a habit and a policy. If every citizen saves a little and every government plans for the long term, Pakistan can meet its needs without robbing future generations.
questions.explanation: Model answer with outline, two developed body paragraphs and a conclusion. The figures a student quotes may vary, so the explanation avoids specific statistics; other answers are acceptable.

questions.question: Work in pairs. One of you should write an essay on any of the following topics. Follow the points discussed above for writing the essay. Topic 4: Scope of English Language
questions.answer:
SCOPE OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE

Outline: Introduction (English as the global lingua franca; central argument that its scope is wide but should not displace the mother tongue) — Body 1 (education and research) — Body 2 (business, information technology and freelancing) — Body 3 (diplomacy, travel and international organisations) — Body 4 (its place in Pakistan and the need to keep it alongside Urdu and regional languages) — Conclusion (English is a tool of opportunity, not a substitute for identity).

Developed body paragraph (education and employment): English opens the door to knowledge. Most scientific journals, research databases and textbooks in medicine, engineering and computing are published in English, and a student who cannot read them is cut off from the latest work in his field. In Pakistan, English is the language of higher education, of the superior courts and of most official business, so competence in it directly affects access to universities and to public service. In the private sector it is even more decisive: information technology companies, banks, multinational firms and the growing market for online freelancing all conduct their work in English. A young person who can write a clear email, make a presentation and negotiate in English can compete for jobs not only in Karachi or Lahore but anywhere in the world.

Developed body paragraph (balance): This wide scope, however, does not mean that English should push aside Urdu and the regional languages. A child who loses his mother tongue loses the culture that comes with it. The sensible policy is additive rather than substitutive: strong literacy in the mother tongue in the early years, with English taught well as a second language from the primary stage onward.

(Conclusion) The scope of English is therefore both academic and economic, and it will remain wide for the foreseeable future. Pakistan should teach it confidently and well, while preserving the languages that carry its identity.
questions.explanation: Model answer with outline, two developed body paragraphs and a conclusion; other answers on the same topic are acceptable.

questions.question: Work in pairs. One of you should write an essay on any of the following topics. Follow the points discussed above for writing the essay. Topic 5: Prosperity Lies in Peace
questions.answer:
PROSPERITY LIES IN PEACE

Outline: Introduction (definition of prosperity and peace; central argument that peace is the precondition of development) — Body 1 (peace allows investment, jobs and growth) — Body 2 (peace makes education and health possible) — Body 3 (the cost of conflict: destruction, displacement, fear, lost opportunities) — Body 4 (internal peace requires justice, tolerance and rule of law) — Conclusion (the Quaid’s vision of cooperation and equal citizenship).

Developed body paragraph (economic argument): No factory, bank or foreign investor will risk money in a city where bombs explode and markets close at noon. Peace is therefore the first condition of prosperity. Where law and order prevail, businesses expand, employment grows and the government can collect taxes to build schools, hospitals and roads. Tourism, which depends entirely on safety, can earn foreign exchange and support thousands of families. In contrast, a single year of conflict can destroy infrastructure that took a decade to build and drive away the investment that would have paid for the next decade’s development.

Developed body paragraph (social and moral argument): Peace is also the condition of a good society. Children can go to school, patients can reach hospitals, and families can plan their future only when they are not afraid. Conflict breeds displacement, poverty and hatred that outlive the fighting. But peace is not merely the absence of war; it requires justice. The Quaid-e-Azam told the Assembly that every citizen, “no matter to what community, colour, caste or creed he/she belongs is first, second and last a citizen of this State with equal rights, privileges and obligations”. Where people are treated fairly, they have no reason to take up arms.

(Conclusion) Prosperity lies in peace because peace protects the investment, education and trust on which prosperity is built. Pakistan must guard internal harmony, settle disputes through law and dialogue, and remember the Quaid’s advice to work “in co-operation, forgetting the past, burying the hatchet”.
questions.explanation: Model answer with outline, two developed body paragraphs and a conclusion that quotes the reading text. The examples chosen may vary; other answers are acceptable.

questions.question: Work individually and prepare a presentation on the topics given below. Use above table to introduce yourself and the topic of presentation. 1. Gender Equality
questions.answer:
Good morning and a warm welcome to you all. My name is Ayesha Khan and I belong to Grade XI. It is my privilege to make a presentation on gender equality.

Gender equality means that women and men enjoy the same rights, opportunities and dignity. It does not mean that men and women are identical; it means that a person’s sex should never decide their education, employment or worth.

My first point is education. In many families a daughter is withdrawn from school earlier than a son. If we keep half the population out of classrooms, we lose half the talent of the nation. My second point is economic participation. Women work in fields, factories and homes, yet often without pay, property or a bank account in their own name. Equal pay and safe workplaces would add greatly to national income. My third point is decision-making. Women should be present in village councils, boards and legislatures, because decisions made without them are decisions made for only half the society. Finally, the Quaid-e-Azam reminded the first Constituent Assembly that all citizens are equal, “no matter to what community, colour, caste or creed” they belong; gender is part of that same principle of equal citizenship.

To conclude, gender equality is not a favour to women but a condition of national progress. Thank you for your patient hearing. I shall be happy to answer your questions.
questions.explanation: The script follows the book’s three-part frame: greeting (“Good morning and a warm welcome to you all”), self-introduction (“My name is … and I belong to Grade XI”), and topic introduction (“It is my privilege to make a presentation on …”), followed by body points and a closing with thanks and an invitation for questions. Students should substitute their own names and details.

questions.question: Work individually and prepare a presentation on the topics given below. Use above table to introduce yourself and the topic of presentation. 2. Proper Use of Time
questions.answer:
Good morning and a warm welcome to you all. I am Bilal Ahmed from grade XI, and today my topic is the proper use of time.

Time is the only resource that cannot be stored, borrowed or bought. Once a minute has passed, it is gone forever; this is why the proverb says that time and tide wait for no man.

My first point is planning. A student who writes down his tasks for the day, and marks the most important ones, finishes more in two hours than a careless student finishes in five. My second point is punctuality. Arriving on time for class, for prayers and for appointments shows respect for others and saves the whole group from delay. My third point is avoiding distractions. The mobile phone is the greatest thief of time in our age; a short video becomes an hour, and the homework is still undone. Fixed study hours with the phone switched off can recover that lost time. My fourth point is balance. Time spent on rest, exercise, family and worship is not wasted; a tired mind learns nothing. The Quaid-e-Azam advised us to think a hundred times before a decision, but once it is taken, to stand by it — and that includes deciding firmly how we will use our hours.

To conclude, proper use of time is the secret of achievement. If we plan, keep our word, resist distraction and keep our lives balanced, we can achieve far more than we imagine. Thank you for listening; I welcome your questions.
questions.explanation: Model presentation using the printed opening phrases (greeting, “I am … from grade XI”, “today my topic is …”), four body points and a closing. Other content and personal details are acceptable.

questions.question: Work individually and prepare a presentation on the topics given below. Use above table to introduce yourself and the topic of presentation. 3. Healthy Life Style
questions.answer:
Good afternoon and a warm welcome to you all. My name is Hina Raza and I belong to Grade XI. The subject of my presentation is a healthy life style.

A healthy life style is a set of daily habits that keep body and mind fit. It is built not in a hospital but at home, in the kitchen, the playground and the bedroom.

My first point is food. A balanced diet contains fruit, vegetables, pulses, milk and whole grains, and limits oil, sugar and junk food. Skipping breakfast or drinking soft drinks instead of water slowly damages health. My second point is exercise. Thirty minutes of walking, cycling or games every day strengthens the heart, controls weight and improves mood. My third point is sleep. Seven to eight hours of undisturbed sleep is as important as food; late-night scrolling leaves a student tired and unable to concentrate. My fourth point is cleanliness and avoidance of harmful substances. Washing hands, keeping food covered and refusing cigarettes, paan and drugs protect us from disease. My fifth point is mental health. Talking to parents or a teacher when we feel low, and taking time to relax, is part of being healthy.

To conclude, a healthy life style is not a difficult prescription; it is a series of small, repeated choices. If we eat well, move daily, sleep on time and stay clean, we can enjoy a long and productive life. Thank you for your attention. I shall be glad to answer your questions.
questions.explanation: The script uses greeting, self-introduction and topic-introduction phrases from the book’s table, gives five body points and closes with thanks and an invitation to questions. Individual details and examples may vary.

questions.question: There is only one reason for this problem he never learned to drive properly.
questions.answer: There is only one reason for this problem: he never learned to drive properly.
questions.explanation: The colon is placed after “problem” because it introduces the explanation of what the one reason is. A colon draws attention to the specific information that follows.

questions.question: My morning routine looks like this wake up, brush my teeth, and run to school.
questions.answer: My morning routine looks like this: wake up, brush my teeth, and run to school.
questions.explanation: The colon follows “looks like this” to introduce a list of items — the three actions that make up the morning routine.

questions.question: We have set a house rule do your homework before watching television.
questions.answer: We have set a house rule: do your homework before watching television.
questions.explanation: The colon after “rule” introduces the content of the rule — an explanation of what the rule says.

questions.question: My final answer still stands “No!”
questions.answer: My final answer still stands: “No!”
questions.explanation: The colon comes after “stands” to introduce a quotation, which is one of the standard uses of the colon listed in the book.

questions.question: I enjoy reading novels by Jane Austen they are among my favourites.
questions.answer: I enjoy reading novels by Jane Austen: they are among my favourites.
questions.explanation: The colon after “Austen” introduces an explanation of why the speaker enjoys those novels. It separates two independent clauses, which a colon is able to do when the second explains the first.

questions.question: I gave you the spray bottles for one reason to clean the windows.
questions.answer: I gave you the spray bottles for one reason: to clean the windows.
questions.explanation: The colon after “reason” introduces the explanation of that reason — the purpose for which the spray bottles were given.

questions.question: You will need the following ingredients milk, sugar, flour, and eggs.
questions.answer: You will need the following ingredients: milk, sugar, flour, and eggs.
questions.explanation: The words “the following ingredients” signal a list, so the colon is placed immediately before the list begins — after “ingredients”.

questions.question: Sara found the purse.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Found” takes the direct object “the purse”: Sara found what? — the purse.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “found”. It transfers the action to an object (“the purse”), so it is transitive.

questions.question: I lived in Islamabad for a very brief period.
questions.answer: Intransitive. “Lived” has no object; “in Islamabad” and “for a very brief period” are adverbial phrases.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “lived”. Nothing receives the action of living — “in Islamabad” tells where, not what — so the verb is intransitive.

questions.question: I make an excellent chicken curry.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Make” takes the direct object “an excellent chicken curry”: I make what? — an excellent chicken curry.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “make”. It transfers the action to the thing produced, so it is transitive.

questions.question: Nabeel heard a lovely song in the morning.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Heard” takes the direct object “a lovely song”: Nabeel heard what? — a lovely song.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “heard”. “A lovely song” receives the action of hearing; “in the morning” is only an adverbial of time.

questions.question: The prosecution proved the defendant’s guilt.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Proved” takes the direct object “the defendant’s guilt”: the prosecution proved what? — the defendant’s guilt.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “proved”. It transfers the action to “the defendant’s guilt”, which is the object.

questions.question: He delivered presentation. [sic]
questions.answer: Transitive. “Delivered” takes the direct object “presentation”: he delivered what? — a presentation.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “delivered”. The printed sentence omits the article (“delivered presentation”); the natural form is “delivered a presentation”. The verb is transitive regardless, because “presentation” is its object.

questions.question: I worked for ten hours yesterday.
questions.answer: Intransitive. “Worked” has no object; “for ten hours” and “yesterday” are adverbials of duration and time.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “worked”. No noun phrase receives the action — “for ten hours” is a prepositional phrase, not an object — so the verb is intransitive.

questions.question: She advised me to consult a doctor.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Advised” takes the direct object “me”; the infinitive phrase “to consult a doctor” completes the meaning as an object complement.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “advised”. “Me” is the object of advising, so the verb is transitive; the infinitive clause tells what she advised me to do.

questions.question: Let us invite your cousins as well.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Invite” takes the direct object “your cousins”: invite whom? — your cousins.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “invite”. It transfers the action to the people invited, so it is transitive.

questions.question: I waited for an hour.
questions.answer: Intransitive. “Waited” has no object; “for an hour” is an adverbial phrase of time.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “waited”. “Wait” is an intransitive verb; it cannot take a direct object, and “for an hour” merely tells how long.

questions.question: I received your letter in the morning.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Received” takes the direct object “your letter”: I received what? — your letter.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “received”. “Your letter” receives the action; “in the morning” is only an adverbial of time.

questions.question: I am going to send her some flowers.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Send” takes two objects: “her” (indirect object) and “some flowers” (direct object).
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “send”. This is a double-object verb: the direct object “some flowers” is what is sent, and the indirect object “her” is the receiver.

questions.question: He has changed a lot since he got married.
questions.answer: Intransitive. “Changed” has no object; “a lot” is an adverbial of degree and “since he got married” is an adverbial clause of time.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “changed” in the sense of becoming different. Nothing receives the action of changing, so it is intransitive here. (In “He changed his shirt” the same verb would be transitive.)

questions.question: Suddenly the child woke up.
questions.answer: Intransitive. The phrasal verb “woke up” has no object; the child woke by himself.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “woke up”. “Wake up” used without an object is intransitive. (Compare “The noise woke me up”, where it is transitive.)

questions.question: The loud noise awoke me.
questions.answer: Transitive. “Awoke” takes the direct object “me”: the noise awoke whom? — me.
questions.explanation: The italicised verb is “awoke”. Here it is causative and transfers its action to “me”, so it is transitive.

questions.question: Verb “Start”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively, following the example of “Move”.
questions.answer:
Transitive: The driver started the engine with a jerk.
Intransitive: The film starts at seven o’clock.
questions.explanation: In the first sentence “the engine” is the direct object receiving the action of starting, so “started” is transitive. In the second there is no object — the film simply begins — so “started” is intransitive.

questions.question: Verb “Change”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: She changed her dress before dinner.
Intransitive: The weather changed suddenly in the afternoon.
questions.explanation: “Her dress” is the direct object of “changed” in the first sentence. In the second, “changed” means “became different” and has no object.

questions.question: Verb “Close”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: Please close the door when you leave.
Intransitive: The shop closes at nine every night.
questions.explanation: “The door” is the direct object in the first sentence; in the second “closes” describes the shop’s own action and takes no object.

questions.question: Verb “Open”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: He opened the window to let in fresh air.
Intransitive: The exhibition opens tomorrow morning.
questions.explanation: “The window” is the direct object of “opened”; in the second sentence “opens” has no object and simply reports when the exhibition begins.

questions.question: Verb “Stop”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: The guard stopped the car at the barrier.
Intransitive: The bus stopped at the corner.
questions.explanation: “The car” receives the action of stopping in the first sentence; in the second the bus stops of its own accord and there is no object.

questions.question: Verb “Walk”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: She walks her dog every morning.
Intransitive: I walk to school every day.
questions.explanation: “Her dog” is the direct object of “walks” (she walks the dog); in the second sentence “walk” describes the subject’s own movement and takes no object.

questions.question: Verb “Run”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: He runs a small bookshop in the market.
Intransitive: The children run in the park after school.
questions.explanation: In the first sentence “a small bookshop” is the direct object (he manages it). In the second “run” means move quickly and has no object.

questions.question: Verb “Live”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: She lived a simple and honest life.
Intransitive: They live in a small village near Thatta.
questions.explanation: “A simple and honest life” is the direct object of “lived” (to live a life). In the second sentence “live” is intransitive and “in a small village” is an adverbial of place.

questions.question: Verb “Wash”: make one sentence using it transitively and one using it intransitively.
questions.answer:
Transitive: Please wash the dishes before you go out.
Intransitive: This woollen shirt washes easily.
questions.explanation: “The dishes” is the direct object in the first sentence. In the second, “washes” describes how the shirt behaves when washed and has no object.

questions.question: Work individually. Brainstorm and make a list of the verbs in middle used in both transitive and intransitive in a Venn diagram other than list of verbs given in exercise 3 & 5. [sic]
questions.answer:
TRANSITIVE ONLY: make, build, carry, discuss, invite, receive, admire, destroy, create, examine.

BOTH TRANSITIVE AND INTRANSITIVE: break, burn, grow, fly, ring, hang, increase, improve, melt, turn, begin, finish, hurt, smell, taste.

INTRANSITIVE ONLY: arrive, die, sleep, sneeze, cough, come, go, laugh, happen, occur, rise, sit.

Verbs for the middle (overlapping) part of the Venn diagram, with proof: break — “She broke the glass” (transitive) / “The glass broke” (intransitive); grow — “Farmers grow wheat” / “Children grow quickly”; fly — “The pilot flies the plane” / “Birds fly south”; ring — “Ring the bell” / “The telephone rang”; turn — “She turned the key” / “The leaves turn yellow”; begin — “He began the meeting” / “The meeting began”. The lists avoid the ten verbs of Exercise 3 (move, start, change, close, open, stop, walk, run, live, wash) and the word bank of Exercise 5.
questions.explanation: A verb is transitive when it takes an object and intransitive when it does not; many English verbs can be used both ways. The exact contents of the diagram will vary from student to student. The printed instruction says “verbs in middle used in both transitive and intransitive” — i.e. the middle, overlapping part of the diagram; marked [sic].

questions.question: In pairs, make sentences of any ten verbs given below with direct and indirect objects. After completing, share your work with your partner. An example has been done for you. Word bank: award, offer, send, feed, promise, grant, mail, present, lend, post, bake, pour, book, prepare, build, knit, reserve, sing, order, provide.
questions.answer:
1. award — The principal awarded Sana the first prize. (indirect object: Sana; direct object: the first prize)
2. offer — The company offered him a job in its Karachi office. (indirect object: him; direct object: a job)
3. send — I sent my brother a birthday card. (indirect object: my brother; direct object: a birthday card)
4. feed — The farmer fed the cattle fresh grass. (indirect object: the cattle; direct object: fresh grass)
5. grant — The university granted her a scholarship for two years. (indirect object: her; direct object: a scholarship)
6. mail — Please mail me the signed contract today. (indirect object: me; direct object: the signed contract)
7. present — The students presented the chief guest a bouquet of flowers. (indirect object: the chief guest; direct object: a bouquet)
8. lend — Could you lend me your umbrella for an hour? (indirect object: me; direct object: your umbrella)
9. bake — My aunt baked us a chocolate cake on Sunday. (indirect object: us; direct object: a chocolate cake)
10. order — I ordered my sister a cup of tea. (indirect object: my sister; direct object: a cup of tea)

Alternative pattern (direct object first, indirect object in a prepositional phrase): The principal awarded the first prize to Sana. / The company offered a job to him. / I sent a birthday card to my brother. / Please mail the signed contract to me. / My aunt baked a chocolate cake for us.
questions.explanation: A transitive verb may take two objects: the direct object (the thing given, sent, made, etc.) and the indirect object (the person who receives it). The usual pattern is verb + indirect object + direct object, or verb + direct object + to/for + indirect object. Note: the book’s example is printed as “My mother bought me a new dress. (direct object)” and “My mother bought a new dress for me. (indirect object)”; the labels are reversed [sic] — in the first sentence “me” is the indirect object and “a new dress” the direct object.

questions.question: Look at the pictures and compare and contrast them.
questions.answer:
The left-hand picture shows a mountain lake that is still unspoiled: clear turquoise water, a pine forest along the shore, snow-capped peaks reflected in the lake, and no people or litter in sight. The right-hand picture shows a city waterway that has been badly polluted: grey, muddy water, heaps of plastic bags and rubbish on the bank and in the water, a concrete bridge and high-rise buildings behind, and people picking through the waste.

Similarities: both are inland water bodies with banks and shallow edges; both are fed by rain and streams and would normally support fish, birds and plants; both are part of a landscape that people use for travel, work or leisure.

Differences: the lake is clear and silent, the waterway is grey and noisy; the lake is framed by trees and mountains, the waterway by concrete and traffic; the lake is clean, the waterway is choked with plastic; the lake suggests solitude, the waterway suggests overcrowding. In short, the first picture shows nature preserved and the second shows nature degraded by human waste.
questions.explanation: Open-ended pre-reading task: any two valid similarities and two differences are acceptable. The aim is to activate the language of comparison and contrast (both, whereas, unlike, in contrast) and to predict the unit theme. Encourage students to notice colour, clarity, setting and human presence.

questions.question: Guess the theme of the text you are going to study.
questions.answer: The theme is the preservation of nature, seen through a personal return to a childhood lake. The pair of pictures sets an unspoiled lake against a polluted city waterway, the unit is titled 'Preservation of Nature', and the text is called 'Once More to the Lake'. The title suggests a nostalgic journey back to a natural place that may have been changed by modern life. The extract confirms this: the writer revisits a lake in Maine after many years, wonders how time and the new tarred road have 'marred' it, and is disturbed by outboard motors and crowds. So the text is about memory, the passing of time, and the need to protect natural places.
questions.explanation: Open-ended prediction. A good answer names the theme (preservation of nature / nostalgia for an unspoiled place) and supports it with the unit title, the text title and the picture contrast.

questions.question: Work in pairs and deduce the meaning of words given in column A and write their contextual meaning in column B.
questions.answer:
No. | Column A | Column B (contextual meaning)
1 | marred | spoilt, damaged or disfigured in appearance - the writer fears time has spoilt 'this unique, this beautiful spot'
2 | tarred | covered with tar, a black sticky substance used to make a hard road surface - 'the tarred road' that now reaches the lake
3 | grooves | narrow tracks or ruts; here, the familiar channels or paths of memory that the mind follows - 'return into the grooves which lead back'
4 | sneak | move quietly and secretly so as not to be noticed - he would 'sneak out into the sweet outdoors' before the others woke
5 | illusion | a false impression or belief; something that seems real but is not - 'the illusion that he was I'
6 | creepy | causing an uneasy, frightened, 'goose-flesh' feeling - 'It gave me a creepy sensation'
7 | moss | a small, soft green plant that grows in damp places - 'the same damp moss covering the worms'
8 | jollity | cheerful, merry, lively happiness - 'There had been peace and goodness and jollity'
9 | sedative | calming, soothing, making a person sleepy - the inboard motors' noise was 'a sedative, an ingredient of summer sleep'
10 | petulant | irritable, bad-tempered, peevish - the outboard motors made 'a petulant, irritable sound'
questions.explanation: Meanings are deduced from context, not copied from a dictionary: each word is defined by the phrase in which it appears. Accept close synonyms (marred = spoiled; grooves = familiar tracks/patterns; jollity = cheerfulness; sedative = soothing; petulant = cranky).

questions.question: The writer in the essay 'Once More to the Lake' is accompanied by his ______.
questions.answer: (b) son
questions.explanation: Text: 'I took along my son, who had never had any fresh water up his nose and who had seen lily pads only from train windows.' The boy is with him throughout the return visit, so (b) is correct; no brother, wife or pet is mentioned as making the trip.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) brother   (b) son   (c) wife   (d) pet

questions.question: In the beginning of 'Once More to the Lake', the writer characterizes himself as ______.
questions.answer: (c) salt-water man
questions.explanation: In the essay White says he has 'since become a salt-water man' - as an adult he lives by the sea - though in summer he longs for the placidity of a lake in the woods. The abridged textbook extract omits that sentence, but the question tests it, so the intended answer is (c). He is not a pond-water man, and 'ordinary man' ignores the specific phrase.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) lake-water man   (b) pond-water man   (c) salt-water man   (d) ordinary man

questions.question: The writer has referred the word "placidly" in the context of ______.
questions.answer: (b) calmness
questions.explanation: 'Placid' means calm, still and undisturbed. The extract describes the lake as 'cool and motionless', as water that 'had not stirred', 'this constant and trustworthy body of water'. 'Calmness' is therefore the closest meaning; 'peacefulness' is related but refers more to mood than to the water's stillness, while loneliness and idleness are unrelated.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) peacefulness   (b) calmness   (c) loneliness   (d) idleness

questions.question: The ______ were/was tapping on the roof of the camp of writer.
questions.answer: (c) squirrel
questions.explanation: Text: 'in the morning, the red squirrel would be on the roof, tapping out his happy routine.' Mosquitoes appear only in a simile for the whine of outboard motors at night, and no swarm or mouse is mentioned.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) mosquitoes   (b) swarm   (c) squirrel   (d) mouse

questions.question: The writer felt in the end of the essay ______.
questions.answer: (c) happy
questions.explanation: The extract closes with 'We had a good week at the camp', sunshine 'day after day', sleep that 'would come easily' and the squirrel's 'happy routine', while the writer lies in bed 'remembering everything' - a mood of contentment. (The unabridged essay ends more darkly with a thunderstorm, but that passage is not in the printed text.)
questions.optionsRaw: (a) the fear of storm   (b) the danger of life   (c) happy   (d) the loneliness

questions.question: ______ caught two fish before lunch.
questions.answer: (c) both son & father
questions.explanation: Text: 'We caught two fish. When we got back for a swim before lunch...' The pronoun 'we' refers to the writer and his son fishing together, so both caught the fish. A spinner is only the lure the writer bought; it cannot catch fish by itself.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) son   (b) father   (c) both son & father   (d) spinner

questions.question: The writer revisited the lake with his son in ______ season.
questions.answer: (a) summer
questions.explanation: The family went 'for the month of August' and 'returned summer after summer--always on August 1st'; the writer's own return with his son is also a summer visit.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) summer   (b) winter   (c) autumn   (d) spring

questions.question: The writer's son has seen ______ while travelling by train.
questions.answer: (b) lily pads
questions.explanation: Text: 'who had seen lily pads only from train windows' - the boy knew lily pads only as a glimpse from a train, never up close.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) weeds   (b) lily pads   (c) sheltered bay   (d) wet woods

questions.question: The writer used to visit lake ______.
questions.answer: (b) in Maine
questions.explanation: Text: 'my father rented a camp on a lake in Maine'; the title and the whole return journey point to that lake in Maine. New York, his former house and his school are not named as the lake's location.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) in New York   (b) in Maine   (c) near his form house   (d) in his school

questions.question: For ______, the writer used to go to the lake.
questions.answer: (a) fishing
questions.explanation: Text: 'returned to the lake where we used to go, for a week's fishing and to revisit old place.' Fishing is the stated purpose; waves, cool water and swimming are incidental pleasures, not the reason given.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) fishing   (b) seeing waves   (c) enjoying cool water   (d) enjoying swimming

questions.question: Read the text individually. First, write the five things that writer observed and loved in the past. Then, write five changes that took place later on.
questions.answer:
Past scene of lake | Later scene
1. Cool, motionless early mornings, with the bedroom smelling of lumber and wet woods and the lake misty and still. | 1. The mornings are still calm, but the silence is broken by 'an unfamiliar nervous sound of the outboard motors'.
2. Canoeing alone close to the shore 'in the long shadows of the pines' before the others woke. | 2. The writer now comes as a father with his son, and feels that he is his own father - 'I seemed to be living a dual existence'.
3. Inboard one- and two-cylinder motors: 'The one-lungers throbbed and fluttered, and the twin-cylinder ones purred and purred' - a sleepy, sedative sound. | 3. 'But now the campers all had outboards', which make 'a petulant, irritable sound' by day and 'whined about one's ears like mosquitoes' at night.
4. A quiet, half-wild lake with cottages 'sprinkled around the shores', where the family lived at the shore and ate meals at the farmhouse. | 4. The tarred road now 'led to within half a mile of the shore', and other campers crowd the shore and the water - the place is easy to reach and no longer remote.
