questions.explanation: This page prints the sample without an exercise number (the next exercise is numbered 2); the task is to identify how the narrative elements are illustrated, which is answered element by element with quotations from the sample.

questions.question: Work individually and narrate a happy/ sad or surprising incident of your life in the light of elements given in the sample. After you have written, share your work with your class fellows.
questions.answer:
The Night the Lights Went Out

I have never been so grateful for a power cut.

It was a hot evening in June, three weeks before my scholarship test. The test was online, and our area had already lost electricity twice that day. At six o'clock I sat at the dining table with my laptop at ninety per cent, my notes spread around me like a fan, and my mother frying pakoras in the kitchen because, she said, 'A hungry boy cannot think.' My father had gone to the market to buy candles. My younger brother, Bilal, was drawing racing cars on the back of my revision sheet.

At ten minutes to seven the ceiling fan slowed, clicked, and stopped. The tube-light died with a small tick. For a second nobody spoke. Then Bilal said, 'Load-shedding,' in the calm voice of a child who has grown up with it, and I felt my throat close. Of all the evenings, I thought. Of all the evenings.

I ran to the window. The whole lane was dark. My laptop showed sixty per cent and the clock showed 6:52. I could hear my mother's slippers hurry behind me and my own heart in my ears.

Then a voice came from the gate. 'Areeba! Beta!' It was Uncle Rashid from the house opposite, standing in his doorway with a torch. 'Bring your laptop here. My UPS is charged.' I did not even put on my shoes. I crossed the lane holding the laptop against my chest like a baby, and my mother followed with my rough notebook and a stool.

For the next hour and a half I wrote my test on Uncle Rashid's dining table while his generator hummed in the courtyard. My mother held a torch over my shoulder until her arm ached and then Uncle Rashid's daughter held it. At 8:32 I pressed submit and sat back, and only then did I notice that the whole family had been sitting silently around me, afraid to make a sound. My mother's eyes were wet.

I passed that test. But what I remember is not the result; it is a lane full of dark houses and one lit doorway. I had always believed that success was something a person achieves alone, with hard work and discipline. That evening taught me otherwise. A power cut that I had cursed all my life turned out to be the kindest thing that happened to me that year, because it showed me how many people were quietly holding a torch for me.
questions.explanation: Model narrative of a surprising/happy incident, written to the sample's structure: hook, scene, thesis, show-don't-tell detail, chronological transitions, dialogue, climax and a reflective conclusion.

questions.question: You have already read the story diagram in post-reading of the Unit 3.1. Now, work in pairs and analyse the sample story according to that diagram and write down its elements. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
Exposition: Morning at Hina's home. Mom wakes Hina and Sara, tells Hina to walk Sara to school on her first day of Kindergarten and to 'make sure she gets there O.K.' Hina feels her mother is treating her 'like such a baby' and wants to prove she can be responsible.

Rising Action: Hina takes Sara's hand, asks if she is excited, and feels 'proud to be the older sister' as they pass gardens and leafy trees. Then she hears a growl: a big, fierce-looking dog with long sharp teeth is walking towards them, and no owner is in sight. Hina's hand becomes sweaty and Sara stops, saying, 'I'm scared, Hina.' The dog steps closer, 'the size of small horse-with red eyes and sharp teeth', and Hina tells herself, 'Be brave, be brave.'

Climax: Hina grabs Sara's hand and shouts 'RUN!' - the moment of decision when the outcome is decided.

Falling Action: They sprint down the sidewalk, Sara breathing hard, the dog coming behind them. Hina glances back, urges 'Come on', and silently prays 'Please let us make it.' Then they see the bright red door of the school.

Resolution: 'We made it!' Hina gives Sara a high-five and says, 'Let's not tell mom about this, okay? I think we'll go to school a different way tomorrow.' The narrator has proved she is grown-up by protecting her sister, and the joke about the different route closes the story on a warm, relieved note.
questions.explanation: The sample on page 45 is mapped onto the five-part story diagram from page 43, with quotations for each stage.

questions.question: Work individually and use pre-writing strategies to write an incident that changed you in a significant way. List the incidents and indicate how each changed you. After writing it, exchange it with your partner.
questions.answer:
Step 1 - List of incidents and how each changed me:
No. | Incident | How it changed me
1 | Failed the class VII scholarship test by two marks | Stopped believing that talent alone is enough; began making a weekly study timetable that I still follow.
2 | My grandmother's illness and her three months in hospital | Decided to become a doctor; learnt to stay calm in a crisis and to help with practical things (forms, medicines, shifting beds) instead of only feeling sorry.
3 | Losing my father's camera on a school trip | Learnt to confess immediately; became careful with borrowed things and honest even when honesty is expensive.
4 | Being made captain of the school cricket team in class IX | Learnt that leadership is mostly listening and giving others credit; my temper improved.
5 | The flood of 2022, when our street was under water for four days | Understood how quickly comfort can disappear; began volunteering with a relief group every winter.

Step 2 - Choosing and narrowing: I chose incident 3 because it has a clear single scene, a strong conflict (truth versus hiding), and a visible change in me.

Step 3 - Outline (beginning, middle, end): borrowing the camera; the trip and the fall at the stupa; the silent bus journey home; confessing at the gate; paying for the repair from my savings and working at my cousin's shop.

Step 4 - Draft (short version): 'The Lens' - I borrowed my uncle's camera for the Mohenjo-daro trip and smashed its lens climbing down from the stupa. I hid it in my bag all the way home and rehearsed a lie about a thief. At our gate my uncle was waiting with tea, and the lie died in my mouth. I told him everything. He was silent for a long minute, then said, 'The camera can be repaired. You, I was worried about.' I paid for the repair over two months. I have never since been able to enjoy anything I obtained by hiding the truth.
questions.explanation: Open-ended task: the pre-writing list, the choice of one incident, the outline and a short draft are all shown, as the exercise demands.

questions.question: Now, work in pairs and check the story of your partner written while doing Exercise 4. Make sure the story has all the elements and has followed the sample given on previous page.
questions.answer:
Peer-check checklist (to be applied to the partner's story, with the result of each check):

No. | Element to check | What to look for | Comment on the draft
1 | Hook | Does the first sentence catch attention (a line of dialogue, a sound, a surprising statement)? | Yes - 'The camera can be repaired' idea works, but the opening should be sharper; suggest beginning with the sound of the lens cracking.
2 | Scene | Are the characters, place, time and situation clear in the first paragraph? | Yes - Mohenjo-daro, the school trip, the uncle, the narrator.
3 | Thesis / purpose | Is it clear what the incident meant to the writer? | Yes - honesty is cheaper than a lie; state it more directly near the start.
4 | Show, don't tell | Are there concrete details (sounds, objects, physical reactions) instead of labels like 'I was scared'? | Mostly - add one detail of the bus ride home (the bag on the knees, the noise) to build tension.
5 | Supporting evidence | Do the events actually prove the lesson learnt? | Yes - the confession, the uncle's reply, the two months of work.
6 | Passage of time and transitions | Are 'at first', 'then', 'by the time', 'after that' used to guide the reader? | Needs work - the middle jumps from the stupa to the gate; add a transition sentence.
7 | Dialogue | Is there some direct speech that reveals character? | Yes - the uncle's line is the best sentence in the piece; add one line of the narrator's own words at the confession.
8 | Paragraphing | Does each new paragraph mark a change of action or of reflection? | Yes, but paragraph 2 is too long; split it at the fall.
9 | Conclusion / moral | Does the ending reflect on the significance of the event, not just report it? | Yes - the last sentence does this well.
10 | Language and mechanics | Spelling, tense consistency, punctuation, commas around non-restrictive clauses? | A few past-tense slips ('I hide' for 'I hid') and one missing comma before 'which'; correct them before the final copy.
questions.explanation: Pair-work evaluation task; the answer is a completed checklist that shows what to look for and gives sample comments on a partner's draft.

questions.question: Work in group of three. Take turns and acknowledge orally the contribution of the following people for the community. Remember to use the phrases given in the table above. Scenario 1: The forest officer of the area visits your college for further plantation drive.
questions.answer:
Student A (host): Assalam-o-Alaikum, sir. Thank you for sparing time from your busy schedule to visit our college today.

Student B: Sir, our college has planted two hundred saplings this year, and the whole drive began because of the guidance your office gave us last spring. On behalf of the students, I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you for the saplings, the fencing wire and, above all, the training your staff gave our volunteers.

Student C: I agree with my friend. This would not have been possible without your support and nurturing, so I would like to extend my deepest appreciation and thanks to you and your team. I am also thankful to you for visiting us personally today, when a single phone call would have been enough. Your presence here tells every student that the work we are doing matters.

Student B: Sir, your department's contribution has been instrumental in making our college one of the greenest campuses in the district. Special thanks to you for arranging the drip irrigation that kept the plants alive through the summer.

Forest Officer: Thank you, students. A forest officer plants trees; you keep them alive. That is the harder work.

Student A: Sir, we are deeply indebted to you for that encouragement. We look forward to working with your office in the next drive as well.
questions.explanation: Role-play task; the dialogue uses the strong ('I would like to express my deepest appreciation', 'This would not have been possible without', 'deeply indebted', 'instrumental in'), the milder ('I am also thankful', 'Special thanks') and the reason-giving phrases from the table on page 47.

questions.question: Work in group of three. Take turns and acknowledge orally the contribution of the following people for the community. Remember to use the phrases given in the table above. Scenario 2: An event organized and managed by your college principal to develop awareness about the environmental cleanliness.
questions.answer:
Student A: Respected Principal, teachers and friends, before we begin today's programme I would like to say a few words about the person because of whom this event is possible.

Student B: Ma'am, when the idea of a cleanliness awareness week was first discussed, many of us thought it was too ambitious for a college with no extra funds. You arranged the whole event yourself - the guest speakers, the banners, the street-cleaning teams and even the gloves and bags. On behalf of the students' council, I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you.

Student C: I also wish to thank you, ma'am, for trusting us with real responsibility instead of simply lecturing us about cleanliness. Your encouragement and patience throughout the planning of this event taught us more than any speech could. You were instrumental in turning an idea into a campaign that has reached four neighbouring streets.

Student B: Special thanks are also due to you for persuading the shopkeepers' association to join us; without their support the campaign would have remained inside our college gate.

Principal: Thank you. But the credit belongs to you - I only signed the letters. What you have done this week has made our neighbourhood cleaner and, I hope, our habits better.

Student A: Ma'am, we are deeply indebted to you for your leadership, and we promise that this will not be a one-week event.
questions.explanation: Second role-play scenario; the acknowledgement follows the three-level pattern of the table (very strong appreciation, less strong but appreciative, reason for the acknowledgement) and is specific to the event described.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Acknowledge and appreciate the contribution of any one of the following philanthropists: (a) Dr. Adeeb Rizvi
questions.answer:
Dr. Adeeb Rizvi is a kidney and transplant surgeon who, with his team at the Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation (SIUT) in Karachi, has built one of the largest free kidney-care centres in the world. Patients who cannot pay are treated free of charge - dialysis, surgery, medicines and follow-up - and no one is turned away for lack of money. He has also trained hundreds of doctors and nurses and has spoken out for the dignity of the poor patient, insisting that treatment should be a right and not a charity.

A spoken acknowledgement: 'Sir, I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you and your team. In a country where illness so often means debt, you have shown that a hospital can run on trust rather than on bills. I am deeply indebted to you for the example you have set for my generation: that a professional can use his skill not to become rich but to make the poor feel human. This would not have been possible without your patience and your refusal to give up, and your work has been instrumental in saving thousands of lives. Special thanks to you for proving that service is the highest form of success.'
questions.explanation: Open-ended oral task on a named philanthropist; the answer gives accurate background plus a model appreciation using the table's phrases.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Acknowledge and appreciate the contribution of any one of the following philanthropists: (b) Abdul Sattar Edhi
questions.answer:
Abdul Sattar Edhi began with a single hand-cart in Karachi and built the Edhi Foundation, which now runs the country's largest ambulance network, along with orphanages, shelters for the destitute, homes for the mentally ill, blood banks and free clinics. He lived in two small rooms beside his office, owned almost nothing, and refused government money so that the service would remain free and independent. He himself picked up abandoned babies and washed the dead, insisting that 'no religion is higher than humanity'.

A spoken acknowledgement: 'I would like to express my deepest appreciation to the family and workers of the Edhi Foundation for the service they have given this nation for more than sixty years. Abdul Sattar Edhi taught us that greatness is not in wealth but in what you give away. This would not have been possible without the thousands of unnamed volunteers who drive ambulances at midnight and hold the hands of strangers. I am also grateful to the foundation for the shelter it gives to children nobody else wanted. Your work has been instrumental in keeping alive our belief in human kindness, and special thanks are due to you for asking for nothing in return.'
questions.explanation: Open-ended oral task; factual background on Edhi plus a model spoken appreciation that follows the phrase patterns in the table.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Acknowledge and appreciate the contribution of any one of the following philanthropists: (c) Any philanthropist of your community
questions.answer:
Model: Mr. Ahmed Ali, a hardware merchant in our neighbourhood, pays the school fees of eleven children - none of them his relatives - and last year he donated the science equipment for our school laboratory. He never allows his name to be written on the equipment and asks the head teacher not to mention him at functions.

A spoken acknowledgement (for example, at a school assembly): 'Respected sir, I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you on behalf of the students of this school. Many of us would not be sitting in this hall today if you had not quietly paid our fees, term after term, without ever asking for anything in return. This would not have been possible without your support and generosity, and I would like to extend my deepest appreciation and thanks to you. I am also thankful to you for the laboratory equipment, which has made our practical classes real instead of imaginary. Sir, your contribution has been instrumental in keeping eleven children in school, and your example has taught us that charity does not need a stage. Special thanks to you for showing us what a neighbour should be.'
questions.explanation: Open-ended task about a local philanthropist; a concrete model person and a full spoken appreciation are provided so the pattern can be adapted to any real person in the student's community.

questions.question: Work in pairs and read the following paragraph. Look especially for errors in agreement between pronouns and their antecedents. When you find a pronoun error, cross out the incorrect pronoun and write the correct one above it. There will not be a mistake in every sentence. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
1. Kathy has always liked dollhouses, and she got an idea for a business from their hobby. WRONG: their -> her (antecedent: Kathy, singular feminine). Corrected: ...from her hobby.
2. Now, she and her brothers make dollhouses for sale. CORRECT - no pronoun error.
3. Neither she nor her brothers give all of her time to the business. WRONG: her -> their (with neither...nor the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, 'her brothers', plural). Corrected: ...all of their time...
4. Still, the team makes all its spending money from their sales. WRONG: their -> its (the team is acting as a single unit, so the singular 'its' must be used consistently). Corrected: ...from its sales.
5. Kathy's elder brother assembles the pieces. CORRECT - no pronoun error.
6. He chooses the plywood, cuts it to scale, and assembles the pieces. CORRECT - 'He' agrees with 'Kathy's elder brother'; 'it' refers to the plywood.
7. Her younger brother, Max, paints the houses inside and out, giving it details like doors, windows, and shutters. WRONG: it -> them (antecedent: houses, plural). Corrected: ...giving them details...
8. While Murray and Max do his jobs, Kathy buys miniature furniture. WRONG: his -> their (compound subject, plural). Corrected: ...do their jobs...
9. Then she sews curtains, rugs, tablecloths, and bedspreads to make each house special. CORRECT - no pronoun error.
10. From October until mid-December, the crew takes turns selling its products at craft sales. CORRECT as printed ('the crew' as a unit - its products). If the writer thinks of the members acting individually (they take turns), 'their products' would also be acceptable.

Summary: five sentences contain errors - 1, 3, 4, 7 and 8; sentences 2, 5, 6, 9 and 10 are correct.
questions.explanation: Each pronoun is tested against its antecedent in number, gender and person; collective nouns (team, crew) take a singular pronoun when the group acts as one unit.

questions.question: Each of the boys on the team is wearing (his, their) new uniform. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: his. Antecedent: Each (of the boys) - an indefinite pronoun that is always singular, so the singular masculine pronoun 'his' is used.
questions.explanation: Indefinite pronoun 'each' is always singular.

questions.question: Many have expressed (his or her, their) support for our plan. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: their. Antecedent: Many - 'many' is always plural, so the plural pronoun 'their' is required.
questions.explanation: Indefinite pronoun 'many' is always plural.

questions.question: Neither of the women has told me (her, their) opinion. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: her. Antecedent: Neither (of the women) - 'neither' is singular, and the antecedent is feminine, so 'her' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is always singular; the verb 'has' confirms the singular reading.

questions.question: When the team scored a touchdown, the crowd threw (its, their) hats in the air. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: their. Antecedent: the crowd - here the members of the crowd are acting individually (each person throws his own hat), so the collective noun takes the plural pronoun 'their'.
questions.explanation: A collective noun takes a plural pronoun when the members act individually.

questions.question: Neither Ali nor his sisters have bought a gift for (her, their) brother. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: their. Antecedent: his sisters - with neither...nor the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, which is plural.
questions.explanation: Rule for 'or/nor': the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent.

questions.question: Scuba divers are taught that (you, they) should check (your, their) equipment. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: they ... their. Antecedent: Scuba divers - third person plural, so 'they' and 'their' are needed; 'you' would wrongly shift to the second person.
questions.explanation: The pronoun must agree in person as well as number with its antecedent.

questions.question: Samar and Qavi will present (his, their) routine before the other gymnasts do. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: their. Antecedent: Samar and Qavi - two nouns joined by 'and' form a compound plural subject, so a plural pronoun is used.
questions.explanation: Compound subjects joined by 'and' take a plural pronoun.

questions.question: Not one hiker would set out without (his or her, their) compass. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: his or her. Antecedent: Not one hiker - singular and of unknown gender, so 'his or her' is the correct singular form.
questions.explanation: 'Not one' is singular; 'his or her' is treated as a singular pronoun.

questions.question: Yasmeen and her sisters shop for clothes here because (you, they) can find good bargains. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: they. Antecedent: Yasmeen and her sisters - third person plural; 'you' would shift the person and is incorrect.
questions.explanation: Pronoun and antecedent must agree in person (third person plural here).

questions.question: Anyone who wants a job should bring (his or her, their) application to me. Encircle the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence. Also, underline the antecedent(s) of the pronoun.
questions.answer: his or her. Antecedent: Anyone - an indefinite pronoun that is always singular, so the singular 'his or her' is used. ('their' is common in informal speech, but the textbook rule requires the singular form.)
questions.explanation: 'Anyone' is always singular; 'his or her' is considered a singular pronoun.

questions.question: Work in pairs and read the following text. Spot the errors of Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement. After you have completed, share your work with your partner. (Text: 'One of the most popular sports in Sindh is Malakhiro...')
questions.answer:
Errors of pronoun-antecedent agreement and their corrections:

1. 'The renowned Malakhiro players participate in this traditional event to showcase his strength' - his -> their. 'Players' is plural, so the pronoun must be plural.
2. '...to pull down its opponent players' - its -> their. The antecedent is 'players' (plural), not 'event'.
3. 'Each one then holds onto the opponent's waist cloth and tries to throw them to the ground' - them -> him. 'Each one' is singular, so the object pronoun must be singular.
4. 'Many of the players are professionals who earn its living by participating in this sport' - its -> their. 'Many of the players ... who' is plural.
5. 'Almost everybody in Pakistan has heard of this popular and traditional sports, even if they haven't seen it' - they -> he or she (or 'he or she hasn't seen it'). 'Everybody' is always singular, so the singular pronoun is required; 'their' is accepted only in informal modern usage.

Note on wording (not a pronoun error): 'this popular and traditional sports' should be 'this popular and traditional sport', because 'this' is singular.

Corrected opening for reference: 'The renowned Malakhiro players participate in this traditional event to showcase their strength to pull down their opponent players ... Many of the players are professionals who earn their living by participating in this sport.'
questions.explanation: Each error is decided by the number and person of the antecedent; singular indefinite pronouns (each one, everybody) take singular pronouns.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 1. Siddiq Mirza a lawyer may be appointed for governor.
questions.answer: Siddiq Mirza, a lawyer, may be appointed for governor.
questions.explanation: 'a lawyer' is a non-restrictive appositive renaming Siddiq Mirza and must be set off with commas on both sides. Note: the printed book skips the number Exercise 4 in this grammar section (Exercise 3 on page 52 is followed directly by Exercise 5 on page 53); nothing is missing from this solution set.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 2. If you ever need a ride a slower one please let me know.
questions.answer: If you ever need a ride, a slower one, please let me know.
questions.explanation: 'a slower one' is an appositive explaining 'a ride'; it interrupts the sentence and is enclosed in commas. (A dash - 'a ride - a slower one -' would also be correct.)

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 3. The winner of the contest who arrived from the US last week will receive 1 million.
questions.answer: The winner of the contest, who arrived from the US last week, will receive 1 million.
questions.explanation: The clause 'who arrived from the US last week' is non-restrictive - it adds information about a winner already identified - so it is set off by commas.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 4. Kabir a writer and a poet is very obedient to his parents.
questions.answer: Kabir, a writer and a poet, is very obedient to his parents.
questions.explanation: 'a writer and a poet' is a non-restrictive appositive and needs a comma on each side.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 5. The captain ordered the troops to assemble the navy boat a large rowboat.
questions.answer: The captain ordered the troops to assemble the navy boat, a large rowboat.
questions.explanation: 'a large rowboat' is an appositive renaming 'the navy boat'; one comma is enough because it ends the sentence.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 6. Oliver Twist which was Dicken's second novel is a classic.
questions.answer: Oliver Twist, which was Dickens's second novel, is a classic.
questions.explanation: The 'which' clause is non-restrictive (the novel is already named) and is enclosed in commas; 'Dicken's' should be 'Dickens's'.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 7. The lamp which my friend gave me is beside my bed.
questions.answer: No comma is needed: The lamp which my friend gave me is beside my bed.
questions.explanation: The clause 'which my friend gave me' is restrictive - it identifies which lamp is meant - so it is not set off by commas; adding commas would wrongly suggest there is only one lamp.

questions.question: Insert commas wherever necessary in the following sentences. 8. Mr. and Mrs. Kareem our neighbours for the past eight years are moving to the Turkey.
questions.answer: Mr. and Mrs. Kareem, our neighbours for the past eight years, are moving to the Turkey.
questions.explanation: 'our neighbours for the past eight years' is a non-restrictive appositive and is enclosed in commas. (The printed phrase 'to the Turkey' is itself faulty English - it should be 'to Turkey'.)

questions.question: Work individually and combine the following sentences using comma around a dependent word or a group of words. One example has been done for you. Set 01: a. Gawadar coastline is the longest in the region. b. Gawadar coastline is a national treasure.
questions.answer: Gawadar coastline, a national treasure, is the longest in the region.
questions.explanation: This is the book's worked example: sentence (b) becomes an appositive placed in commas inside sentence (a).

questions.question: Work individually and combine the following sentences using comma around a dependent word or a group of words. Set 02: a. Kobe makes millions of dollars a year. b. Kobe is a basketball player.
questions.answer: Kobe, a basketball player, makes millions of dollars a year.
questions.explanation: The noun phrase from (b), 'a basketball player', is inserted as an appositive in commas after the subject of (a).

questions.question: Work individually and combine the following sentences using comma around a dependent word or a group of words. Set 03: a. A giant plane is launched in 1970. b. A Boeing 474 is launched in 1970.
questions.answer: A giant plane, a Boeing 474, was launched in 1970.
questions.explanation: 'A Boeing 474' renames 'a giant plane' and is set off by commas. The printed sentences use the present tense 'is launched'; in a finished sentence about 1970 the past tense 'was launched' is correct.

questions.question: Work individually and combine the following sentences using comma around a dependent word or a group of words. Set 04: a. My brother's car is the envy of my friends. b. My brother's car is sporty red convertible with bucket seats.
questions.answer: My brother's car, a sporty red convertible with bucket seats, is the envy of my friends.
questions.explanation: The description in (b) is reduced to the appositive 'a sporty red convertible with bucket seats' and placed in commas after the subject of (a).

questions.question: Work individually and combine the following sentences using comma around a dependent word or a group of words. Set 05: a. The head surgeon took her nephew on a hospital tour. b. The head surgeon was an expert in organ transplant procedures.
questions.answer: The head surgeon, an expert in organ transplant procedures, took her nephew on a hospital tour.
questions.explanation: The predicate nominative from (b) becomes an appositive in commas after 'The head surgeon' in (a).

questions.question: What does this picture show? Think out a minute and write down the names of devices.
questions.answer: The picture shows a collection of modern digital devices, most of them small, portable and wireless. Reading from the top left I can name: an action camera fixed on a selfie stick or gimbal; a small wearable camera clipped to clothing; a pair of true-wireless earbuds in their blue charging case; a group of mobile phones, including an old keypad phone, a touchscreen smartphone and a portable music player (the white device with the circular control pad); a handheld gaming console with a controller attached on each side; a smart speaker with a rounded screen displaying the word 'Hello'; a tablet held upright in a black stand; a small smart display or mini tablet on a stand; a camera mounted on a handheld gimbal stabiliser; a set of hexagonal smart-light panels; a phone or VR viewer lying flat; and a small streaming stick or USB dongle.
questions.explanation: The pre-reading task asks students to look at the picture and identify the gadgets. The list is read off the picture, which groups communication, photography, gaming, music, lighting and home-assistant devices together to introduce the theme of the unit.

questions.question: How has technology evolved over the period of time?
questions.answer: Technology has evolved from simple mechanical tools to connected digital systems, and each stage has made information easier and cheaper to handle. The passage itself traces the line from Gutenberg's invention of movable type, which made the mass printing of information possible, to the telephone and the mobile phone, which made information travel over distance. Early devices recorded information on paper and in analogue form, as 'atoms'; the digital stage converted it into 'bits' - binary digits of 1s and 0s - so that it could be copied, stored, manipulated and transmitted instantly. The materials revolution then produced automobiles, planes, appliances and telecom systems, and today sensors, wearables, smart phones, cloud conferencing, telemedicine and artificial intelligence are merging into one network. In short, the evolution has been from tools that extended human muscle, to machines that extended human senses, to networks that extend human thought.
questions.explanation: Open-ended but anchored in the text: the first paragraph gives the historical sequence (movable type, telephone, mobile phone) and the analogue-to-digital shift; the remaining paragraphs supply the modern examples.

questions.question: List down technologies recently discovered/invented.
questions.answer: A list of recent technologies: smartphones and 5G mobile networks; wireless earbuds and smart watches that track health; smart speakers and other smart-home devices (smart bulbs, smart locks, security cameras); tablets, smart displays and handheld gaming consoles; drones and action cameras with gimbals; electric and self-driving vehicles; solar panels and wind-power systems; virtual-reality and augmented-reality headsets; cloud computing and video-conferencing platforms; online learning (teleschool, e-learning portals) and telemedicine; e-commerce and digital payment systems; artificial intelligence, machine translation and chatbots; three-dimensional printing; gene-editing (CRISPR) and mRNA vaccines; reusable rockets and satellite internet; and quantum computers.
questions.explanation: This is an open-ended recall task. The list deliberately includes the technologies named in the unit text (smart phones, wearables, cloud conferencing, teleschool, telemedicine, e-commerce) so that the pre-reading answer links to the reading that follows.

questions.question: Work in pairs and deduce the meaning of words given in column A and write their contextual meaning in column B. Share with your partner once you have completed.
questions.answer:
No. | Word | Contextual meaning
1 | innovation | a new idea, method or device; here the new developments and products that the technological revolution keeps producing.
2 | optimists | people who look on the bright side and expect good results; here those who greeted the new era of technology hopefully.
3 | manipulate | to handle, arrange or control something skilfully; here to work with and process information - to develop, organise, store and transmit it.
4 | heralded | announced or proclaimed the arrival of something; here the optimists announced that a new era had begun.
5 | hazards | dangers or risks; here natural dangers such as storms and earthquakes that can turn into disasters.
6 | hurricanes | violent tropical storms with very strong winds and heavy rain, named in the text among natural phenomena that technology helps to manage.
7 | proliferated | increased quickly in number, multiplied; here games that also teach have spread widely.
8 | impending | about to happen very soon; here problems that are coming and that drivers are warned about in real time.
9 | calamities | great disasters that cause widespread damage and suffering; here outbreaks and natural disasters.
10 | lessen | to make smaller or weaker; here to reduce the impact of a pandemic.
questions.explanation: Meanings are deduced from the sentences in which the words occur (for example 'proliferated' is used of learning games, 'impending' of problems drivers are warned about), not from a dictionary alone.

questions.question: Read the text carefully. There are certain words that are related to word 'Tele' means 'far'. First, underline these words in the texts and then write description of these words. An example has been given for you.
questions.answer:
All the words below contain the prefix tele- (from Greek 'far, at a distance') and are taken from the unit text.

No. | Word from the text | Description
1 | Telephone | A device used for speaking to distant places by means of electrical signals (the example given in the book).
2 | Tele-pointers | New-generation pointing or input devices that work at a distance and have replaced the pen, the pencil and older pointer models.
3 | Telecom (telecommunication) system | A system that carries messages - voice, text, images or data - over a distance, through cables, radio waves or satellites.
4 | Television (spectrum) | A system that sends moving pictures and sound from a distant studio to receivers; its spectrum (radio frequencies) is also used for public-safety networks.
5 | Teleschool | Schooling at a distance: lessons and course material delivered to students who stay at home instead of going to a classroom.
6 | Telemedicine | The practice of medicine at a distance: a patient gets information or advice about a medical condition through a network instead of visiting the doctor physically.
7 | Telepresence | The technology that makes a person feel present, and able to act, in a distant or extreme place without travelling there.
8 | Telework | Work done at a distance from the office, with the help of computers and the Internet.
9 | Telemarketing | Marketing carried out over the telephone or the Internet, reaching customers far away instead of meeting them at a shop.
questions.explanation: The task is a word-detective exercise: students underline every 'tele-' word in the reading text and then explain it. The nine words above are exactly those that occur in the text; each description shows how the idea of 'far' is present in the word.

questions.question: 1. Digital revolution mainly depends on________.
questions.answer: (c) hardware innovations. The text says that 'many advances in the technology depend on hardware innovations made possible by continued advancement in materials technology'.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly names hardware innovations, supported by materials technology, as the base on which technological advances rest; improved life is the result, not the base.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) physical nature   (b) improved life   (c) hardware innovations   (d) integrated Circuit

questions.question: 2. During World War-II, transmission of information was in________ form:
questions.answer: (b) analogue. The text explains that information processing 'relied on atoms to record or transmit information in analog form rather than the bits ... used to record or transmit information in digital form'.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts analogue ('atoms') with digital ('bits') and places the analogue stage before the digital one; 'analogue' in the option is the British spelling of the text's 'analog'. Electric waves were only the means used by telephones, not the form of the information.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) material   (b) analogue   (c) electric   (d) catalogue

questions.question: 3. ________ is the technological option to work in dangerous situation.
questions.answer: (c) Telepresence. The section on public safety says: 'Telepresence is possible option to work in any extreme condition'.
questions.explanation: Telepresence lets a person act in a distant place without being physically there, which is exactly what working in an extreme or dangerous condition requires.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Telephone   (b) Telecom   (c) Telepresence   (d) Television

questions.question: 4. It is technology that people get things better according to their____.
questions.answer: (c) needs. The commerce section says the revolution is 'enabling them to get the kinds of products and services that fit their needs'.
questions.explanation: The text speaks of products and services that 'fit their needs'; market demand, environment and work are not the words used in that sentence.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) market demand   (b) environment   (c) needs   (d) work

questions.question: 5. E-learning can only be possible through__________.
questions.answer: (b) internet. The text says parents use 'e-leaning via Internet' and that flexible online classes give access to education that 'would never have been possible before the Internet'.
questions.explanation: Portals, apps and smart systems are tools that run on the Internet; the passage names the Internet itself as the enabling medium of e-learning. (The printed option is set as 'b)internet' without a space.)
questions.optionsRaw: (a) portals   (b)internet   (c) smart adaptation   (d) innovative system

questions.question: 6. People get information through ________ to help them better understand a medical condition.
questions.answer: (c) telemedicine. The text states: 'People get information through telemedicine to help them better understand a medical condition'.
questions.explanation: This is a direct quotation from the 'Technology in Education & Health' section, so no inference is needed.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) internet   (b) integrated apps   (c) telemedicine   (d) visual images

questions.question: 7. Bits used to record or transmit information in ________ form.
questions.answer: (b) digital. The text describes the bits as being 'used to record or transmit information in digital form'.
questions.explanation: Option (a) is tempting because the text calls bits 'binary digits', but the phrase to be completed is 'in ... form', and the passage's exact phrase is 'in digital form'. Follow the text, not the association with binary.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) binary   (b) digital   (c) analogue   (d) logical

questions.question: 8. ________ is an example of hydrological disaster.
questions.answer: (c) floods. A hydrological hazard is one connected with water, and floods are the water-related disaster among the options.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions hazards 'of atmospheric, geological, hydrological, and biological origins' and lists hurricanes, wildfires, tsunamis and landslides, but gives no example of a hydrological one. Floods are the standard hydrological example; an earthquake is geological, a hurricane atmospheric and a wildfire is not water-related at all.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) earthquake   (b) hurricane   (c) floods   (d) wildfire

questions.question: 9. ________ technology assesses environmental changes and disease predictions.
questions.answer: (a) remote sensing. The passage says: 'The remote sensing technology could monitor environmental changes and disease predictions'.
questions.explanation: Satellite images are one of the tools used, but the sentence that names environmental changes and disease predictions attributes them to remote sensing technology.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) remote sensing   (b) satellite   (c) circuit   (d) visual images

questions.question: 10. A bulk of population at disaster risks may be located by________.
questions.answer: (b) satellite images. The text says satellite images, aerial photographs and on-the-ground inspections 'can be used to locate populations in dangerous or environmentally unstable places'.
questions.explanation: Telecom, actuators and phones are listed among smart-city devices, but locating populations at risk is linked in the text to satellite images, aerial photographs and ground inspections.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) telecom   (b) satellite images   (c) actuators   (d) smart phones

questions.question: Work individually. Read the text again and mark (√) for true, and (X) for false against each statement given below.
questions.answer:
No. | Statement | Answer | Reason
1 | Use of technology can be harmful for our environment. | X | The text presents technology as 'the key enabler of' an 'efficient environment' and as making cars more energy efficient through renewable energy; it does not claim that technology harms the environment.
2 | First use of technology was related to waves. | X | The first advance the text names is Gutenberg's movable type; electric waves appear much later, when 'telephones translated voices into electric waves'.
3 | During World War II, the use of technology was not familiar. | √ | The text says information remained scarce and hard to use because it was handled in analogue form, and that 'many innovations arose after the World War II' - so advanced technology was not yet familiar in that period.
4 | All tele devices may function with traditional type. | X | Telepresence, telework, teleschool and telemedicine all depend on modern digital networks; they cannot work with traditional, analogue devices.
5 | An e-learning can only be possible without internet. | X | The text says e-learning is done 'via Internet' and that online classes would never have been possible before the Internet.
6 | People can also purchase and sell things via internet. | √ | The commerce section describes e-commerce, which 'lets people buy a vast array of goods and services' online - buying and selling through the Internet.
7 | Renewable things are those which cannot be utilized again. | X | The opposite is true: renewable sources such as wind power and solar energy are continuously available and can be used again and again.
8 | Telework and telepresence are the internet ways to work in hazardous situation. | √ | Telepresence is described as the option 'to work in any extreme condition' and telework gives people the chance to work beyond the limits of a workplace.
questions.explanation: Each judgement is tied to a sentence in the reading text. Items 3 and 8 require inference rather than a direct quotation, so the reasoning is shown in the table.

questions.question: 1. What do you mean by technological revolution?
questions.answer: The technological revolution means the continuing transformation of life and work brought about by technology. The text calls technology 'the major driving force of both economic growth and improved quality of life' and says that it is this revolution 'that is driving innovation and enabling billions of people to live better and safer lives'. It is also 'the key enabler of better education, health care, efficient environment, safer and secure communities and nations'. At its centre is a change in the way information is handled: from analogue 'atoms' to digital 'bits'. In short, it is the ongoing shift, based on hardware and materials innovation, by which every field of life - education, health, commerce, safety, entertainment - is reshaped by technology.
questions.explanation: The definition is built from the opening paragraph of 'Technological Revolution', quoting its key phrases.

questions.question: 2. Why did innovation information remain scare at the time of World War-II?
questions.answer: Information remained scarce because it was still processed in analogue form. The text explains that although 'many innovations arose after the World War II', information 'remained scarce and hard to use and transmit'. The reason given is that 'the processing of information relied on atoms to record or transmit information in analog form rather than the bits (binary digits of 1s for on and 0s for off) used to record or transmit information in digital form'. Without digital bits, information had to be carried by physical records such as paper, so it could not be copied, stored, searched or sent quickly and cheaply. The equipment of the time - copiers, printers, telephones - was also limited, and the materials revolution that produced modern devices had not yet arrived.
questions.explanation: The answer follows the causal sentence in the first paragraph: analogue, atom-based processing is given as the reason why information was scarce and hard to use and transmit.

questions.question: 3. How is the technology boon for students?
questions.answer: Technology is a boon for students mainly because it puts education within reach. Course material is provided online through teleschool, so students can study 'without leaving homes'; flexible online classes 'give people access to education that would never have been possible before the Internet'. Parents can follow their child's school assignments and academic progress through web portals and innovative applications, which keeps the home and the school connected. Games designed to double as learning tools have proliferated, so learning becomes interactive and engaging, especially for young children. Information of every kind is at the students' fingertips, and they can revise a lesson, watch a demonstration or consult a library at any time.
questions.explanation: The answer gathers the education-related sentences from the 'Technology in Education & Health' and 'Technology & Entertainment' sections.

questions.question: 4. What are the benefits of E-commerce in today's world?
questions.answer: E-commerce gives people 'a wide variety of choices' and enables them 'to get the kinds of products and services that fit their needs'. It lets them 'buy a vast array of goods and services that previously might have been difficult to find at local stores', so a small town shopper can reach the same market as a city customer. Prices can be compared before buying, and goods are delivered to the door. On the employment side, telework and telemarketing give people 'the chance to move beyond the limits' of their local job market, and businesses can sell to customers far away without opening branch after branch. In short, e-commerce widens choice, saves time and travel, and connects producers and consumers across distances.
questions.explanation: The commerce paragraph supplies the quotations; the points about comparison, delivery and saving time are reasonable extensions of 'a vast array of goods and services' bought online.

questions.question: 5. How does technology work in environmentally risk areas?
questions.answer: In environmentally risky areas technology works as an early-warning and protection system. Remote sensing technology monitors environmental changes and disease predictions; satellite images, aerial photographs and on-the-ground inspections are used 'to locate populations in dangerous or environmentally unstable places and determine how to respond after disaster strikes'. Smart cities are equipped with sensors, processors, wearables, electronics, software, actuators, vehicles, cell phones and computers that collect and send data. Cellular, wireless, satellite and television-spectrum networks keep communications open when ordinary links fail, and the Internet is used 'to coordinate recovery efforts'. Technology also helps scientists understand the mechanism of atmospheric, geological, hydrological and biological hazards and how they turn into disasters.
questions.explanation: The answer combines the 'Disaster Risk Reduction' paragraph with the epidemics paragraph, where remote sensing and satellite data are described.

questions.question: 6. How has technology greatly supported doctors & medical practitioners?
questions.answer: Technology supports doctors and medical practitioners by giving them information and reach. Through telemedicine, people 'get information ... to help them better understand a medical condition', so patients in remote areas can be guided before they ever reach a hospital. Technology 'has helped improve medical care by making it easier for doctors to provide evidence-based medicine' - treatment based on recorded data, test results and research rather than guesswork. Online systems let doctors consult specialists at a distance and share reports and images quickly, and wearable devices and sensors supply continuous data about a patient's condition so that problems are noticed early.
questions.explanation: The quotations come from the health part of the 'Technology in Education & Health' section; the point about specialists and wearables follows from the telemedicine and smart-device sentences.

questions.question: 7. How does technology secure humans from calamities?
questions.answer: Technology secures humans from calamities by predicting, monitoring and managing them. Disasters forecasting, predictions, monitoring, risk assessment and damage assessment are 'the open grounds for integrating technology', and satellite images, aerial photographs and on-the-ground inspections are used to manage hurricanes, wildfires, tsunamis and landslides. Public safety networks built on cellular, wireless, satellite and existing analogue television spectrum keep warnings and instructions flowing, and communities use the Internet 'during an emergency to coordinate recovery efforts'. During epidemics and pandemics technology enables secure access to data, virtual meetings and cloud conferencing, and although it 'cannot prevent the onset of the pandemics', it can 'help prevent the spread, educate, warn, and empower those on the ground' and 'noticeably lessen the impact'.
questions.explanation: The answer draws on both the disaster-reduction and the epidemics paragraphs; the text itself limits the claim by saying technology cannot prevent a pandemic's onset.

questions.question: 8. Some people have opinion that youngsters are not safe in the technological era? Give reasons for your agreement or disagreement.
questions.answer: I partly agree, but I do not accept the opinion as it stands. It is true that the technological era exposes young people to real dangers: strangers can contact them through games and social media; cyberbullying can follow them into their bedrooms; false information and deepfakes can mislead them; endless scrolling damages sleep, eyesight and concentration; and personal data can be collected and misused. Yet the same technology keeps them safer in many ways - emergency alerts, location sharing with parents, online learning when schools are closed, health information and contact with family members far away. The danger lies less in the technology than in its unguided use. With digital literacy, privacy settings, agreed screen-time limits and open conversation at home and school, youngsters can enjoy the benefits and avoid most of the harm. I therefore disagree with the blanket claim that they are 'not safe'.
questions.explanation: This is an opinion question, so more than one answer is possible. The model answer gives a balanced judgement with reasons on both sides and a clear final position, which is what the task requires.

questions.question: 9. Which technology innovation has impacted you profoundly and how?
questions.answer: The innovation that has affected me most is the smartphone connected to the Internet. Before it, study meant waiting for a library book or for the teacher's next lesson; now a doubt about a formula or a date can be answered in a minute by a video lesson or a reliable website, and our class group shares notes and reminders every evening. It has also changed my relationships: I can speak to my cousins abroad and see my grandparents' faces whenever I wish. At the same time it has taught me a caution I did not need before - to check a fact before forwarding it, and to put the phone away when I am reading or talking to someone. So the impact has been both practical and character-forming: it has made learning and communication immediate, and it has made self-control a daily necessity.
questions.explanation: This is a personal-response question. The model answer names one innovation and shows both its practical effects and its effect on habits, which is what 'how' requires.

questions.question: 10. How did technology contribute in keeping peoples' lives safe during the recent pandemic or disaster?
questions.answer: During the recent pandemic technology kept life going while people were kept apart. It enabled 'secure access to data, enterprise applications, virtual meetings and cloud conferencing', so offices, courts and classrooms moved online. Schools used teleschool and online classes, patients used telemedicine, and families used video calls to stay in touch with isolated relatives. Remote sensing and satellite images helped authorities monitor the spread of disease and 'locate populations in dangerous or environmentally unstable places'. E-commerce and digital payments delivered food and medicine to doorsteps, reducing crowds in markets. Public-health messages could be broadcast widely to 'educate, warn, and empower those on the ground', and the result, as the text says, was to 'noticeably lessen the impact' of the crisis.
questions.explanation: The epidemics/pandemics paragraph supplies the quotations; the examples of online classes, telemedicine and e-commerce are the applications described elsewhere in the same text.

questions.question: Though use of technology has many advantages to ease living, it has some disadvantages too. Now, work in groups. First make outlines related to only disadvantages of technology, and then expand each outline in short paragraphs.
questions.answer:
Outline of the disadvantages of technology
1. Unemployment caused by automation.
2. Addiction to screens and damage to health.
3. Loss of privacy and the growth of cybercrime.
4. The rapid spread of false information.
5. The weakening of face-to-face relationships.
6. Environmental damage from electronic waste and energy use.

1. Unemployment caused by automation. Machines and software now do work that once employed people - billing clerks, ticket sellers, assembly-line workers and even junior office staff. When a factory installs robots or a bank installs cash machines, the owner saves money but the employees lose their incomes. Unless workers are retrained for new kinds of jobs, technology widens the gap between those who own the machines and those who are replaced by them.

2. Addiction to screens and damage to health. Phones, games and streaming sites are designed to hold attention, and many young people sit for hours with bent necks and sleepless eyes. This leads to weak eyesight, back and neck pain, obesity from inactivity and constant tiredness in class. Addiction also makes people restless and irritable when they cannot check their devices, so it harms mental health as well as the body.

3. Loss of privacy and the growth of cybercrime. Every click, purchase and location leaves a trace, and companies and criminals collect these traces. Hacked accounts, stolen passwords, fake calls and online fraud cost people their savings and their reputation. Because the crime crosses borders and leaves little physical evidence, it is very hard to trace and punish.

4. The rapid spread of false information. A rumour or a doctored video can reach millions of people within minutes, and it is often shared before anyone checks it. False news about health, elections or religion can cause panic, violence and deep divisions in society. Technology gives every user a microphone, but not every user the training to use it responsibly.

5. The weakening of face-to-face relationships. When people spend their evenings messaging, they may stop visiting, listening and sitting together. Families can be in the same room while each member is lost in a separate screen. Manners such as greeting, waiting one's turn and reading another person's face are learned only in real company, and these skills weaken when devices replace conversation.

6. Environmental damage from electronic waste and energy use. Old phones, chargers and computers are discarded in huge quantities, and much of this e-waste is burned or dumped, releasing poisonous metals into soil and water. Data centres and cryptocurrency mining consume enormous amounts of electricity, much of it still produced from coal and gas. Technology must therefore be designed to be repaired, recycled and powered by clean energy.
questions.explanation: The group task is open-ended. The model answer keeps strictly to disadvantages, as instructed, and expands each outline point into a short paragraph with a cause, an effect and, where possible, a remedy.

questions.question:
Work in pairs. Write the précis of the following paragraph and suggest a suitable title. Remember to use steps given above. After completing, share the précis with your partner.
Trees give shade for the benefit of others, and while they themselves stand in the sun and endure the heat, they produce the fruit of which others profit. The character of good human is like that of trees. Sandalwood, the more it is rubbed, the more scent does it yield. Sugarcane, the more it is peeled and cut up into pieces, the more juice does it produce. What matters whether other people praise them or not? What difference does it make whether they die at this moment or whether lives are prolonged? Happen what may, those who tread in the right path will not set foot in any other. Life itself is unprofitable to a human being who does not live for others. To live for the mere sake of living one's life is to live the life with no purpose.
questions.answer:
Title: Trees - The Model of Selfless Service

Précis: Trees bear heat to give others shade and fruit. Good people resemble them, like sandalwood that yields more fragrance when rubbed and sugarcane that gives more juice when crushed. Praise or death hardly matters to such people, who never leave the right path. A life lived only for itself is purposeless.
questions.explanation: The passage is 141 words, so a précis of about one-third (the book's rule) is roughly 47 words; the model is 51 words. It keeps only the central idea (selfless service), drops the rhetorical questions and repeated examples, uses fresh wording, adds no opinion, and supplies the required title.

questions.question: Practise the following dialogue in groups of three. Three friends, Babar, Akmal and Zeeshan, were discussing about their future plan after completing intermediate. One dialogue has been left blank for each of the character. Each one should think of one more dialogue related to situation and say it; the others can agree or state another view point.
questions.answer:
Model added turn for each character, to be spoken after the printed dialogue:

Babar: In my opinion, we should also think about the cost. Medical and engineering both need long years of study and heavy fees, while a legal career needs years of reading before it pays. Speaking personally, I would rather choose a field where I can serve people and support my family at the same time.
Akmal: I agree with Babar that cost matters, but I have the feeling that talent and hard work attract scholarships. As far as I am concerned, a good student should not give up a difficult field only because it is expensive; he should apply for every scholarship and then prove himself.
Zeeshan: My own opinion on the subject is that the field must suit the person, not the family's wish or the fashion of the year. It is my impression that a lawyer who hates courts, or a doctor who faints at the sight of blood, will serve nobody. So each of us should test his aptitude first and then decide.

Agreement and counter-view (spoken by the other two after each turn): 'I agree with you, but ...' or 'That is true, however, in my view ...'. For example, after Zeeshan's turn Babar may reply: 'I agree that aptitude matters, but in my view aptitude can also be built by hard work once the choice is made.'
questions.explanation: The printed dialogue already gives each friend two turns; this task asks each student to add one further turn using the phrases for expressing a point of view, while the others agree or state another view. The model shows all three added turns and one sample agreement-and-counter-view exchange, so the dialogue remains a genuine three-way discussion.

questions.question: Two dialogue activities should be presented in the class. The topics must be of any common interest like: 1. Personal Business and Employment
questions.answer:
A dialogue on 'Personal Business and Employment' (three speakers: Ayesha, Bilal, Sameer):

Ayesha: In my opinion, a young person should first take a job and learn how a business actually runs before risking his own money. I think that a salaried start teaches discipline, accounting and dealing with customers.
Bilal: I would say that is too slow. As far as I am concerned, a small personal business - a repair shop, an online store, a tailoring unit - can be started with modest capital and grown step by step. Speaking personally, I would rather earn from my own effort than wait for a promotion.
Sameer: It is my impression that both of you are partly right. My own opinion is that the choice depends on the person's savings, skills and family responsibilities. A person with dependents should keep a job and test a small business in the evenings; a person with a useful skill and some capital can begin at once.
Ayesha: I agree with Sameer, but in my view a business without bookkeeping fails within a year, so anyone starting one should first learn basic accounts.
Bilal: That is true; however, I still believe that waiting too long destroys the courage to start. I am of the opinion that a carefully planned small beginning is better than a lifetime of hesitation.
Sameer: Then we agree on the essentials: skill, planning, savings and honest accounts - whether one begins with a job or with a business.
questions.explanation: Open-ended speaking task. The model dialogue uses the phrases for presenting a point of view given on the page (in my opinion, I think, I would say, as far as I am concerned, it is my impression, speaking personally, I am of the opinion) and shows agreement plus a counter-view, as the task requires.

questions.question: Two dialogue activities should be presented in the class. The topics must be of any common interest like: 2. Manual Book Readings and Digital Readings
questions.answer:
A dialogue on 'Manual Book Readings and Digital Readings' (three speakers: Hina, Omar, Farah):

Hina: In my opinion, a printed book is still the best way to read seriously. I find that I remember a page better when I can turn it, underline it and see it lying open on the table, and my eyes do not ache after an hour.
Omar: I would say that digital reading has advantages a paper book cannot offer. As far as I am concerned, a single tablet can hold a whole library, the text can be searched in seconds, and the font can be enlarged. Speaking personally, I read more now because a book is always in my pocket.
Farah: It is my impression that the purpose decides the medium. My own opinion is that for deep study - a novel, a poem, a long argument - paper is calmer and less distracting, while for quick reference, news and research, digital text is far more efficient.
Hina: I agree with Farah, but in my view the temptation of notifications makes digital reading difficult for young students unless the device is kept offline while reading.
Omar: That is true; however, I am of the opinion that the same device can carry a dictionary, notes and audio, which helps weaker readers instead of harming them.
Farah: So we conclude that neither medium is perfect: paper gives concentration, digital gives access, and a good reader uses each for what it does best.
questions.explanation: Open-ended speaking task. The model presents three clear viewpoints with the target phrases, one agreement, one counter-view and a concluding synthesis, which is what a classroom dialogue presentation needs.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Look at the picture below and illustrate the use of prepositions of place and time and fill in the blanks. After completing, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
Completed sentences (the filled prepositions are shown in brackets):

No. | Completed sentence
1 | There is a doll on the sofa that was purchased on Monday last. [place: on; time: on]
2 | There is a ball on the table. It will be taken to play in half an hour. [place: on; time: in]
3 | There is a cat on the armchair. [place: on]
4 | There is an apple on the table. [place: on]
5 | There is a dog under the table. [place: under]
6 | There is an umbrella behind the sofa. [place: behind]
7 | There is a picture on the wall. [place: on]
8 | There is a vase on the table. [place: on]
9 | There is a robot on the floor. [place: on]
10 | There is a car under the armchair. [place: under]
11 | There is a lamp beside the sofa and will be lit at 10 pm. [place: beside; time: at]
12 | There is a teddy on the armchair. It will go to sleep at 11 pm. [place: on; time: at]

Note on prepositions: 'on' is used for a surface (sofa, table, wall, floor) and for days and dates (on Monday); 'in' for a period of time in the future (in half an hour); 'at' for exact clock times (at 10 pm, at 11 pm); 'under', 'behind' and 'beside' for position relative to an object. 'Beside' may be replaced by 'next to'.
questions.explanation: The answers are read from the picture: the doll is seated on the sofa, the ball and the apple stand on the tables, the dog and the toy car are tucked under the furniture, and the lamp stands beside the sofa. The picture is small in print, so where a toy is partly hidden, a near-synonym (for example 'next to' for 'beside') is equally acceptable; the grammar point being tested is the choice of place preposition versus time preposition.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Look at the picture below and illustrate the use of prepositions of place & movement and fill in the blanks. After completing, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
Completed sentences:

No. | Completed sentence
0 | He is walking from the post office to the bank. [movement: from ... to]
1 | The ladder is standing against the wall. [place: against]
2 | The post office is next to the travel agency. [place: next to]
3 | The aeroplane is flying over the town. [movement: over]
4 | The bank is between the post office and the library. [place: between]
5 | My flat is above the bank. [place: above]
6 | They are standing in front of the building. [place: in front of]
7 | The flat is near the park. [place: near]
8 | The park is behind the library. [place: behind]
9 | The library is next to the bank. [place: next to]
10 | He is standing outside the library. [place: outside]
11 | She is walking along the road. [movement: along]
12 | They are sitting on the bridge. [place: on]
13 | He is walking across the road. [movement: across]
14 | He is driving over the bridge. [movement: over]
15 | The bus stop is in front of the bank. [place: in front of]
16 | She is walking towards the market. [movement: towards]
17 | She is walking up the stairs. [movement: up]
18 | He is walking down the steps. [movement: down]
questions.explanation: The numbered labels and arrows on the town map show where each person or object is and which way the arrows point: the ladder leans on the wall, the plane flies above the town, the car crosses the bridge, the woman climbs the stairs and the man comes down the steps. The map is printed faintly, so a few blanks (for example 5, 7 and 10) can take another suitable place preposition - above/near, near/opposite, outside/in front of - provided the sentence remains true to the picture; the essential distinction is between position (in, on, at, between, behind, next to) and movement (from ... to, along, across, over, towards, up, down).

questions.question: Now, work individually and fill in the gaps with the verbs followed by appropriate prepositions to complete the sentences given below. You can choose from the above given table.
questions.answer:
i. Since Sara is arrogant, she never apologises for her rude behaviour. [apologise for]
ii. The luggage belongs to the man in black hat. [belong to]
iii. She asked for the second chance to rectify her mistake. [ask for]
iv. Last year, Moiz arrived at Mirpur Khas and stayed at his home town for a month. [arrive at]
v. In today's session, he commented on the current situation of Pakistan. [comment on]
vi. The committee consists of Mr. Ali Miral, Mr. Zohair Anees, and Ms. Saima Huq. [consist of]
vii. The nation suffers from the inflation and poverty. [suffer from]
viii. The Prime Minister did not agree with his cabinet's opinions. [agree with]
ix. When she participates in races, she only concentrates on the time. [concentrate on]
x. Now, it is the time to invest in as many companies as possible. [invest in]
questions.explanation: Each answer uses a verb plus the preposition that the table on book page 67 lists for it: for (purpose/reason), to (direction/connection), about, with (relationships), of, in (involvement), at (place), on (with certain verbs such as comment on) and from (origin). Note: 'arrive in' is also used with large cities, but the table gives 'arrive at'; in (iv) 'at' also matches the printed 'at his home town'. In (ix), 'cares about' would also fit the blank, but 'concentrates on' matches the sense of a runner's attention to time.

questions.question: Now, work individually and fill in the blanks with the appropriate words in the box below. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
Word box: forecast, disinfect, semiformal, nonverbal, biannual, rejoice, substandard

No. | Completed sentence | Word used
1 | The cleaning staff disinfects the area to avoid the spread of Corona Virus. | disinfect
2 | The problem is that he expected you to understand his nonverbal communication. | nonverbal
3 | Her wedding was semiformal, so everyone just dressed neat and tidy. | semiformal
4 | Living conditions such as substandard housing have a major impact on health. | substandard
5 | You have just forecast how quickly people would accept this information and how supportive they would be while learning to accept this 'change'. | forecast
6 | The biannual dental and medical check-ups are offered if you take total coverage medical policy. | biannual
7 | His victory was rejoiced by the political analyst due to his commitment and promises with the nation. | rejoice (used as rejoiced)
questions.explanation: Each blank is filled from the meaning of the prefix: dis- (opposite), non- (not), semi- (half), sub- (under/below), fore- (before), bi- (twice) and re- (again). Note on 7: the only word left is 'rejoice', so the expected answer is 'rejoiced'; standard usage, however, prefers the intransitive 'rejoiced at/over his victory', so the printed passive 'was rejoiced by the political analyst' is awkward. If the sentence is to be fully idiomatic, the analyst's action is better expressed as 'His victory was hailed/celebrated by the political analyst'. In 1, 'disinfect' is also acceptable if 'staff' is treated as a plural collective.

questions.question: Work in pairs and identify the words which have prefixes in any news from a newspaper which is provided by the teacher. After completing, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
Model worked on this short news item: 'The government has announced an unprejudiced inquiry into the disagreement between the two provinces over the sharing of canal water, which had been disinfected before supply. Officials said the situation was unprecedented and that misinformation on social media had worsened it. A spokesperson promised to reopen the case and to review the substandard construction of the canal, calling the delay unacceptable and the repair work overdue.'

No. | Word | Prefix | Root word | Suffix | Meaning of the word
1 | unprejudiced | un- (not) | prejudice (judge beforehand) | -ed | not influenced by prejudice; fair
2 | disagreement | dis- (opposite of) | agree | -ment | failure to agree; quarrel
3 | disinfected | dis- (opposite of) | infect | -ed | freed from infection; cleaned of germs
4 | unprecedented | un- (not) + pre- (before) | cede/cedent (go) | -ed | never known or done before
5 | misinformation | mis- (wrongly) | inform | -ation | false or wrong information
6 | reopen | re- (again) | open | - | to open again
7 | review | re- (again) | view (look) | - | to look at again; to examine
8 | substandard | sub- (below) | standard | - | below the accepted standard; of poor quality
9 | unacceptable | un- (not) | accept | -able | not able to be accepted; intolerable
10 | overdue | over- (too much/beyond) | due | - | not paid or done by the due time; late

Method: underline each word, mark the prefix at the beginning and, if there is one, the suffix at the end, and then remove them to find the root word; the meaning of the whole word is the meaning of the root changed by the prefix and suffix.
questions.explanation: This exercise is open-ended because the newspaper passage is supplied by the teacher, so the answer gives a short model news item and a fully worked table. The table also distinguishes prefix, root and suffix, as the teacher's note on the page requires.

questions.question: Pre-reading 1. Look at the pictures and quickly describe different activities.
questions.answer:
Picture 1: A young man with a shoulder bag stands at an ATM (automated teller machine). He has inserted his card, is pressing the keys to enter his PIN and is about to collect the cash that the machine will dispense. He is doing his own banking - withdrawing money - without going to a clerk at a counter.

Picture 2: The busy hall of a bank. A customer in a red shawl stands at the counter being served by a clerk behind the grille, while a small child in a red shirt holds on to her. A man in a green shirt waits behind her, and other clients stand in a loose queue holding forms, passbooks and cash. Some are filling in deposit and withdrawal slips, others are waiting for their turn.

Activities shown: withdrawing cash from an ATM, depositing and withdrawing money at the counter, encashing a cheque, filling in bank forms, waiting in a queue and being served by the staff. Both pictures show ordinary civic/banking activities in which people have to wait patiently, take their turn and behave courteously towards staff and fellow customers.
questions.explanation: The task is open-ended picture description; the answer names each activity visible in the two pictures and links them to the unit theme of civic sense (queueing, patience, courtesy).
