questions.question: While-reading Exercise 1. Work in pairs and deduce the meaning of words given in column A and write their contextual meaning in column B. Share with your partner once you have completed.
questions.answer:
No. | Word | Contextual meaning (Column B)
1 | solemnly | in a serious, grave and formal manner; the writer said 'alone' in a solemn, almost solemnly important tone, as though it were a matter of great secrecy.
2 | terrible | extremely bad, dreadful, frightening; 'a terrible secret' is a shocking secret that makes one afraid.
3 | detective | a person whose job is to investigate crimes, especially a private investigator; the manager thought he belonged to Pinkerton's detective agency.
4 | mysterious | strange, secret and puzzling, suggesting that something is being hidden; his frightened look and his demand to see the manager 'alone' seemed mysterious.
5 | whispered | spoke in a very low, soft voice so that other people could not hear; 'Fairly large', I whispered.
6 | painful | causing distress or embarrassment, difficult and unpleasant to do; handing over his money felt 'painful' to the shy writer.
7 | astonished | greatly surprised, amazed; the clerk was astonished that the customer wanted to draw out every cent at once.
8 | hollow | empty, dull and without real feeling or strength; a 'hollow shaking voice' is a voice that sounds lifeless and trembling.
9 | temper | a person's tendency to become angry; 'a man with a fearfully quick temper' means a man who loses his temper very easily.
10 | rival | a competitor; a rival agency is another detective agency competing with Pinkerton's.
questions.explanation: Each meaning is deduced from the sentence in which the word occurs in 'My Bank Account' (pages 73-75), not from a dictionary, as the task asks for contextual meaning.

questions.question: While-reading Exercise 2. Work in pairs. Match the following bank-related words of column A with their meanings given in column B and write answers in Column C. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
No. | Column A | Column C (answer) | Meaning matched from Column B
1 | bank manager | F | one who has control of all resources in the bank
2 | accountant | E | one who maintains audits business accounts
3 | clerk | A | one who maintain all written record
4 | cheque | G | a written order directing a bank to pay money
5 | transactions | C | dealings and exchanges
6 | deposits | B | to put money in the account
7 | cheque book | D | a small book having checks to draw money
questions.explanation: Every word is paired with exactly one meaning, so the matching is one-to-one (manager F, accountant E, clerk A, cheque G, transactions C, deposits B, cheque book D). Note: the printed definitions are loosely worded - 'clerk' is defined as 'one who maintain all written record' (grammatically faulty in the book) and 'deposits' is defined by the act 'to put money in the account'; the intended pairing is still clear.

questions.question: Exercise 3. Read the statements and encircle the right option. 1. The writer visited the bank________________.
questions.answer: The writer visited the bank for the first time.
questions.explanation: He knows nothing about bank procedure - he believes that anyone opening an account must consult the manager, is frightened by the clerks, the desks and the very sight of money, and behaves like an 'irresponsible fool'. Such complete unfamiliarity shows that this was his first visit to open an account; nothing in the text suggests frequent, monthly or yearly visits.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) frequently   (b) first time   (c) in a month   (d) yearly

questions.question: Exercise 3. 2. The writer's salary was raised to_____________ a month.
questions.answer: The writer's salary was raised to fifty dollars a month.
questions.explanation: The text says: 'my salary had been raised to fifty dollars a month and I felt that the bank was the only place for it.' Fifty-six dollars is the sum he deposited, not his salary.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) sixty dollars   (b) fifty dollars   (c) thirty dollars   (d) fifty-six dollars

questions.question: Exercise 3. 3. ____________ presumed the writer to be a detective.
questions.answer: The manager presumed the writer to be a detective.
questions.explanation: In the private room the manager says, 'You are one of Pinkerton's detectives, I suppose,' and the writer adds, 'My mysterious manner had made him think that I was a detective.'
questions.optionsRaw: (a) clerk   (b) manager   (c) accountant   (d) rich man

questions.question: Exercise 3. 4. The writer first met the ____________ in the bank.
questions.answer: The writer first met the accountant in the bank.
questions.explanation: He 'went up to a place marked Accountant', asked that official to let him see the manager, and the accountant 'brought him'. The manager was met afterwards.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) accountant   (b) manager   (c) clerk   (d) security guard

questions.question: Exercise 3. 5. The writer had____________ dollars at the time of opening the account.
questions.answer: The writer had fifty-six dollars at the time of opening the account.
questions.explanation: He 'held my fifty-six dollars, pressed together in a ball, in my pocket' and told the manager he intended to place 'the sum of fifty-six dollars' in the bank.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) six   (b) fifty six   (c) fifty   (d) sixty

questions.question: Exercise 3. 6. Mr. Montgomery was a/ an____________.
questions.answer: Mr. Montgomery was the accountant.
questions.explanation: The manager opened the door and called to the accountant, 'Mr. Montgomery ... this gentleman is opening an account.' So Montgomery is the accountant to whom the writer later pushes his money.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) manager   (b) accountant   (c) clerk   (d) detective

questions.question: Exercise 3. 7. The ____________ of the author made the manager think that he was a detective?
questions.answer: The mysterious manner of the author made the manager think that he was a detective.
questions.explanation: The text states it directly: 'My mysterious manner had made him think that I was a detective.' The demand to see the manager 'alone' and the writer's frightened secrecy produced this impression; he was neither simple, harsh nor bold - he was terrified.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) mysterious manner   (b) simplicity   (c) harsh behaviour   (d) boldness

questions.question: Exercise 3. 8. The author wrote fifty-six dollars instead of six dollars due to____________.
questions.answer: The author wrote fifty-six dollars instead of six dollars because of anxiety (nervous confusion).
questions.explanation: The text says, 'I was too upset to reason now. I had a feeling that it was impossible to explain the thing. All the clerks had stopped writing to look at me.' His hand was shaking, his face 'terribly pale' and the bank 'seemed to swim' before his eyes - acute nervous anxiety made him write the larger figure. Fear is the general mood of the story, but the immediate cause stated is being too upset to think; the answer is not madness.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) fear   (b) haste   (c) anxiety   (d) madness

questions.question: Exercise 3. 9. The text 'My Bank Account' is an example of_______ tale.
questions.answer: The text 'My Bank Account' is an example of a humorous tale.
questions.explanation: The comedy arises from the gap between the narrator's terror and the ordinary business of opening an account, from the manager mistaking him for a detective, and from the comic climax of depositing fifty-six dollars and instantly withdrawing the whole amount while the clerks roar with laughter. The detective element is only a misunderstanding, and the story teaches no explicit moral.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) detective   (b) humorous   (c) moral   (d) fictitious

questions.question: Exercise 3. 10. After returning from the bank, the writer put his savings in____________.
questions.answer: After returning from the bank, the writer put his savings in a sock.
questions.explanation: The last lines say: 'Since then I use a bank no more. I keep my money in my pocket and my savings in silver dollars in a sock.'
questions.optionsRaw: (a) bank   (b) pocket   (c) silver box   (d) sock

questions.question: Exercise 4. Work in pairs. Read the text again carefully and write the sequence of events of the story. After completing, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
Firstly | The writer's salary is raised to fifty dollars a month, so he decides to keep the money in a bank. He walks into the bank frightened by the clerks, the desks and the sight of money, asks the accountant to let him see the manager 'alone', and is taken to a private room.
Secondly | The manager, alarmed by his strange behaviour, locks the door and asks whether he is one of Pinkerton's detectives; the writer denies it and explains that he has come only to open an account and deposit fifty-six dollars, plus fifty dollars every month.
After That | Relieved and now convinced that he is a rich man, the manager calls the accountant, Mr. Montgomery, and tells him that the gentleman is opening an account; the writer hands over his ball of money and signs the sum on a slip, and is given a cheque book.
Then | Wishing to draw six dollars for present use, he writes the cheque for fifty-six dollars by mistake; when the clerk asks in surprise whether he is drawing it all out again, he is too upset to explain and says, 'Yes, the whole thing.'
Later | The astonished clerk asks whether he will not put any more money in the account; the writer answers 'Never', and the clerk pays him a fifty-dollar note and six one-dollar notes, and he rushes out of the bank.
Finally | As the big door swings behind him he hears a roar of laughter rising to the roof of the bank; since then he never uses a bank and keeps his savings in silver dollars in a sock.
questions.explanation: The six stages follow the chronological order of 'My Bank Account': decision and entry, interview with the manager, opening of the account, the mistaken cheque, the withdrawal, and the comic exit and resolution.

questions.question: Exercise 5. Read the text and answer the following questions. 1. What is effect upon the author of entering the bank to do business?
questions.answer: Entering the bank destroys the author's confidence and turns him into, in his own words, an 'irresponsible fool'. The clerks frighten him, the desks frighten him, the very sight of money frightens him, and 'everything frightens' him. His voice sounds 'as if it came from the grave', his face is 'terribly pale', the bank seems to swim before his eyes and he loses the power to reason, which is why he behaves so oddly and finally makes the mistake with the cheque.
questions.explanation: The text opens with the author's confession of fear and repeatedly shows its physical effects (voice, pale face, swimming bank, inability to reason), so the effect is loss of nerve and of clear thinking.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 2. Why did the author decide to open an account?
questions.answer: He decided to open an account because his salary had been raised to fifty dollars a month and he felt that 'the bank was the only place for it'. In other words, he had a regular monthly income that he thought would be safe and sensible to keep in a bank rather than carry about or hoard at home.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives the reason directly: the raised salary made a bank account seem the proper place for his money.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 3. What was the manager's reaction when the author told him that he would like to see him alone?
questions.answer: The manager 'looked at me with some anxiety', because he felt that the visitor had 'a terrible secret to tell'. He said, 'Come in here,' led the way into a private room, turned the key in the lock and, telling the writer that they were safe from interruption, invited him to sit down. Later, in the locked room, he guessed aloud that the visitor must be one of Pinkerton's detectives.
questions.explanation: The text describes the manager's anxious look, his belief that a terrible secret was about to be revealed, and his dramatic locking of the door - all reactions to the word 'alone'.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 4. Why did the manager look relieved when he knew the purpose of the author's visit?
questions.answer: The manager looked relieved because the visitor turned out to be neither a detective nor a criminal, but an ordinary customer who had come only to open an account and deposit money. His fear that some serious or dangerous matter was about to be disclosed disappeared. In fact he was so pleased that he convinced himself the visitor was 'a very rich man, perhaps a son of Baron Roth's child', and he treated him with sudden respect.
questions.explanation: The text says the manager 'looked relieved but still serious; he felt sure now that I was a very rich man' - relief at the harmless purpose plus satisfaction at gaining a wealthy client.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 5. What is the equivalent of fifty American dollars in Pakistani currency?
questions.answer: Fifty American dollars are equivalent to roughly fourteen thousand Pakistani rupees at an exchange rate of about Rs. 280 to a dollar (50 x 280 = Rs. 14,000). The exact figure changes every day with the interbank rate, so the current rate on the day of answering should be used; for example at Rs. 275 the amount is Rs. 13,750, and at Rs. 285 it is Rs. 14,250.
questions.explanation: This is a real-world conversion question, not one answered by the text. The answer gives the method (50 x the current dollar-rupee rate) and a figure based on the approximate 2025-26 rate of about Rs. 280 per dollar.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 6. What mistake did the author make when he wrote the cheque?
questions.answer: He intended to draw only six dollars for present use, but in his nervous confusion he wrote 'fifty-six dollars' on the cheque instead of 'six'. When the clerk asked in surprise, 'What! Are you drawing it all out again?', he was too upset to explain his error; he lost his nerve, pretended it was deliberate, and said 'Yes, the whole thing' - so he withdrew the entire amount he had just deposited.
questions.explanation: The text states, 'I realized that I had written fifty-six dollars instead of six. I was too upset to reason now', and his refusal to explain turns a slip of the pen into a withdrawal of the whole deposit.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 7. Explain the meaning of the clerk's question, 'How will you have it?'
questions.answer: The clerk is asking in what form or denominations the writer wants his money - that is, which currency notes should be counted out to him. The writer does not understand at first ('What?'), and when he does, he answers 'in fifty-dollar notes', after which the clerk gives him a fifty-dollar note and asks how he wants the remaining six, which the writer asks for 'in six-dollar notes' - meaning six one-dollar notes.
questions.explanation: The following exchange ('in fifty-dollar notes', 'And the six?') shows that the question concerns the denominations of the notes in which the amount is to be paid.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 8. Why was there a roar of laughter when the author left the bank?
questions.answer: There was a roar of laughter because the clerks had just watched a ridiculous performance. A trembling customer had deposited fifty-six dollars, signed the slip as if he were a millionaire, then immediately written a cheque for the entire amount, refused to explain, insisted on drawing out 'every cent' and asked for the money 'in fifty-dollar notes' and 'in six-dollar notes' before rushing out. To the staff the whole transaction was pointless and absurd, and the nervous, secretive manner in which it was carried out made it irresistibly funny, so the laughter 'went up to the roof of the bank'.
questions.explanation: The comedy is the contrast between the writer's terror and the trivial sum involved; the clerks' laughter follows his hasty exit after drawing out everything he had just paid in.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 9. The author, Stephen Leacock, was a respected university teacher and a highly successful writer. Do you think this is a true story?
questions.answer: It is most probably not literally true. Leacock was a professor of political economy and a famous humorist, and the piece is a comic sketch in which the narrator is exaggerated for effect: his terror of 'everything', his belief that an account-holder must see the manager 'alone', the manager's guess that he is a Pinkerton detective, the locked room, the instant withdrawal of the whole deposit and the final roar of laughter are all too neatly arranged to be a plain record of fact. The small sum of fifty-six dollars contradicting the manager's idea of 'a very rich man' is a further comic invention. What is true is the feeling described - the nervousness of an ordinary person facing unfamiliar bank formalities - which is why readers find the story convincing even while laughing at it.
questions.explanation: The question invites a personal, evidence-based judgement. The answer takes the position that the sketch is fictional in detail but true in feeling, and supports it with the exaggerations and coincidences in the text.

questions.question: Exercise 5. 10. Why is it wiser to keep one's money in a bank than to hoard it in one's home?
questions.answer: Keeping money in a bank is wiser for several reasons. (i) Safety: cash at home can be stolen, burnt or lost, whereas a bank account is protected and, in Pakistan, deposits are also insured up to a limit. (ii) No loss in value: money kept in a sock earns nothing, while a savings account or term deposit earns profit and helps the savings keep pace with inflation. (iii) Convenience and record: cheques, ATM cards, mobile and internet banking make payments and transfers easy, and the bank statement is proof of every transaction. (iv) Protection from one's own weakness: money at home is easily spent, whereas withdrawing from a bank takes a deliberate effort. (v) Legal and official use: salary payments, fees, scholarships and government transactions require a bank account. The narrator of 'My Bank Account' keeps his savings 'in silver dollars in a sock' - safe from the bank's clerks perhaps, but earning nothing and exposed to theft.
questions.explanation: The answer draws the moral contrast implied by the story's ending (savings in a sock) and gives practical reasons that go beyond the text, as the question asks for the reader's own reasoning.

questions.question: Exercise 7. There are many advantages of using Bank. Work in groups, first collect some points on the topic: Advantages of Using Bank. Then, present these opinions in front of the class.
questions.answer:
Points for the presentation - Advantages of Using a Bank
1. Safety of money: cash kept at home can be stolen, lost or destroyed in a fire or flood; a bank keeps it in a secure vault and the deposit is recorded in the bank's books.
2. Profit on savings: a savings or fixed deposit account earns profit/interest, so money grows instead of lying idle.
3. Easy payments: cheques, debit cards, ATM cards and mobile/internet banking let a person pay bills, fees and shopkeepers without carrying large amounts of cash.
4. Record of every transaction: the passbook and statement show when money came in and went out, which helps in budgeting and in settling disputes.
5. Safe money transfer: money can be sent to another city or country in minutes through online transfer or demand draft - impossible with hoarded cash.
6. Access to loans and credit: banks give loans for education, business and housing, and issue credit/debit cards, but only to account holders.
7. Receipt of salary, pension, scholarships and zakat: employers and the government pay through bank accounts, so an account is almost a necessity today.
8. Protection from theft and impulse spending: a thief cannot steal what is in the bank, and money is not spent carelessly because it is not in one's pocket.
9. Utility bills and taxes: bills can be paid by direct debit, autopay or mobile banking, saving time and queues.
10. Financial discipline and documentation: regular deposits encourage the habit of saving and the statement serves as proof of income for visas, admissions and loans.

Presentation outline for the class: greet the audience, state the topic in one sentence, present the points in three groups (safety, growth and convenience), give one real example for each group (for instance, a family whose house was burgled but whose savings were in the bank), then end with the advice to prefer a bank account over hoarding cash at home and invite questions.
questions.explanation: The exercise is a group discussion and oral presentation task; the answer gives the substantive points the group should collect and a structure for presenting them, including a conclusion and an invitation for questions.

questions.question: Exercise 1. Work in pairs and write a letter to the National Book Foundation for provision of English Grammar books for your library. Follow the tips and format provided above. After completing, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
14 August 20XX

The Director,
National Book Foundation,
Islamabad.

Subject: Request for the provision of English Grammar books for our college library

Dear Sir,

I am writing on behalf of the Students' Library Committee of Government Degree College, Latifabad, Hyderabad, to request the provision of English Grammar books for our library.

Our library serves more than twelve hundred students of Classes XI and XII. At present we have only two copies of an old grammar book, and both are in poor condition. As a result, students preparing for the Board examinations in English cannot practise the grammar exercises they are given in class, and many of them have to buy expensive books that they cannot afford. We therefore need about fifty copies of a modern, board-oriented English Grammar and Composition book, together with twenty copies of its workbook, so that whole classes can work from the same text.

We shall be grateful if the Foundation supplies these books under its book-aid scheme or at its concessional rate. Kindly let us know the procedure for placing the order, the price of the titles available, the discount allowed to educational institutions and the mode of payment. Our committee is prepared to deposit the amount as soon as the quotation is received, and we can also arrange for the books to be collected from your regional office in Karachi.

An early reply will be highly appreciated.

Thanking you in anticipation.

Yours faithfully,
Ayesha Khan
Secretary, Students' Library Committee
Government Degree College, Latifabad, Hyderabad
Mobile: 0300-1234567
questions.explanation: The letter follows the block format of the sample on page 80 (date, inside name and address, greeting, opening paragraph, concluding paragraph, closing and signature), uses simple formal language without abbreviations, and asks for the books in the manner suggested by the tips.

questions.question: Exercise 2. You went to a commercial bank for account opening. However, you are not satisfied with their services. Now, work individually and write a letter to the Manager of the bank complaining about the unprofessional behaviour of the staff. Follow the tips and the format provided above.
questions.answer:
5 September 20XX

The Manager,
National Commercial Bank,
Branch Latifabad No. 4,
Hyderabad.

Subject: Complaint about the unprofessional behaviour of the branch staff

Dear Sir,

I opened a savings account (No. 0412-778899) at your branch on 28 August 20XX, and I regret to say that I have been deeply disappointed by the behaviour of the staff.

First, although I arrived at ten in the morning, I had to wait for more than an hour because the clerk at the account-opening counter was busy chatting with a colleague and attending to personal phone calls. Secondly, when my turn came he did not greet me or ask me to sit, and he spoke to me in a rude and dismissive tone when I asked which form I should fill in. I would also be grateful for a written confirmation that my account details have been verified.

I hope you will take prompt action so that other account holders do not face the same treatment.

Thanking you.

Yours sincerely,
Bilal Ahmed
House No. 15, Block C, Latifabad No. 4, Hyderabad

questions.question: Exercise 1. Work in groups of three and practise the following dialogue. You will have to practise the dialogue three times, each time taking the role of one another.
questions.answer:
Model performance of the printed dialogue
The three friends are planning a farewell party for their seniors. Their negotiation runs as follows:

Bashir (proposal): 'I think we should arrange a farewell party for all our seniors.'
Zamir (partial disagreement): 'I agree, but we have so many seniors and we have collected limited amount of money.'
Kashif (reason): every year Class XI arranges a farewell, so it must be done.
Bashir (proposal): invite all the seniors if the menu is kept limited.
Zamir (disagreement + reason): the problem is not only the menu - many guests need a big venue, and that needs a lot of money.
Kashif (reason): a farewell is held in honour of the seniors and for fun, so all of them should be invited.
Bashir (concession): but we must be careful not to spend too much.
Zamir (agreement + proposal): 'You have a strong point here. Let's make a list of all the participants including teachers. Then we can decide how many people to invite and who to invite.'
Kashif (acceptance): 'I think that would be acceptable. Once we know for sure how many people we are inviting, we can then decide about venue and menu.'

Consensus reached: a farewell party will be held; a complete list of invitees, including teachers and all seniors, will be prepared first; only after the number is known will the venue and a limited menu be decided within the money collected.

How to perform it three times: in round one take the role of Bashir (the proposer - use 'I think we should...', 'I would like to propose that...'); in round two take Zamir (the questioner - use 'I agree, but...', 'I'm afraid we have some reservations on that point', 'You have a strong point here'); in round three take Kashif (the reconciler - use 'This is because...', 'One of the key reasons for this is...', 'I think that would be acceptable'). Each time, keep your tone polite, let the other speaker finish, stress the words that carry the argument (all, limited, venue, list) and close the dialogue by summing up the agreement.
questions.explanation: The printed task is a speaking/role-play task, so the answer supplies a model performance: the moves made by each speaker, the consensus the group reaches, and role-specific phrases to use in each of the three rounds.

questions.question: Exercise 2. After you have practised the above dialogue, work in same group of three and develop a dialogue on one of the following topics. You need to come to a consensus and then role play as above. Remember to use phrases given above. Topic 1: Organising a college debate competition (discuss and agree on what will be done, when will the programme be, how long will it be, who will be invited as a chief guest, etc.)
questions.answer:
Kashif: I would like to propose that our class organise an inter-class English debate competition this term.
Bashir: I agree with you on that point - we have not held one for two years - but I am afraid we have some reservations about the time. Our monthly tests begin in three weeks.
Kashif: That is exactly why I am suggesting the last Friday of this month. One of the key reasons for this is that it falls before the tests, so nobody will be busy.
Zamir: Perhaps a better idea would be to keep it on a Saturday morning, because on Friday many students leave after the prayer break.
Bashir: You have a strong point there. A Saturday gives us a full morning and parents can also come.
Kashif: All right, Saturday the 26th, from nine to eleven - about two hours. Now, what exactly will be done?
Zamir: I propose two rounds: a prepared speech round of four minutes for each speaker and a rebuttal round of two minutes. Two speakers from each section, so eight speakers in all.
Bashir: Concerning your proposal, our basic position is that four minutes is too long for eight speakers. Could we make it three minutes and a one-minute rebuttal?
Zamir: I can't quite agree with you on that. Three minutes is hardly enough to develop an argument with evidence.
Kashif: Let us look at the points we agree on: two rounds, two speakers per section. Why not three minutes for the speech and two for the rebuttal? That gives us eight speeches of three minutes and a rebuttal session of about sixteen minutes.
Bashir: I think that would be acceptable, and the whole programme will still finish within two hours.
Zamir: Agreed. What about the motion and the chief guest?
Kashif: I suggest the motion 'Social media has done more harm than good', and for chief guest our Principal, with the Head of the English Department as a second judge.
Bashir: I agree with you on that point. But the Principal may be busy; may I suggest that we invite the retired Professor of English, Mr. Saleem Akhtar, as chief guest, and request the Principal to preside?
Zamir: That sounds better. A retired professor is a neutral judge and will attract a bigger audience.
Kashif: So we are agreed: the competition will be held on Saturday the 26th from 9 to 11 a.m. in the college hall; eight speakers, two from each section; a three-minute speech and a two-minute rebuttal; the motion on social media; Mr. Saleem Akhtar as chief guest and the Principal presiding.
Bashir: I think we have reached an agreement here. I will prepare the notice and the registration sheet.
Zamir: And I will write the invitation letters. This agreement is acceptable to us.
questions.explanation: The dialogue is built entirely from the negotiation phrases on page 82 (proposing, giving reasons, partial disagreement, conceding a strong point, accepting and summing up) and settles every element the topic asks for: what will be done, when, how long, and who the chief guest will be.

questions.question: Exercise 2. Topic 2: Having a college trip (discuss and agree on where will you go, only students or teachers also, how much money will be required and what will be the share on each student, etc.)
questions.answer:
Zamir: I would like to propose a one-day college trip to Keenjhar Lake and the ruins of Makli this month.
Bashir: I agree in principle, but we have to be careful about the cost. Last year's trip was cancelled because the share per student became too high.
Zamir: One of the key reasons for choosing Keenjhar and Makli is that both places are within three hours of Hyderabad, so we do not need to pay for a hotel.
Kashif: I agree with you on that point, and it is educational as well - Makli is a World Heritage site and our history teacher can explain it on the spot.
Bashir: My reservation is about safety. If only students go, parents will not allow it. I propose that three teachers, including at least one female teacher, accompany us.
Zamir: You have a strong point there. I accept that. Let us say forty-five students and three teachers.
Kashif: Then we must work out the money. A fifty-seater bus for the day will cost about thirty thousand rupees; lunch at about two hundred and fifty rupees a head for forty-eight people is twelve thousand; entry tickets at fifty rupees for forty-eight people come to two thousand four hundred; and water and first aid about two thousand. The total is about forty-six thousand four hundred.
Bashir: If we round it to forty-nine thousand five hundred and add a small contingency, and request four thousand five hundred from the college welfare fund, each of the forty-five students will pay one thousand rupees. That is affordable.
Kashif: I think we should also collect the money in advance, by the twentieth, so that the bus can be booked. Those who do not pay by then cannot be counted.
Zamir: Perhaps a better idea would be to allow instalments of five hundred rupees, because some students cannot pay a thousand at once.
Bashir: I can't quite agree with you on that - instalments will make the accounts difficult to maintain in one week. Instead, those who cannot pay in time may apply to the welfare fund for a concession.
Zamir: That is acceptable to me.
Kashif: So, to sum up the main points of our discussion: the trip will be to Keenjhar Lake and Makli on the last Sunday of this month; forty-five students and three teachers, including one female teacher, will go; the total cost is about forty-nine thousand five hundred rupees; the college fund will give four thousand five hundred; each student will pay one thousand rupees by the twentieth; and consent letters from parents are compulsory.
Bashir: I think we have reached an agreement here. I will draft the consent letter tonight.
Zamir: And I will get the bus quotation. This agreement is acceptable to us.
questions.explanation: The dialogue covers each point the topic lists - destination, whether teachers accompany, total cost, per-student share - and shows the arithmetic behind the figures, while using the polite proposal, disagreement, concession and consensus phrases from page 82.

questions.question: Exercise 1. Each of the following sentences has an error in the use of comparative or superlative adjectives. Work individually and identify the error, and write corrected sentences in your notebook.
questions.answer:
1. My bed is more big than my desk. -> My bed is bigger than my desk. (Error: 'more big' doubles the comparison. A one-syllable adjective takes -er, not 'more'.)
2. Zaheer can run fast than me. -> Zaheer can run faster than I can. (Error: 'than' needs a comparative form, so 'fast' must become 'faster'.)
3. You are most generous than my brother. -> You are more generous than my brother. (Error: a superlative ('most generous') cannot be followed by 'than'; a two-syllable adjective with -ous forms its comparative with 'more'.)
4. Of all our luggage, mine is the heavier. -> Of all our luggage, mine is the heaviest. (Error: 'of all' compares one thing with the whole group, so the superlative is required.)
5. The weather during the summer is the most hot than during the winter. -> The weather during the summer is hotter than during the winter. (Errors: 'most hot' is a doubled/wrong comparative-superlative form, and 'than' requires the comparative 'hotter'.)
6. The Earth is closest to the moon than the sun. -> The Earth is closer to the moon than to the sun. (Error: 'than' requires the comparative; 'closest' is superlative. 'to the sun' is repeated after 'than' to avoid an ambiguous comparison.)
7. You should always turn in your work because some points are best than no points. -> You should always turn in your work because some points are better than no points. (Error: 'than' requires the comparative 'better', not the superlative 'best'.)
questions.explanation: The seven sentences illustrate the errors listed on pages 84-85: doubled comparisons, a missing comparative before 'than', a superlative before 'than', a comparative where 'of all' requires a superlative, and a missing second element of comparison.

questions.question: Exercise 2. In the following sentences, some parts have been labelled A, B, C and D. Work in pairs and identify the part that contains an error. If there is no error in any part of the sentence, mark your answer as E. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
1. Part E (No Error) - 'Nadeem and Saleem are comparatively weaker in English as assessed by their teacher.' 'Comparatively' is an adverb of degree modifying the comparative 'weaker'; it is not a doubled comparison like 'more weaker'.
2. Part D - 'of all other friends' -> 'of all friends' (or: 'richer than all other friends'). A superlative ('the richest') already includes the whole group, so 'other' is wrong with 'of all'.
3. Part B - 'more good' -> 'better'. 'Good' has the irregular comparative 'better'; 'more good' is wrong.
4. Part D - 'the most charming of all other areas in Pakistan' -> 'the most charming of all the areas in Pakistan' (or 'more charming than all other areas in Pakistan'). 'Most ... of all other' mixes a superlative with 'other'.
5. Part B - 'the most smartest' -> 'the smartest'. 'Most' and '-est' cannot both be used (doubled superlative).
6. Part A - 'The most happiest man' -> 'The happiest man'. Doubled superlative: 'happy' takes '-est', not 'most'.
7. Part A - 'more intelligent' -> 'the most intelligent' (so the phrase reads 'the most intelligent among her class fellows'). With 'among' (a group of three or more) the superlative is required, and the superlative needs 'the'.
8. Part C - 'than any actor of Pakistani films' -> 'than any other actor of Pakistani films'. Javed Shaikh is himself an actor of Pakistani films, so 'other' is needed; otherwise he is compared with himself.
9. Part A - 'A most hard working student' -> 'The most hard-working student'. The superlative takes the definite article 'the', not 'a'.
10. Part E (No Error) - 'Mr. Najeeb was the tallest among the four brothers and the three sisters.' The superlative 'the tallest' is correct with 'among' plus a group of more than two.
questions.explanation: Each answer names the printed labelled part, quotes the faulty words and gives the correction with the rule applied (pages 84-85: comparative vs superlative, doubling, 'other' after a comparative, the definite article with superlatives). In item 7 the printed labels are A = 'more intelligent', B = 'among', C = 'her class', D = 'fellows'; the error is the comparative in Part A. Item 1 is answered E because 'comparatively weaker' is standard English, though a very strict reading of the 'doubling' rule would make B the intended error.

questions.question: Exercise 3. Work individually and rectify the following sentences with proper use of degrees of adjectives, and write corrected sentences in your notebook.
questions.answer:
i. Shahid's motivation to succeed in this program seems to be great than his sister. -> Shahid's motivation to succeed in this program seems to be greater than that of his sister. (A comparative is needed before 'than', and 'that of' prevents comparing a motivation with a person.)
ii. Either you will make serious study than your sister or risk failing the exam. -> Either you will make a more serious study than your sister or risk failing the exam. (The comparison with 'than' requires the comparative 'more serious'.)
iii. A few students are found the more interested in mathematics in whole class. -> A few students are found the most interested in mathematics in the whole class. (The group is the whole class, so the superlative with 'the' is required, and 'the whole class' needs the article.)
iv. My travelling partner's journey was long than mine. -> My travelling partner's journey was longer than mine. (Comparative 'longer' before 'than'.)
v. My income is little than that of my brother. -> My income is less than that of my brother. (The comparative of 'little' is 'less'.)
vi. Among all my colleagues, Mr. Altaf is the more regular. -> Among all my colleagues, Mr. Altaf is the most regular. (With 'among all' the superlative is needed.)
vii. Karachi is the more populous city in Pakistan. -> Karachi is the most populous city in Pakistan. (Superlative used for one city compared with all cities of the country.)
viii. She is intelligent than her cousin so she has taken many marks. -> She is more intelligent than her cousin, so she has taken many marks. (Comparative 'more intelligent' before 'than'; two-syllable adjective takes 'more'.)
ix. Azizia in Libya is the hot place in the world. -> Azizia in Libya is the hottest place in the world. (Superlative '-est' with 'in the world'.)
x. The Jupiter is the large planet in the solar system. -> Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system. (Superlative 'the largest'; 'the' is not used before the name of a planet.)
questions.explanation: The ten sentences are corrected according to the five error types taught on pages 84-86, with the reason given for each change.

questions.question: Exercise 4. Work in pairs and spot the errors in degree of adjective and rewrite the correct conversation in your notebook. Share your work with your partner after completing the exercise.
questions.answer:
Errors corrected:
1. 'old than all the other phones' -> 'older than all the other phones' (comparative form needed before 'than').
2. 'a latest phone' -> 'the latest phone' (the superlative takes 'the').
3. 'more cheaper than' -> 'cheaper than' (doubled comparative).
4. 'much happiest' -> 'much happier' (comparison with the other phone needs the comparative; 'much' also modifies a comparative).
5. 'a more big memory card' -> 'a bigger memory card' (one-syllable adjective takes '-er', not 'more').
6. 'much nice than mine' -> 'much nicer than mine' (comparative before 'than').
7. 'a lot largest' -> 'a lot larger' (comparing two screens, so the comparative is needed).
8. 'a newer and a good version' -> 'a newer and better version' (parallel comparative; 'good' -> 'better').
9. 'more advanced features among all new smart phones' -> 'the most advanced features among all new smart phones' (superlative with 'among all').
10. 'the most new version' -> 'the newest version' (doubled/wrong superlative; 'new' takes '-est').

Corrected conversation:
Mateen: My phone is working the worst ever! And it's older than all the other phones I see, too. I want the latest phone.
Laiba: Take a look at my phone. It was cheaper than my last phone, and I'm much happier with it. When I'm traveling, I listen to music more often than I do when I'm at home, so I wanted a phone with a bigger memory card.
Mateen: Wow, it's much nicer than mine! The screen is a lot larger, too. I want one like that!
Laiba: Yeah, you need a big screen, because you watch videos on your phone more frequently than I do.
Mateen: I need to check my emails; do you think a newer and better version will help me out?
Laiba: Why not, Mateen. Since it has the most advanced features among all new smart phones in the market, this mobile phone will not only help you to receive and send emails but you can also download different applications.
Mateen: Thank you, Laiba, for helping me out to buy this newest version of the mobile phone.
questions.explanation: All ten numbered errors are corrected and the whole conversation is rewritten, since the task asks for both error-spotting and a corrected conversation.

questions.question: Exercise 5. Work in pairs and make at least five sentences of each model verb according to its nature. After you have completed, share your sentences with your partner.
questions.answer:
CAN (ability / possibility / permission)
1. Sana can speak three languages fluently.
2. Can you solve this algebra problem in five minutes?
3. A trained nurse can dress this wound properly.
4. You can borrow my dictionary for the weekend.
5. Heavy rain can damage the wheat crop.

COULD (past ability / polite request / possibility)
1. My grandfather could walk ten miles when he was young.
2. Could you please pass me the salt?
3. She could read English before she joined school.
4. The road is blocked, so the bus could be late.
5. Could I use your phone for a minute?

MAY (permission / possibility)
1. May I come in, sir?
2. You may leave the class after finishing the test.
3. It may rain in the afternoon, so take an umbrella.
4. The results may be announced next week.
5. May I borrow your notes for one day?

SHOULD (advice / expectation)
1. You should revise your notes every evening.
2. Patients with high blood pressure should avoid salt.
3. You should apologise to your teacher for coming late.
4. The train should reach Karachi by eight o'clock.
5. We should plant trees to keep the air clean.

MUST (strong obligation / certainty)
1. Every citizen must obey the traffic rules.
2. You must submit the assignment before Friday.
3. She must be tired after the long journey.
4. We must not waste water in summer.
5. Candidates must bring their original CNIC to the examination hall.

HAVE TO (external obligation)
1. I have to wear a uniform at my school.
2. She has to catch the seven o'clock bus every morning.
3. We had to wait two hours for the doctor.
4. You have to take off your shoes before entering the prayer room.
5. They will have to renew the licence next month.

MIGHT (possibility)
1. It looks cloudy; it might rain tonight.
2. She might join the debate competition if her exams are over.
3. The shop might be closed on Sunday.
4. He might not agree to our proposal.
5. We might visit our uncle during the holidays.
questions.explanation: The table on page 88 lists seven modal verbs under five uses (ability, permission, advice, obligation, possibility); five sentences are supplied for each verb, and each sentence follows the use named in brackets.

questions.question: Exercise 6. Use appropriate modal verbs from the box given below and fill in the following conversation. An example has been done for you. Two colleagues, Sara and Zoya, are at a lunch meeting. They are waiting for their co-worker, Noor, who is late.
questions.answer:
1. 'No, she may be on her way,' replies Sara. (possibility)
2. 'Yes, she said she left the office 30 minutes ago,' says Zoya. 'She must be about to arrive.' (strong deduction)
3. 'Traffic could be bad during this hour of time, because it usually doesn't take too long to reach here,' Sara says. (weak possibility)
4. 'She must feel bad about being late since I know her so well,' Sara says. (confident deduction from knowing her)
5. 'Well, that's alright! We shouldn't be impatient, don't you think?' Zoya smiles. (advice / disapproval)
6. 'Remember her rule: the one who is late must buy lunch!' (obligation fixed by Noor's own rule)
7. 'What should we order?' asks Noor. (asking for advice)
8. 'I think we should take some light meals since we all are on diet,' says Zoya. (advice / suggestion)
9. 'Could we order a large serving of salad with steamed chicken?' asks Noor. (polite proposal / request for permission)
10. 'But I would rather prefer to take a bowl of humus since its very healthy and scrumptious,' adds Zoya. (preference)
11. 'Well, girls, we mustn't waste time, now it's already late...' yells Sara. (prohibition / necessity not to)
12. '...we should place an order,' yells Sara. (advice / what is right to do)

Completed opening line as given: 'We must wait for Noor before we start,' says Zoya.
All the box words are used: may, must, shouldn't, would, should, could, mustn't.
questions.explanation: Each blank is filled from the given box (may, must, shouldn't, would, should, could, mustn't) according to the meaning required by the speaker's line: possibility (may, could), deduction (must), advice (should, shouldn't), preference (would), and prohibition (mustn't).

questions.question: Exercise 7. Insert proper modal verbs in the following blanks.
questions.answer:
1. When Sara was five, she could read and write. (past ability)
2. I need not get up early today, because it is Sunday. (absence of obligation; 'don't have to' is also correct)
3. Birds can fly but lions cannot. (ability / inability; 'can't' is also correct)
4. This bag is too heavy for you. Shall I help you? (offer; 'May I help you?' or 'Can I help you?' are also acceptable)
5. I have to wear school uniform at my school. (obligation imposed by the school's rule)
6. You must not smoke here. It is forbidden. (prohibition)
7. Could you turn on the lights, please? (polite request; 'Would' or 'Will' are also correct)
8. I should help my mother with the housework. She is tired. (advice / moral duty)
9. If you go to bed late, you may be late for the school. (possibility; 'might' or 'will' are also correct)
10. You must do your homework if you want to go out. (obligation laid down as a condition)
questions.explanation: Each blank is filled with the modal that matches the meaning of its sentence (ability, absence of obligation, offer, obligation, prohibition, polite request, advice and possibility); acceptable alternatives are given in brackets.

questions.question: Think of an event occurred in your life that has positively impacted you and share it with the class.
questions.answer: One event that changed the way I work happened in Class IX. I had prepared for a physics test by memorising solved examples, and I failed it with 28 marks out of 75. Instead of hiding the paper I took it to my teacher and asked her where I had gone wrong. She made me solve two problems on the board every day for a month and explain every step aloud to the class. The first week was humiliating; by the fourth week it was easy. In the annual examination I scored 68. What stayed with me was not the marks but the discovery that I learn best when I have to explain a thing to somebody else. Since then I have used the same method for mathematics and chemistry, and I have begun helping two younger children in my street with their science homework. The failure itself was small; the habit it gave me has shaped three years of my studies.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response task. The model answer is a short first-person narrative of one specific event and states clearly what changed in the speaker's attitude or habits, which is what the task asks students to share with the class.

questions.question: According to you, what is required to succeed in the life?
questions.answer: Nothing succeeds without a mixture of a clear aim, steady effort and the willingness to fail and try again. The book puts 'To succeed in life' at the centre of six hexagons, and if I had to fill those hexagons I would write: a definite goal, because effort without direction is only noise; hard work and discipline, because talent without practice rarely lasts; self-belief, because a person who does not trust his own judgement gives up at the first criticism; knowledge and skill, because good intentions cannot replace competence; health and patience, because success is a long race and not a sprint; and honesty towards the people who help us, because nobody rises alone. Luck may open a door, but these qualities decide whether we can walk through it and stay in the room. The reading text that follows makes the same point in its own way: the power that is in a person 'is new in nature' and only he can discover it by trying.
questions.explanation: Open-ended opinion task linked to the hexagon diagram 'To succeed in life'. The answer fills the six hexagons with named qualities and gives a reason for each, so it can be spoken aloud as the pre-reading discussion the teacher's note asks for.

questions.question: Work in pairs. Find at least ten new words from the text and write their meaning contextually. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
No. | Word | Contextual meaning
1 | latent | existing but not yet expressed or acted upon; here the belief a man holds silently in his heart before he dares to speak it ('Speak your latent conviction')
2 | conviction | a firmly held belief; the thing a person is convinced is true, as opposed to a mere opinion
3 | lustre | shine, brilliance, fame; the inner 'ray of light' is said to matter more than the lustre of the spheres of bards and sages
4 | alienated | separated from oneself, no longer felt as one's own; our rejected thoughts return to us as something distant and majestic
5 | arduous | needing great effort, difficult; the rule 'what I must do is all that concerns me' is equally arduous in practical and in intellectual life
6 | meanness | pettiness, smallness of mind or character; the opposite pole to greatness in the phrase 'the whole distinction between greatness and meanness'
7 | aboriginal | original, native, belonging to the earliest natural condition; the 'aboriginal strength' the civilized man has lost
8 | barbarous | uncivilized, savage, crude; one of the passing conditions of society ('it is barbarous, it is civilized')
9 | solstice | either of the two times of the year when the sun is at its greatest distance from the equator, giving the longest and shortest days; the civilized man never observes it
10 | almanac | a book or table of dates, astronomical data and forecasts for the year; the civilized man owns one and therefore never learns to read the sky
11 | recedes | moves back, falls away; society 'recedes as fast on one side as it gains on the other'
questions.explanation: Open-ended vocabulary exercise; the table gives ten words (plus one) actually taken from the excerpt with meanings that fit the sentence in which each occurs, not dictionary meanings in the abstract.

questions.question: Work individually and write the antonyms of the following words. After completing, share your work with your class fellows.
questions.answer:
No. | Word | Antonym
1 | arduous | easy (also: effortless, simple)
2 | Barbarous | civilized (also: refined)
3 | betray | conceal (also: hide, keep secret; the text uses 'betraying their perception' in the sense of 'revealing')
4 | solitude | company (also: companionship, society, togetherness)
5 | noble | base (also: mean, ignoble, low)
6 | Aboriginal | foreign (also: imported, alien, introduced)
7 | civilized | barbarous (also: uncivilized, savage)
8 | Temporary | permanent (also: lasting, enduring)
9 | Ignorance | knowledge (also: wisdom, awareness)
10 | Recedes | advances (also: proceeds, moves forward)
questions.explanation: Vocabulary exercise. Each antonym is the true opposite of the word as it is used in the excerpt, e.g. 'recedes' is opposed by 'advances' because society is said to recede on one side as it gains on the other.

questions.question: In every work of genius, we recognize our own rejected ______.
questions.answer: (b) thoughts - 'In every work of genius, we recognize our own rejected thoughts; they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty.'
questions.explanation: The sentence is quoted almost word for word from the first paragraph of the excerpt, where the writer says that in a work of genius we recognise 'our own rejected thoughts'. 'Ideas', 'concepts' and 'motives' are plausible synonyms but are not the word printed in the text.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) ideas   (b) thoughts   (c) concepts   (d) motives

questions.question: According to the author, envy is ______.
questions.answer: (d) ignorance - 'he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that imitation is suicide'.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names the two faults separately: envy is ignorance and imitation is suicide. Option (c) is the trap, because 'suicide' is the word attached to imitation, not to envy.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) bliss   (b) evil   (c) suicide   (d) ignorance

questions.question: Insist on yourself; never ______.
questions.answer: (a) imitate - the paragraph begins 'Insist on yourself; never imitate.'
questions.explanation: Direct quotation from the paragraph that opens 'Insist on yourself; never imitate.' The other options look and sound similar but are different verbs with no support in the text. Note that the printed page has (c) circled, which is wrong; the word in the text is 'imitate', so (a) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) imitate   (b) indicate   (c) initiate   (d) imply

questions.question: According to the author, it is ______ in the world to live after the world's opinion.
questions.answer: (c) easy - 'It is easy in the world to live after the world's opinion; it is easy in solitude to live after our own; but the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude.'
questions.explanation: The text contrasts two easy things (following the world's opinion, and following one's own in solitude) with the one difficult thing: keeping one's independence in the middle of the crowd. So the blank needs 'easy', not 'difficult'.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) important   (b) unimportant   (c) easy   (d) difficult

questions.question: Society undergoes ______ changes.
questions.answer: (b) continual - 'It undergoes continual changes; it is barbarous, it is civilized, it is religious, it is rich, it is scientific; but this change is not for better.'
questions.explanation: The printed word is 'continual' (repeated, going on again and again). 'Continuous' would mean going on without any pause at all, which is not what the text says or means.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) continuous   (b) continual   (c) collective   (d) creative

questions.question: Every great man is ______.
questions.answer: (b) unique - 'Every great man is a unique. Shakespeare will never be made by the study of Shakespeare.'
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the list of masters who could not have been taught (Shakespeare, Franklin, Washington, Bacon, Newton) and states that every great man is 'a unique', i.e. one of a kind. The printed page numbers this item twice ('6. 6.'); the duplicate numeral is a printing slip and does not affect the question or the answer.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) simple   (b) unique   (c) rare   (d) common

questions.question: Society acquires new arts, and loses old ______.
questions.answer: (c) instincts - 'Society acquires new arts, and loses old instincts.'
questions.explanation: Direct quotation from the paragraph on society. The word is 'instincts', which supports the argument that the civilized man has gained tools but lost natural strength and skill.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) ways   (b) methods   (c) instincts   (d) approaches

questions.question: Civilized man has lost his ______ strength.
questions.answer: (a) aboriginal - 'compare the health of the two men, and you shall see that the civilized man has lost his aboriginal strength.'
questions.explanation: The text uses the word 'aboriginal' (native, belonging to the earliest condition) in the comparison between the naked savage and the well-clad civilized man. 'Original' is close in meaning, which is why it is offered as a distractor, but it is not the printed word.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) aboriginal   (b) original   (c) real   (d) physical

questions.question: The civilized man has lost the use of his feet because he has built ______.
questions.answer: (b) coach - 'The civilized man has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet.'
questions.explanation: The sentence is the opening of the last paragraph. 'Crutches' appears in the very next sentence, but the man is supported on crutches because he has lost muscle, not because he built them; the car is a modern equivalent and is not in the text.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) car   (b) coach   (c) crutches   (d) castle

questions.question: A solstice is a ______.
questions.answer: (b) position of sun - a solstice is the point in the year at which the sun reaches its greatest distance north or south of the equator, giving the longest and shortest days; the text pairs it with the equinox, which is also a position of the sun: 'The solstice he does not observe; the equinox he knows as little.'
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the civilized man's watch and almanac with his ignorance of the sun's positions in the sky; the solstice and equinox are the two solar markers he no longer observes. Option (d) 'period of year' describes the effect of a solstice rather than what the sentence is contrasting, so (b) is the intended answer.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) position of moon   (b) position of sun   (c) time of the day   (d) period of year

questions.question: Work individually. Read the text again and mark (✓) for true, and (X) for false against each statement given below.
questions.answer:
No. | Statement | Answer
1 | In Self-Reliance, he urges people to trust themselves. | ✓ True - the essay opens with trust in one's own thought ('to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men') and repeats 'Trust thyself'.
2 | According to the author, the greatest obstacle to trust yourself is society. | ✓ True - the difficulty comes from other people: 'you will always find those who think they know what is your duty better than you know it', and the impression must be kept 'when the whole cry of voices is on the other side'.
3 | The author exhorts human beings to strive for absolute consistency. | X False - the excerpt nowhere asks for absolute consistency; it asks us to 'abide by our spontaneous impression' and to 'obey your heart'. Emerson's fuller essay in fact calls 'a foolish consistency' the hobgoblin of little minds.
4 | We should abide by our own thoughts and opinions. | ✓ True - 'They teach us to abide by our spontaneous impression with good-humoured inflexibility' and 'Abide in the simple and noble regions of thy life, obey your heart'.
5 | Great man always remains in solitude for perfection. | X False - the great man is not the man who lives alone: 'the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude'.
6 | Society always undergoes constant changes from better to worse and vice versa. | X False - the changes are continual, but the text denies that they are improvement: 'but this change is not for better. For everything that is given, something is taken.'
7 | Every man is responsible to make for himself and his own. | ✓ True - 'he must take himself for better, for worse, as his portion'; 'Do that which is assigned to you'; 'Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.'
questions.explanation: Table exercise; every printed statement is answered with a tick or cross and the words from the excerpt that decide it. Statements 3, 5 and 6 are the traps: each contains a partly true phrase ('changes', 'solitude', 'consistency') that the text qualifies or reverses.

questions.question: In 'Self-Reliance' Ralph Waldo Emerson distinguishes between internal and external causes of behaviour. Work in groups. Read the text again and re-write the two internal causes and two external causes of behaviour and note these behaviours in your notebook. Compare the written responses with another group.
questions.answer:
No. | Type of cause | Cause named in the text | Behaviour it produces (with the words of the text)
1 | Internal | A man's own thought and private conviction - 'To believe your own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men' | Originality and self-trust: he speaks his 'latent conviction', trusts his 'spontaneous impression' even when 'the whole cry of voices is on the other side', and does his own work with his whole heart.
2 | Internal | The power seated in the heart - 'the absolutely trustworthy was seated at their heart, working through their hands, predominating in all their being'; 'The power which resides in him is new in nature' | Reliance on inner judgement: he tries what he alone can do ('nor does he know until he has tried'), obeys his heart, and is 'relieved and happy' when he has done his best.
3 | External | The opinion of the world and the voice of the crowd - 'It is easy in the world to live after the world's opinion'; 'the whole cry of voices'; those 'who think they know what is your duty better than you know it' | Conformity and shame: he dismisses his own thought, lives 'after the world's opinion', and is 'forced to take with shame our own opinion from another'.
4 | External | Imitation of other men's gifts and dependence on society's instruments - 'Insist on yourself; never imitate'; the coach, the watch, the almanac, the note-book | Borrowed behaviour: he holds 'the borrowed talent of another' in 'temporary and incomplete possession', and though he has built a coach he 'has lost the use of his feet', and his note-books 'impair his memory'.
questions.explanation: The excerpt opposes what comes from inside a person (his own thought, the power in his heart) to what comes from outside him (public opinion and imitation, together with the tools society supplies). The behaviours named in the last column are all phrased in Emerson's own words so that the group work can be checked against the text.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 1. What makes a man great according to the author?
questions.answer: For Emerson greatness is not rank, wealth or learned reputation but fidelity to one's own thought. The essay opens with the claim that 'to believe your own thought... that is genius', and it ends the argument with the sentence 'the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude'. A great man therefore does two things: he refuses to live 'after the world's opinion', and he does the particular work that is given to him with his whole heart - 'Do that which is assigned to you, and you cannot hope too much or dare too much.' Because 'every great man is a unique', he cannot be produced by copying another; Shakespeare 'will never be made by the study of Shakespeare'. Greatness, in short, is self-trust put into action, and the distinction between greatness and meanness is exactly the distinction between doing what I must do and doing what people think.
questions.explanation: Comprehension answer built from three places in the text: the definition of genius in the first paragraph, the sentence about the great man in the crowd, and the closing paragraph on doing what is assigned to you.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 2. Why is self-reliance important for one's development?
questions.answer: Self-reliance is important because the power a person has is his own and cannot be supplied by anybody else: 'The power which resides in him is new in nature, and none but he knows what he can do, nor does he know until he has tried.' Unless a person relies on himself he never tests that power, and so he never discovers what he is capable of. Whatever he borrows remains second-hand - 'the borrowed talent of another, you have only temporary and incomplete possession' - and imitation is called 'suicide' because it kills the original self before it can grow. Self-reliance is also the condition of good work and of peace of mind: 'A man is relieved and happy when he has put his heart into his work and done his best; but what he has said or done otherwise, shall give him no peace.' Development, then, means cultivating one's own gift 'with the full force of a whole life's cultivation' rather than living on another man's talent.
questions.explanation: The answer collects the sentences in paragraphs two, three and five that explain why the individual must depend on his own power; the borrowed-talent sentence supplies the contrast.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 3. What is mark of genius according to the author?
questions.answer: The mark of genius, says the author in his very first sentence, is 'to believe your own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men'. A man of genius trusts the 'ray of light which flashes across his mind from within' more than 'the lustre of the spheres of bards and sages', and he speaks his 'latent conviction' instead of suppressing it, because 'always the inmost becomes the outmost'. The proof of such genius is that other people recognise themselves in it: 'In every work of genius, we recognize our own rejected thoughts; they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty.' In other words, genius is not extraordinary cleverness imported from outside but the courage to say aloud what everyone else has felt and timidly thrown away.
questions.explanation: Answer drawn from the opening paragraph, which defines genius directly and then describes how a work of genius affects its readers.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 4. What happens when a person doesn't value one's own qualities?
questions.answer: When a person does not value what is his own, he throws away his best thoughts before they can become anything: 'Yet he dismisses without notice his thought, because it is his.' The consequence is twofold. First, he loses the credit for his own insight - 'tomorrow a stranger will say with masterly good sense precisely what we have thought and felt all the time, and we shall be forced to take with shame our own opinion from another.' Second, he loses his peace of mind, for 'what he has said or done otherwise, shall give him no peace.' Having rejected his own gift, he can only live on borrowed talent, which is 'temporary and incomplete possession', and he ends by measuring himself by other people's opinions instead of his own.
questions.explanation: The question is answered from the end of paragraph one (the dismissal of one's own thought and the stranger who says it later) and from paragraph two (the man who has not done his best has no peace).

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 5. Why does the author emphasize on developing one's own individuality?
questions.answer: The author insists on individuality because each person is given a particular plot of ground to cultivate and a particular power to use: 'nothing of substance can come to him but through his toil bestowed on that plot of ground which is given to him to till'. That power 'is new in nature' and nobody else can know or exercise it for him. If he does not develop it, he can only borrow, and a borrowed gift is held in 'temporary and incomplete possession'. Emerson proves the point with the example of the greatest men: no master could have taught Shakespeare, Franklin, Washington, Bacon or Newton, because 'every great man is a unique' and 'Shakespeare will never be made by the study of Shakespeare'. Individuality is therefore not vanity; it is the only route by which a person can 'reproduce your own creative world again' and add something to the world that did not exist before.
questions.explanation: The answer combines the 'plot of ground' image of paragraph two with the argument against imitation in paragraph five, where the Shakespeare example is given.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 6. How can a person be happy according to the author?
questions.answer: According to the author happiness is not something that is given from outside; it follows from work done with one's whole heart and from confidence in oneself. 'A man is relieved and happy when he has put his heart into his work and done his best', whereas anything done half-heartedly 'shall give him no peace'. The last two lines of the excerpt make the same point in a stronger form: 'Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.' So a person is happy when he stops measuring himself by other people's approval, trusts his own thought, does the work assigned to him and lives by his principles. Since 'envy is ignorance' and 'imitation is suicide', comparing oneself with others and copying them are the surest ways to remain unhappy.
questions.explanation: The answer uses the explicit statement about happiness in paragraph two and the closing couplet about peace, and links them to the essay's rejection of envy and imitation.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 7. "What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think." Do you agree to this statement? Give reasons for your agreement or disagreement.
questions.answer: I agree with the first half of the statement and accept the second half only with a qualification. Emerson is right that a person must finally decide what his duty is: if he waits for public approval before doing what he believes to be right, he will never act at all, because 'you will always find those who think they know what is your duty better than you know it'. History is full of people who were mocked and later proved right, and the student who chooses a subject or a career only to please relatives often ends up miserable. But 'not what the people think' cannot mean that other people's opinions are worthless. Parents and teachers often see our faults more clearly than we do, and a person who never listens becomes arrogant rather than independent. The balanced reading, I think, is the one the text itself supplies: the great man keeps 'the independence of solitude' in the midst of the crowd. He listens to the crowd and then decides for himself, and he is answerable for the consequences of that decision.
questions.explanation: Open-ended evaluative question. The model answer agrees with the text's core claim, gives reasons from the passage, and adds a reasoned qualification, which is what the task (agree or disagree with reasons) demands.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 8. What kind of changes does a society undergo according to the author?
questions.answer: According to the author society undergoes 'continual changes': 'it is barbarous, it is civilized, it is religious, it is rich, it is scientific'. But he denies that these changes are progress - 'this change is not for better' - because society 'recedes as fast on one side as it gains on the other'. The rule is exchange rather than improvement: 'For everything that is given, something is taken. Society acquires new arts, and loses old instincts.' His illustration is the civilized man with his watch, pencil and bill of exchange beside the naked savage with his club and spear: the civilized man has gained comfort and information but 'has lost his aboriginal strength'. He has built a coach and lost the use of his feet, owns an almanac and cannot read a star, keeps note-books and damages his memory. Social change, then, is a trade-off in which new skills are paid for by old capacities.
questions.explanation: The answer follows the paragraph beginning 'Society never advances' and the following paragraph on the coach and the watch, quoting the phrases that define the direction of change.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 9. How do you relate the message of essay to your life?
questions.answer: The message of the essay reaches me most sharply in the classroom. I have often known the answer to a teacher's question and said nothing because the clever boys in the front row were silent; a minute later one of them said the same thing and was praised for it. That is exactly Emerson's 'tomorrow a stranger will say with masterly good sense precisely what we have thought and felt all the time, and we shall be forced to take with shame our own opinion from another.' The essay also warns me about imitation in small daily matters: choosing a field of study because a cousin chose it, copying a friend's notes instead of making my own, dressing and speaking like a group so as not to stand out. What I take from the text is not a command to ignore advice but a rule for my own work: prepare my own answers, form my own opinion before a discussion, and judge myself by whether I have done my best rather than by applause. That is the 'independence of solitude' I can practise in the middle of my class.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the answer connects specific sentences of the essay to concrete school experiences, as the 'respond to the text' objective of the unit requires.

questions.question: Read the text and answer the following questions. 10. Write a brief summary of the arguments presented in the text?
questions.answer: Emerson argues that truth begins in the individual. To believe one's own thought, and to trust that what is true in one's private heart is true for all men, is genius; the inmost always becomes the outmost. A man therefore should attend to the ray of light that flashes across his mind rather than to the brilliance of established writers and thinkers, and should not dismiss a thought merely because it is his own, for in every work of genius we recognise our own rejected thoughts. Envy, he says, is ignorance and imitation is suicide: each person must accept himself as his portion and cultivate the plot of ground given to him, since his power is new in nature and only he can discover it by trying. Doing his best brings relief and happiness; doing otherwise brings no peace. Trusting himself, a man should do what he must do rather than what people think, for it is easy to follow the world's opinion and easy to follow one's own in solitude, but the great man keeps the independence of solitude in the midst of the crowd. Insisting on himself and never imitating, he remains unique, as every great man is unique. Society, by contrast, never really advances: it changes continually, acquiring new arts and losing old instincts, gaining the coach and the watch while losing the use of the feet and the knowledge of the stars. The conclusion is that nothing can bring a man peace but himself and the triumph of his principles.
questions.explanation: Summary written in continuous prose, following the order of the excerpt: the definition of genius, the rejection of envy and imitation, self-trust and duty, the uniqueness of great men, the argument about society, and the closing statement about peace.

questions.question: Work in groups. Read the whole text and pick any five ideas that you like the most. Share your work with other groups and check each other's work.
questions.answer:
1. 'To believe your own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men, - that is genius.' I like this because it makes confidence in one's own judgement the beginning of all original work, not a luxury for special people.
2. 'In every work of genius, we recognize our own rejected thoughts.' This explains why a good book or a good speech feels familiar: it says what we already half-knew but were afraid to say.
3. 'Envy is ignorance; imitation is suicide.' A short, hard sentence that names the two habits that waste most young lives - measuring oneself against others and copying them.
4. 'The great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude.' I like the word 'sweetness': independence is not rudeness or showing off, it is a quiet quality that can be kept while living among people.
5. 'The civilized man has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet.' This is the most memorable image in the essay, and it is still true of us with our phones and calculators: every convenience quietly takes away a skill.
questions.explanation: Open-ended selection task. The five ideas are quoted exactly from the excerpt, each followed by a short personal reason, which is what the group work and the sharing of responses require.

questions.question: Look at the following passages. First one is draft passage and the other is edited passage. Now, work in pairs and compare the draft and the edited passage and note down the difference. After you have completed, exchange your work with your partner. (Passage 1: the bats passage)
questions.answer:
No. | Draft passage | Edited passage | Difference noted
1 | did you no | Did you know | 'did' is capitalised at the beginning of a question, and 'no' is corrected to 'know'.
2 | mammals. | mammals? | The full stop is replaced by a question mark, because the sentence asks a question.
3 | we no | We know | A new sentence begins with a capital 'We', and 'no' is corrected to 'know'.
4 | becaus | because | Spelling corrected.
5 | warm blooded | warm-blooded | A hyphen is added in the compound adjective.
