questions.explanation: The descriptions in the printed table are deliberately jumbled, so the row-by-row pairing must not be copied: 'realistic' people work with their hands, 'investigative' with ideas, 'artistic' with creation, 'social' with helping, 'enterprising' with leading, and 'conventional' with organizing and checking details.

questions.question: Exercise 6, step a: Make a list of your career-related interests and values.
questions.answer:
My career-related interests:
- Biology, especially the working of the human body, and chemistry.
- Helping people who are ill or worried; first aid and hospital volunteering.
- Reading about medical research and new treatments.
- Explaining difficult things to classmates in simple words.

My career-related values:
- Service to humanity - being useful to people in pain.
- Respect and trust in the community.
- Intellectual achievement - I enjoy understanding how things work.
- Security - a profession in which hard work and honesty are rewarded.
- Continuous learning - a field in which one never stops studying.
questions.explanation: Open-ended self-assessment task; the model list follows the reading text's advice that interest and values should guide the choice of career.

questions.question: Exercise 6, step b: Write down your natural skills and abilities.
questions.answer:
My natural skills and abilities:
1. Good memory and the ability to learn a large amount of factual material (biology, chemistry, anatomy).
2. Patience and a calm manner - I do not panic when somebody is hurt or crying.
3. Clear communication: I can explain an idea in Urdu or English so that a weak student understands it.
4. Careful observation and attention to small details (I notice changes in a patient's condition or in an experiment).
5. Steady hands and neat work in the biology laboratory.
6. Good time management - I keep a study timetable and follow it.
7. Teamwork: I have worked in group projects and in a first-aid camp at school.
questions.explanation: Open-ended self-assessment; the skills listed are the 'strengths' the text asks students to identify before choosing a career.

questions.question: Exercise 6, step c: Consider your personality type and career-related values.
questions.answer: On the personality types listed in Exercise 5, I am mainly 'Social' (like number 6: I like to work with and help other people) with a strong second element of 'Investigative' (like number 5: I like to work with ideas and problems). I am not strongly 'Enterprising', so a career built only on selling, leading or competing would not suit me, and I am not purely 'Conventional', so a desk job of routine checking would bore me. My leading values are service, respect and intellectual achievement. A career in medicine fits all three: it is social because the doctor works with and for people, investigative because diagnosis is a problem-solving activity, and it satisfies my wish to be of use and to keep learning.
questions.explanation: The answer applies the Exercise 5 personality types and the values listed in step a to the career decision, as the text recommends matching career to personality and values.

questions.question: Exercise 6, step d: Make a preliminary career decision and create a plan of action.
questions.answer:
Preliminary career decision: I have decided to become a doctor (MBBS), and later to specialize in paediatrics.

Plan of action:
1. This year: complete FSc (Pre-Medical) with at least 85 per cent marks, with special attention to Biology and Chemistry.
2. Join a good academy and start MDCAT preparation six months before the test; solve one past paper every week.
3. Take at least four online mock tests to find my weak topics, and revise those topics first.
4. Consult two practising doctors and one medical student about the demands of the profession and about the best colleges.
5. Visit the websites of the medical universities to learn the admission criteria, test pattern and closing merits.
6. Keep a backup plan: if I do not get an MBBS seat, I shall apply for BDS, Doctor of Pharmacy or BS Medical Laboratory Technology, all of which use the same subjects and serve the same value of helping patients.
7. Review this plan after every result and redesign it if necessary, as the text advises.
questions.explanation: Open-ended planning task; the model plan follows the steps of the reading text - interest, skills, personality, realistic back-up and constant review.

questions.question: Look at the advertisement and identify its components.
questions.answer:
No. | Component | How it appears in the advertisement
1 | Job title | The post is announced in bold at the very top of the notice, under the company's name and logo: the advertisement is for the position of 'Head of Operations'.
2 | Job location | The place of posting (the company's head office/city) is stated with the company's name and address in the heading of the notice, above the duties.
3 | Duties and responsibilities | A bulleted block headed 'Duties and Responsibilities' lists what the post-holder will do - planning and monitoring the operations of the organisation, supervising and guiding teams, coordinating with other departments, preparing reports, and reporting to senior management.
4 | Job requirements | A second bulleted block headed 'Qualifications & Skill Requirements' gives the required qualification (a degree, preferably in business/engineering), the number of years of relevant experience, and the managerial, communication and computer skills demanded.
5 | Company and benefits | The employer's name and logo stand at the top of the notice, and the block of requirements ends with the terms offered - salary, allowances and other benefits such as medical cover and a congenial working environment.
6 | Applying instructions | The closing lines tell the candidate how to apply: a detailed CV with a covering letter is to be sent (by post or e-mail) to the Human Resources Manager, with the name of the post written on the envelope, before the given closing date.
questions.explanation: The six components are exactly the six boxes of the structure diagram printed beside the advertisement; because the advertisement itself is a low-resolution scan, the answer identifies each part from its heading and position rather than quoting every line.

questions.explanation: Model letter follows the nine-part structure printed in the book - contact details, heading, greeting, introduction, reason for writing, education and previous experience, what makes the candidate ideal, closing statement and sign-off - and is kept to one page. questions.question: Work in pairs and practice the following dialogues. First, one of you should take the role of the interviewer and the other that of interviewee. Then, reverse the roles and practice again.
questions.answer:
Full dialogue for practice:

Interviewer: Tell me briefly about yourself?
Interviewee: I have spent the last six years developing my skills as a customer service manager for OGDCL, where I have won several performance awards and been promoted twice. I love managing teams and solving customer problems and am looking for a new role that will challenge me.

Interviewer: What are your strengths?
Interviewee: I am highly motivated, enthusiastic and work well in team. I also handle pressure smartly which is the key factor of my achievements.

Interviewer: Why are you interested in this position?
Interviewee: I have always admired your company's products. I was really impressed with the recent interview of your CEO where he shared his vision of collaborative company culture. The job responsibilities also emphasize communication skills and leadership which are of my greatest strengths. I really feel that it is the role and organization in which I could excel.

Interviewer: Why are you leaving your current job?
Interviewee: I have already mentioned that I am zealous and keen to abreast myself. Also, I will also seek various opportunities here to learn and grow.

Interviewer: Why should we hire you?
Interviewee: Honestly, with all my great communication and leadership skills, I will prove myself a benefit and an asset to your reputable company.

While practising, keep the etiquette in mind: sit straight only after being asked, keep eye contact with the speaker, do not interrupt, and speak at a moderate speed. Two of the printed sentences are slightly faulty English ('work well in team', 'keen to abreast myself'); in a real interview say 'work well in a team' and 'keen to keep myself abreast of new developments'.
questions.explanation: Role-play task; the printed dialogue is reproduced in full for practice, with a note on the etiquette points and on the two grammatical slips in the book's text.

questions.question: Situation: You have received a call letter for appearing in the job interview. You need to prepare for it. You have to grab this opportunity. Now, work in pairs and play role as an interviewee and interviewer. You can use some of the interview etiquettes/tips given in the box above.
questions.answer:
Preparation before the interview: two copies of the CV and the call letter in a folder, attested academic documents, a pen and a small notepad, formal dress with polished shoes, trimmed hair and nails, mild fragrance, and the office address checked a day earlier so that I reach fifteen minutes early.

Model role play:

Interviewer: Good morning. Please come in and have a seat.
Interviewee: Good morning, sir. Thank you. (sits only after being asked, keeps the folder on the table)
Interviewer: Tell me a little about yourself.
Interviewee: I am Ayesha Khan, a fresh higher secondary graduate from Government College, Karachi. I secured an A grade in Pre-Engineering and I have completed a short course in MS Excel and data handling. For the last two summers I worked in my uncle's stationery business, where I kept the daily accounts and dealt with customers.
Interviewer: Why do you want to work here?
Interviewee: Your company has a reputation for training young people properly, and the advertisement for management trainee asks for exactly the skills I have been building - accuracy with figures, computer work and confidence with people. I would like to learn the business from the ground up in an organisation like yours.
Interviewer: What is your greatest weakness?
Interviewee: I sometimes spend too long checking a piece of work to make it perfect. I am learning to set a time limit for each task and to ask for help when I need it.
Interviewer: Why should we hire you?
Interviewee: Because I am honest, hard-working and quick to learn, and because I will not treat this as a temporary job. I want to grow with the company.
Interviewer: Do you have any questions for us?
Interviewee: Yes, sir. Could you tell me what training a management trainee receives in the first six months?
Interviewer: Certainly. Thank you for coming.
Interviewee: Thank you very much for your time, sir. (stands, thanks the panel and leaves quietly)
questions.explanation: Role-play task; the answer supplies the preparation checklist and a model interview that uses the etiquette points printed in the table (knock, greet, sit when asked, eye contact, polite answers).

questions.question: Work in pairs. Assign the role of an interviewer and an interviewee and present the mock job interview in front of the class.
questions.answer:
Plan for the class presentation (five minutes, two students):

Stage 1 - Entry: the interviewee knocks, waits for the panel to say 'come in', greets the class panel ('Good morning, sir/madam'), and sits only when asked, keeping the file of documents on the table and both feet on the floor.

Stage 2 - Opening: the interviewer introduces the company and the post ('We are interviewing for the post of management trainee'), then asks the first question.

Stage 3 - Questions and answers (four questions):
Interviewer: Tell us briefly about yourself.
Interviewee: I am Bilal Ahmed, a higher secondary graduate in commerce. I have worked part-time in a bank's customer service counter and I am comfortable with figures, computers and people.
Interviewer: What are your strengths?
Interviewee: I am punctual, accurate and calm under pressure; in the bank I handled forty customers a day without a single complaint.
Interviewer: Where do you see yourself in five years?
Interviewee: Working as a branch operations officer, having completed my B.Com and the bank's internal training.
Interviewer: Why should we hire you?
Interviewee: Because I have already done part of this work, I learn quickly, and I will stay long enough to be useful.

Stage 4 - Closing: the interviewee asks one question about training, thanks the panel, and leaves after being told to do so.

Stage 5 - The class observes and comments on dress, posture, eye contact, speed of speech and honesty of answers.
questions.explanation: Performance task; the answer gives a complete, presentable mock interview with stage directions and the points the class should observe.

questions.question: Tell me a little about yourself.
questions.answer: I am Hamza Raza, and I have just completed my Higher Secondary Certificate in Pre-Engineering from Government College, Karachi, with an A grade. For the last two years I have been teaching mathematics to younger students at a neighbourhood academy, which taught me patience and clear communication. I am good with computers, I enjoy solving problems in a team, and I am now looking for a first proper job in which I can learn the work from the beginning and grow with the organisation.
questions.explanation: Open-ended interview-response task; the model answer keeps to the present-post-education-future pattern recommended for a 'tell me about yourself' reply.

questions.question: What is special about you?
questions.answer: What is special about me is that I finish what I start. When our college quiz team lost its captain a week before the district competition, I took over, made a study plan for the remaining members and we still reached the semi-final. I am also unusually accurate with details: in my part-time job I maintained the sales register for eight months without a single entry error. I would not call myself extraordinary, but I am reliable, and in a workplace reliability is rare enough to be special.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; the answer supports the claim with two concrete examples instead of empty adjectives.

questions.question: Why do you want to work here?
questions.answer: I want to work here for three reasons. First, your company has a name for training its junior staff properly, and as a fresh graduate I need that training more than a big salary. Second, the work of this department matches what I enjoy and what I am good at - records, figures and dealing with people. Third, I have spoken to one of your former employees, and he described a working culture in which people are trusted with responsibility early. That is the kind of place where I would work hard and stay long.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; it links the candidate's needs and skills to specific facts about the organisation, which is what interviewers look for.

questions.question: What interests you about this job?
questions.answer: What interests me most is the variety. The advertisement describes a post in which one day is spent checking reports and the next in coordinating with other departments, so the work will never become a fixed routine. I am also interested in the responsibility for a small team, because I enjoy helping people work well together, and in the chance to deal directly with clients, which is the part of my part-time job I liked best.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; it picks out the duties listed in the job advertisement and connects them to the candidate's own preferences.

questions.question: Why are you leaving your current job?
questions.answer: I am leaving my current job because it has no room left for growth. I joined the academy as a part-time teacher, and in two years I have learnt everything the post offers; there is no chance of training, promotion or new responsibility. I am grateful for the experience, and I am leaving on good terms, but I want a position where I can keep learning and take on bigger duties. I am not running away from a problem; I am moving towards an opportunity.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; it gives a positive reason, avoids criticism of the present employer and ends on the future.

questions.question: What are your strengths?
questions.answer: My main strengths are accuracy, punctuality and calmness. Accuracy, because I check every figure twice - my sales register at the academy was audited without a single mistake. Punctuality, because in two years of teaching I never missed a class, even during examinations. Calmness, because when an angry customer once refused to pay his fee, I listened to him, found that the fault was ours and settled the matter without an argument. I am also a quick learner, and I am comfortable with MS Office and basic accounting.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; each strength is followed by evidence, which is the pattern recommended for this question.

questions.question: What are your goals for the future?
questions.answer: In the short term, my goal is to become fully competent in this post within a year - to handle the daily reports and the client correspondence without supervision. In the medium term, I want to complete a B.Com degree in the evening and take on the responsibility of a small team. In the long term, I hope to become an operations manager who trains young people the way I was trained. My goals are all inside this profession, because I believe in growing where I am planted.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; goals are arranged as short, medium and long term and tied to the employer's organisation.

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.answer: In five years I see myself as a senior member of this department, probably handling a team of four or five people and responsible for the monthly operations report. I also see myself having finished my B.Com and possibly a diploma in management. I would like to have earned the trust of my seniors so that new trainees are given to me to train. I do not see myself in another company, because everything I want to learn is available here.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; it shows ambition that is realistic and inside the organisation, not a plan to leave.

questions.question: Why should we hire you?
questions.answer: You should hire me because I can do the work you have advertised and I will not need to be persuaded to do it. I have the computer skills and the record-keeping experience the post requires, I have already worked with customers, and I am used to finishing tasks on time without being reminded. I am also at the beginning of my career, so I am willing to be trained and I am not looking for a stop-gap job. In short, I will be useful from the first month and I will still be useful in five years.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; it summarises the candidate's fit in three points - skills, attitude and long-term commitment.

questions.question: What is your salary range expectation?
questions.answer: As a fresh graduate my first priority is to learn the work properly, so I am flexible about salary. I know that a trainee in this industry usually starts between twenty-five and thirty-five thousand rupees a month, and I would be comfortable anywhere in that range, depending on the responsibilities and the training you offer. What matters more to me is that the pay should be reviewed on performance after the training period. I am sure we can agree on a figure that is fair to both sides.
questions.explanation: Open-ended response; a range is given instead of a fixed demand, and the answer is left open for negotiation.

questions.question: You have already studied about the job advertisement in this Unit (9.2). Now, imagine you are called for the job interview. Work in pairs. Devise your own questions and responses accordingly and practise them.
questions.answer:
Post applied for: Management Trainee (Operations), Sindh Industrial Services (Pvt.) Ltd.

Q1. What do you know about our company?
A. Your company has been in industrial services for over twenty years and handles operations for several manufacturing units in Sindh. I read on your website that you have recently started a training programme for fresh graduates, and that is the programme I am applying for.

Q2. The advertisement asks for a degree and two years of experience. You have neither. Why should we consider you?
A. I have the equivalent in a different form: I am a fresh graduate with an A grade in Pre-Engineering, I have completed a certificate course in MS Excel and data handling, and I have two summers of paid work in a business where I kept accounts and dealt with customers. What I lack in years I make up in willingness to be trained.

Q3. What do you understand by 'operations' in this company?
A. From the duties listed in your advertisement, operations means making sure that the work of the departments runs on time - planning schedules, checking that materials and reports reach the right people, and solving problems before they become delays.

Q4. How would you handle a colleague who is senior to you but keeps missing deadlines?
A. First I would make sure my own part is not delayed. Then I would speak to him politely and privately, ask whether something is blocking his work, and offer help. If the delay continued, I would inform my supervisor, not as a complaint but as a request for guidance.

Q5. Where do you see yourself after the training period?
A. As a confirmed operations assistant handling my own section of the daily reporting, and preparing for a supervisory role within three to four years.

Q6. Do you have any questions for us?
A. Yes - what does the six-month training cover, and will I be rotated through other departments?

Practice these answers aloud with your partner, taking turns as interviewer and candidate, and remember the etiquette: knock, greet, sit when asked, keep eye contact and thank the panel at the end.
questions.explanation: Open-ended role-play task; the answer first turns the 9.2 advertisement into interview material (company, requirements, duties) and then supplies a full model question-and-answer set for practice.

questions.question: The following paragraph is on 'Unsustainable Environment'. Work in group of three. Each group is required to write a paragraph proposing solutions to this issue. After completing, exchange your paragraphs to the other group.
questions.answer: The paragraph tells us that fish is one of Pakistan's favourite foods and that the average person eats about 16 kg of fish a year, but that many kinds of fish in the river are disappearing because people and poachers catch too many of them; environmentalists say that 90 per cent of the biggest fish are already gone from the River Indus, and that if we catch too many big fish now there will be no baby fish in the future. The present way of fishing is therefore not sustainable. If the government enforced a closed season of two or three months every year, the fish would get time to breed. If the fishing nets had a wider mesh, only grown-up fish would be caught and the young ones would slip back into the water. If the wildlife department deployed more guards and speedboats, the poachers would not be able to use explosives and illegal nets. If the fishing communities were given a share of the income from a well-managed fishery, they would themselves report the poachers. If restaurants and buyers refused to buy undersized fish, the market for illegal catch would disappear. If we acted on all these suggestions now, the River Indus would again be full of fish; if we waited another ten years, we would lose this gift for ever.
questions.explanation: The paragraph follows the printed model: it states the problem in the book's own words and then proposes solutions in conditional Type-II sentences, which is the grammar point of this section.

questions.question: Now, read the paragraphs and identify the type of sentence structure your class fellows have used.
questions.answer: The paragraphs written by my class fellows use conditional sentences of Type-II. Each solution is expressed in an 'if' clause in the simple past tense (often with 'were' for all persons, as in 'If the government were stricter ...') followed by a main clause with would, could or might plus the base verb: 'If the fishing nets had a wider mesh, only grown-up fish would be caught.' The past tense after 'if' does not refer to past time; it signals that the condition is unreal or unlikely at present, and the main clause gives its probable result. A comma separates the 'if' clause from the main clause when the 'if' clause comes first; when the order is reversed, no comma is needed ('The fish would recover if we banned netting in the breeding season').
questions.explanation: The answer names the structure taught on book page 157 and shows how the model paragraph uses it, including the 'were' rule and the comma rule.

questions.question: Identify the situation from the following option in which the responses were used. (a) impossible condition in the past and its impossible result in the past (b) unlikely and hypothetical situation with probable result (c) possible condition with possible result
questions.answer: The correct option is (b): 'unlikely and hypothetical situation with probable result'. The solutions in the paragraphs ('If the government enforced a closed season ... the fish would get time to breed') describe a situation that is not true at present and is only imagined; the past tense after 'if' marks it as unreal, and 'would + verb' gives the probable result. Option (a) would need the past perfect ('If the government had enforced ... the fish would have recovered'), and option (c) would need the present tense with 'will' ('If the government enforces ... the fish will get time').
questions.explanation: Type-II conditionals are defined on book page 157 as structures for unreal situations in the present or future with a probable result; the other two options describe Type-III and Type-I structures.

questions.question: Write short paragraphs on the following topics by following the pattern of conditional type-II structures: If you were chairman of the Union Council of your area....
questions.answer: If I were the chairman of the Union Council of my area, I would begin with the two complaints that every street makes - water and rubbish. If the council kept a proper register of every street and every water connection, the tankers would be sent where they are actually needed instead of where the driver prefers to go. If each household paid a small monthly sanitation charge, we could hire two sweepers for every ward and their attendance would be checked by the ward councillor. If the councillors held an open meeting once a month, the people would see where the money was spent and would trust the council more. If I were the chairman, I would also publish the budget on a notice board in simple Urdu, so that even a shopkeeper with no English could read it. None of this would cost a great deal; it would only require honesty and a little organisation.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is built almost entirely of Type-II conditionals: past-tense 'if' clauses with 'would/could' results, including 'were' with 'I'.

questions.question: Write short paragraphs on the following topics by following the pattern of conditional type-II structures: If you were elected the Prime Minister of Pakistan...
questions.answer: If I were elected the Prime Minister of Pakistan, I would treat education as the first emergency. If every child between five and sixteen were actually in school, the country would gain a whole generation of literate workers within ten years. If the government spent even four per cent of the national income on schools instead of on buildings that remain empty, teachers could be paid properly and trained every year. If the provinces agreed on one curriculum for mathematics and science, a student from Larkana would compete with a student from Lahore on equal terms. If I were the Prime Minister, I would also make it compulsory for every ministry to publish its spending every quarter, because corruption would shrink if the public could see the accounts. These things would not happen in one year; but if a beginning were made honestly, the country would change within a decade.
questions.explanation: Uses Type-II conditionals throughout, with unreal past-tense conditions and 'would/could' results; 'If I were' follows the book's rule for the verb 'to be'.

questions.question: Write short paragraphs on the following topics by following the pattern of conditional type-II structures: If you were the Principal of your college....
questions.answer: If I were the Principal of my college, I would make three small changes before spending a single rupee on new furniture. If the library stayed open until seven in the evening, students who have no quiet room at home would have a place to study. If the timetable kept one period a week free for clubs and sports, the students who are weak in studies would discover something they are good at, and their confidence would improve. If the college opened a counselling office with one trained teacher and one senior student from each class, the boys and girls who are depressed or bullied would find someone to talk to before the problem became serious. If I were the Principal, I would also meet the parents of the weakest twenty students every term, because a college cannot succeed alone. If these things were done, the college would be a happier place, and happy students learn faster.
questions.explanation: Each suggestion is framed as an unreal present condition with a probable result, which is the Type-II pattern; the paragraph also models 'were' after 'if' with singular subjects.

questions.question: Now, work in pairs and use the square brackets where required in the following paragraph. After completing, compare it with your partner.
questions.answer: 'He [Kasoma] was born in 1971. At that time, Namibia[,] a poor country[,] has [sic] many problems. The country was at war [from] 1966 to 1990. Because of the fighting, many indigenous [sic] the Namibians had rifles[,] which caused a problem [of] poaching. During that time, poachers killed many wild animals[,] black rhinos[,] for their horns[,] for [sic] their valuable body parts. To make things even worse[,] around 1980 a terrible drought killed [many] people, livestock, and wildlife. By 1995, there were only [a] few wild animals[,] lions and cheetahs[,] left in the Kunene region in the northwest of the country.'
questions.explanation: Square brackets are used as the book teaches: to supply or correct a word not in the original ([Kasoma], [from], [of], [many], [a]), to mark a grammatical error in the original with [sic] ('has' for 'had', 'indigenous the Namibians', 'for ... for'), and to add bracketed punctuation that clarifies the quoted sentence. The passage also mixes the present ('has') with the past, which is why [sic] is needed.

questions.question: Work individually. Use a thesaurus to find the synonyms closest to the meaning of the given words below. Use them in your own sentences separately. Follow the example given above.
questions.answer:
Original Word | Synonyms | Contextual Meaning | Use in Sentence
Afford | - | to have enough money or time for something | My father cannot afford a new car this year, so we shall keep using the old one.
- | bear | to be able to meet the cost of something | The family could not bear the cost of treatment in a private hospital.
- | provide | to give or make available (an opportunity, a view) | The new library affords students a quiet place to study.
- | spare | to be able to give up (time, money) for a purpose | I can afford two hours every evening for revision.
Fine | - | of good quality; excellent | She gave a fine performance in the annual speech contest.
- | excellent | extremely good of its kind | The teacher's explanation was excellent, and the whole class understood the topic.
- | delicate | thin, light and easily damaged | The fine thread broke while my mother was stitching the hem.
- | penalty | a sum of money paid as a punishment | The court imposed a fine of five thousand rupees on the shopkeeper for selling expired goods.
questions.explanation: The printed table merges the 'Contextual Meaning' cell for all four rows of each word, so the answer supplies the meaning sense row by row, as the model table for 'Modest' does. 'Fine' also means 'healthy' ('I am fine') and '(of weather) clear and dry', which are further senses a thesaurus would list.

questions.question:
What comes in your mind after reading following quotations given in the bubbles?
(1) "Patience accomplishes its object, while hurry speeds to its ruin." (Saadi)
(2) "Desires make slaves out of kings and patience makes kings out of slaves." (Al-Ghazali)
(3) "Yesterday, I was clever, so I wanted to change the world. Today, I am wise, so I am changing myself." (Rumi)
(4) "Independence is of more value than any gifts; and to receive gifts is to lose it." (Saadi)
(5) "Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder." (Rumi)
questions.answer:
1. Saadi, "Patience accomplishes its object, while hurry speeds to its ruin": The quotation reminds me that worthwhile things take time. Patience is not idleness; it is steady, purposeful effort, while haste makes us take wrong decisions and spoil our own work.

2. Al-Ghazali, "Desires make slaves out of kings and patience makes kings out of slaves": Real freedom lies in controlling our wants. A person ruled by his desires is a slave even if he is rich and powerful, while a patient person who masters himself rises above his circumstances.

3. Rumi, "Yesterday, I was clever, so I wanted to change the world. Today, I am wise, so I am changing myself": Real change begins from within. Instead of blaming others and trying to reform the whole world, a wise person first corrects his own habits and thinking.

4. Saadi, "Independence is of more value than any gifts; and to receive gifts is to lose it": Self-reliance and self-respect are worth more than any favour. One who lives on gifts and charity slowly loses his independence and, with it, his dignity.

5. Rumi, "Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder": Gentle, well-chosen words persuade people and produce results, whereas shouting and anger achieve nothing. This is exactly the lesson of positive work ethics.
questions.explanation: Open-ended pre-reading task (the teacher's note asks each student to write his first impressions individually); the model answer gives a personal response to each bubble and also predicts the unit's themes: patience, self-control, self-reform, independence and gentle speech.

questions.question:
Exercise 1: Work in pairs and find out the words from the text and match with their corresponding descriptions. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
Descriptions: 1. extremely poor and lacking the means to provide for oneself; 2. shaking slightly in a way that once cannot control; 3. bringing or restoring to a state of peace or tranquillity; 4. happening especially as if by fate; 5. stimulating drug that can cause illusions; 6. decorated or beautified, as by ornaments; 7. the quality of having or showing good powers of judgement; 8. becoming involved with or take part in something; 9. skill or expertise in a particular activity or field; 10. repository for grain, especially after it has been threshed.
questions.answer:
No. | Description | Word from the text (with the phrase where it occurs)
1 | extremely poor and lacking the means to provide for oneself | destitute — "The wealthy man once asked his destitute brother" (Text-I)
2 | shaking slightly in a way that once cannot control | tremble — "He began to cry and to tremble" (Text-II)
3 | bringing or restoring to a state of peace or tranquillity | pacified — "he could not be pacified by kindness" (Text-II)
4 | happening especially as if by fate | happened — "there happened to be a wise man" (Text-II), i.e. chanced to be there
5 | stimulating drug that can cause illusions | ecstasy — "the joy and ecstasy I felt" (Text-III); the word also names a stimulant drug that distorts perception, though in the text it means overwhelming joy
6 | decorated or beautified, as by ornaments | adorned — "his girdle is adorned with pearls" (Text-III)
7 | the quality of having or showing good powers of judgement | shrewdness — "deliberation, intelligence and shrewdness" (Text-V)
8 | becoming involved with or take part in something | partake — "to partake of medicine by guess" (Maxim-II)
9 | skill or expertise in a particular activity or field | prowess — "trying to show his prowess off" (Maxim-III)
10 | repository for grain, especially after it has been threshed | granary — "The granary is but grain upon grain" (Maxim-V)
questions.explanation: The words are taken from Texts I-V and the Maxims; each answer quotes the exact phrase so the matching can be checked. Descriptions 4 and 5 are loosely worded in the print: the only text words that fit are 'happened' (chance/fate) and 'ecstasy' (which also has the drug sense). Description 2 contains the printed typo 'once' for 'one'.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Work individually. Read each text and suggest the appropriate title by writing before each text number. After you have completed, share your work with your class fellows. (Text-I, Text-II, Text-III, Text-IV, Text-V)
questions.answer:
NO. | Text No. | Suggested title
1 | Text-I | The Dignity of Labour (Better to Eat Barley Bread than to Serve)
2 | Text-II | Blessings Are Valued Only After They Are Lost (The Slave, the Boat and the Wise Man)
3 | Text-III | Pearls in the Desert (Wealth Is Worthless in the Wilderness)
4 | Text-IV | A Skill Is Permanent Wealth
5 | Text-V | Think Before You Speak (The Art of Listening and Silence)
questions.explanation: Each title is drawn from the central idea of the text: Text-I contrasts free labour with luxurious service, Text-II shows the slave learning the value of the boat by tasting drowning, Text-III shows an Arab dying of thirst beside pearls, Text-IV is the sage's advice on learning a skill, and Text-V is about not speaking until others have finished. Open-ended: other apt titles are acceptable.

questions.question: The second brother was living by________.
questions.answer: The second (poor) brother gained his livelihood "by the effort of his arm", that is, by doing labour.
questions.explanation: Text-I says: "one of them in the service of the sultan and the other gaining his livelihood by the effort of his arm." The second brother therefore lived by manual labour, not by service.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) serving sultan   (b) doing Govt. service   (c) doing labour   (d) selling belts

questions.question: ________ said that it is better to eat barley than to gird with golden belts.
questions.answer: (a) elder brother. In Text-I the wealthy brother, who is in the service of the sultan, asks his destitute brother why he does not serve the sultan; the destitute brother replies that "it is better to eat barley bread and to sit than to gird oneself with a golden belt and to stand in service."
questions.explanation: The printed options do not name the speaker precisely: the text calls him the "destitute brother", the younger of the two, while the wealthy brother is the one already serving the sultan. Among the four printed choices, (a) elder brother is the only one that refers to a brother and to the family in the anecdote; the key is therefore (a), with the looseness of the printed option noted. (d) servant is wrong because the whole sentence is a refusal to become a servant.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) elder brother   (b) sultan   (c) wealthy man   (d) servant

questions.question: "To gird with golden belts", this phrase indicates to live ________.
questions.answer: A golden belt is an ornament of the rich, so the phrase indicates a wealthy, luxurious life — although, as the speaker adds, that luxury is bought with service.
questions.explanation: The phrase itself pictures a rich, ornamented life; the irony of the passage is that this wealthy life is really 'service'. Option (c) describes what the phrase literally indicates.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) hard life   (b) healthy life   (c) wealthy life   (d) slavery life

questions.question: The________ was fearful during travel in the vessel.
questions.answer: The slave who had never been at sea before was the fearful one; he cried and trembled with fright.
questions.explanation: Text-II opens: "A king was in the same boat with a slave who had never before been at sea... He began to cry and to tremble."
questions.optionsRaw: (a) king   (b) sultan   (c) slave   (d) Wiseman

questions.question: The slave was thrown in the sea to ________.
questions.answer: He was thrown into the water so that he might taste the calamity of drowning and thereby learn, from experience, the safety of the boat.
questions.explanation: The wise man explains afterwards that "before he had tasted the calamity of being drowned, he knew not the safety of the boat"; the purpose was a lesson through experience, not to drown or harm him.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) catch fish   (b) gain experience   (c) go drowning   (d) save boat

questions.question: The Arab became happy after ________.
questions.answer: He was filled with joy when he suddenly caught sight of a bag and hoped it held parched grain; his joy turned to bitterness when the bag proved to contain pearls.
questions.explanation: Text-III: "I suddenly caught sight of a bag. I shall never forget the joy and ecstasy I felt on thinking they might be parched grain... when I discovered them to be pearls." The happiness came at finding the bag, not at the pearls.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) finding bag   (b) gaining grain   (c) finding water   (d) seeing pearls

questions.question: The sage gave advice to his student that________.
questions.answer: The sage advised his students to learn a skill, saying "a profession is itself wealth" and a living fountain, while property and gold can be stolen or spent.
questions.explanation: Text-IV: "Learn a skill because property and riches of the world are not to be relied upon... but a profession is a living fountain and permanent wealth... a profession is itself wealth."
questions.optionsRaw: (a) property can be made   (b) silver and gold are necessary   (c) riches can be relied   (d) profession is wealth

questions.question: "Little drops make an ocean." This proverb is appropriately depicted in________.
questions.answer: Maxim-V: "Drop upon drop collected will make a river. Rivers upon rivers collected will make a sea. Little and little together will become much. The granary is but grain upon grain."
questions.explanation: Counting the maxims in their printed order, the 'drop upon drop' maxim is the fifth. It is the only passage that teaches how small amounts gathered together become great.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Text-I   (b) Text-III   (c) Maxim-V   (d) Maxim-III

questions.question: A group of people travelling together is called as________.
questions.answer: A group of travellers journeying together is a caravan, as in Maxim-II: "to go after a caravan without seeing the road".
questions.explanation: The word is used in the text for a body of travellers on a road; 'crew' is the team working a ship and 'sages' are wise men, not travellers.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) sages   (b) caravan   (c) crew   (d) shrewd men

questions.question: ________may be the suitable message of text-II.
questions.answer: The message of Text-II is that we do not value our safety and blessings until we have tasted the calamity they save us from; the noisy, panicking slave becomes quiet and deep once he understands, and the wise man achieves his purpose by calm action rather than loud words.
questions.explanation: The text states its moral explicitly: "before he had tasted the calamity of being drowned, he knew not the safety of the boat; thus also a man does not appreciate the value of immunity from a misfortune, until it has befallen him." None of the four proverbs expresses this exactly, so the item is ambiguous; (d) has been chosen as the closest, because the slave's loud fear turns into quiet, deep understanding and the wise man wins by silence and action. A key naming a different option should be treated with caution.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 'Self-done is well done,'   (b) 'Brave deeds need no show,'   (c) 'Small wit great boast,'   (d) 'Silent water run deep,'

questions.question: Exercise 4: Read the texts and answers the following questions. 1. What did the wealthy man ask the poor brother and what was his reply?
questions.answer: The wealthy brother, who was in the service of the sultan, asked his destitute brother why he did not serve the sultan in order to be delivered from the hardship of labouring. The poor brother replied that he did not wish to be delivered from the baseness of service, because wise men have said that it is better to eat barley bread and sit free than to gird oneself with a golden belt and stand in service. He added that it is better to leaven mortar of quicklime with one's own hand than to hold it on the breast before the Amir; that his precious life was spent in considering what he would eat in summer and wear in winter; and he asked his 'ignoble belly' to be satisfied with one bread rather than bend his back in service.
questions.explanation: The answer is taken directly from Text-I, including the quoted maxim and the four lines of verse that follow it.

questions.question: Why could the slave not be pacified even though he was in the same boat with the king?
questions.answer: Because the slave had never been at sea before and was feeling the discomfort of a vessel for the first time. He was so terrified of drowning that he cried and trembled to such a degree that no kindness could calm him; the king himself became displeased because the matter could not be remedied.
questions.explanation: Text-II says the slave 'had never before been at sea' and 'could not be pacified by kindness', so his fear, not the king's presence, controlled him.

questions.question: What did the wise man do to make the slave realize about the security of boat?
questions.answer: With the king's permission, the wise man ordered the slave to be thrown into the water. The slave swallowed some water, was caught and pulled by the hair to the boat, and clung to the stern with both his hands; then he sat down quietly in a corner. Having tasted the calamity of drowning, he realised the safety of the boat — as the wise man explained, a man does not appreciate immunity from a misfortune until it has befallen him.
questions.explanation: The wise man used a short, controlled experience instead of advice; the change in the slave's behaviour ('became quiet') proves that he had understood the value of the boat.

questions.question: What kind of virtue the sage wanted to teach to his students?
questions.answer: The sage wanted to teach the virtue of learning a skill or profession. He told his students to learn a skill because property and the riches of the world cannot be relied upon — silver and gold may be stolen by a thief or gradually spent by the owner — whereas a profession is 'a living fountain and permanent wealth' that keeps a man honoured wherever he goes.
questions.explanation: Text-IV is a single piece of advice from a sage to his students, and its subject is the worth of a skill rather than of inherited wealth.

questions.question: How does the professional man earn respect according to the sage?
questions.answer: According to the sage, a professional man earns respect because his profession is itself wealth. Even if he loses his riches it does not matter, since his skill remains with him; wherever he goes he enjoys respect and sits in high places, while a man with no skill must glean crumbs and see hardships.
questions.explanation: The sage contrasts the skilled man, whose profession is 'permanent wealth' and a source of honour, with the unskilled man who is reduced to begging crumbs.

questions.question: Who is lucky and unlucky according to the maxim?
questions.answer: According to the maxim, he is lucky 'who has eaten and sowed' — one who has enjoyed the fruit of his earnings and also planted for the future — and he is unlucky 'who has died and not enjoyed', that is, one who piled up wealth but never used or enjoyed it.
questions.explanation: The sage's reply in Maxim-I links luck with using one's wealth and providing for the future, and bad luck with hoarding it until death.

questions.question: Confide not to a friend every secret thou possess. How know you that he will not some time become thy foe? How far do you agree and why?
questions.answer: I agree with the maxim to a large extent. Human relations change with time and circumstances, and a friend of today may become a rival or foe tomorrow; a secret once told cannot be taken back and can be used against us, so complete self-disclosure to anyone is unwise. Prudence therefore suggests confiding only in a few tested and trustworthy people, and even then only what is necessary. However, I would add that suspicion must not become a habit: friendship grows on trust, and a person who never confides in anybody lives isolated and fearful. The maxim teaches balance — be careful in choosing whom to trust, not that friendship is worthless.
questions.explanation: This is an open-ended opinion question; the answer takes a clear stand ('to a large extent'), gives reasons from the maxim and adds a balanced qualification, as the unit's learning outcome requires.

questions.question: Identify the maxim which reflects the value of real thing never fades or shatters.
questions.answer: The maxim is: "Even after falling into mud, a jewel retains its costliness, and dust, although it may rise into the sky, is as contemptible as before. Capacity without education is deplorable and education without capacity is thrown away." It teaches that a real thing (the jewel, i.e. genuine ability or worth) never loses its value however low it falls, while something worthless (dust) gains nothing even if it rises high.
questions.explanation: The jewel-and-dust image is the maxim's statement that true worth is permanent; the second sentence applies it to capacity and education.

questions.question: What kind of suggestion did Imam Ghazali give to the people?
questions.answer: Imam Ghazali advised people never to feel ashamed of asking about things they did not know. Asked how he had attained such a high degree of knowledge, he replied, "by not being ashamed to ask about things I did not know." His suggestion, therefore, is to ask questions frankly and keep learning, because false shame is the enemy of knowledge.
questions.explanation: The advice is quoted in Maxim-II, where Ghazali's answer explains the method by which he gained his learning.

questions.question: Which tale from the above texts do you like the most? And why?
questions.answer: I like Text-II, the tale of the king, the frightened slave and the wise man, the most. It teaches a truth we all forget — that we do not value our safety and blessings until we have tasted the hardship from which they protect us. The way the wise man cures the slave not with long advice but with one brief, controlled experience is also a memorable lesson in practical wisdom and in handling people intelligently.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the answer names one text and justifies the choice with reference to its theme and method.

questions.question: Exercise 5: Work in pairs and write the concise central theme against each text. After you have completed, share your work with your partner. (Text-I, Text-II, Text-III, Text-IV, Text-V)
questions.answer:
No. | Text | Central Theme
1 | Text-I | Honest labour and independence are better than luxurious servitude; a free man's dry bread is worth more than a golden belt worn in service.
2 | Text-II | We do not value our safety and blessings until we have tasted the calamity from which they save us; experience, not instruction, teaches appreciation.
3 | Text-III | In the wilderness of real need, pearls are worthless; it is necessities, not riches, that decide a man's happiness.
4 | Text-IV | A skill or profession is permanent wealth and honour, whereas property, silver and gold can be stolen or spent.
5 | Text-V | A wise man lets others finish and waits for silence before he speaks; words inserted into the words of others only expose one's folly.
questions.explanation: Each theme is a one-sentence condensation of the text it belongs to, as the exercise asks; the teacher's note requires students to reread the texts before writing these.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Write at least two sentences about each of the following topics in your notebook. Then, exchange your notebooks with your classmates to proofread. After you have completed, exchange your notebook with any of your class mates. Read each other's work and give feedback. Make changes in your work if needed. (Write what you say about……) 1. Getting education is ________
questions.answer: Getting education is the most valuable investment a person can make in himself. It is not only about memorising facts for examinations; it trains the mind to think clearly, to question what is wrong and to choose wisely. An educated person can earn an honourable living, support his family and serve society, and he can stand on his own feet with dignity. In short, education gives us both knowledge and the character needed to use it well.
questions.explanation: Open-ended writing task; the model gives more than the required two sentences on the given opening, then the notebook is to be exchanged for peer proofreading.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Write at least two sentences about each of the following topics in your notebook. Then, exchange your notebooks with your classmates to proofread. After you have completed, exchange your notebook with any of your class mates. Read each other's work and give feedback. Make changes in your work if needed. (Write what you say about……) 2. Your reaction to the food in college canteen ________
questions.answer: The food in our college canteen is cheap and quickly served, which suits students who have short breaks between classes. However, I feel the menu is monotonous and too oily — samosas, pakoras and biryani are repeated almost every day, and fresh fruit or salad is hardly available. I would like the canteen to add fruit, boiled eggs and clean drinking water, and to keep its prices within a student's pocket. On the whole the service is friendly, but the food needs to be healthier.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response topic; the answer states a reaction, gives reasons and ends with a suggestion, which also gives material for the peer-feedback stage.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Write at least two sentences about each of the following topics in your notebook. Then, exchange your notebooks with your classmates to proofread. After you have completed, exchange your notebook with any of your class mates. Read each other's work and give feedback. Make changes in your work if needed. (Write what you say about……) 3. Elders must be respected because________
questions.answer: Elders must be respected because they have already walked the road on which we are only starting. Their experience warns us against mistakes, and their advice usually comes from love rather than self-interest. Respecting them keeps families united and passes our values and culture on to the next generation. Moreover, a society that honours its elders teaches its young people to be patient, humble and grateful.
questions.explanation: Open-ended writing task requiring at least two sentences; the answer completes the given opening with several reasons.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Write at least two sentences about each of the following topics in your notebook. Then, exchange your notebooks with your classmates to proofread. After you have completed, exchange your notebook with any of your class mates. Read each other's work and give feedback. Make changes in your work if needed. (Write what you say about……) 4. Early to bed, early to rise, makes man healthy, wealthy and wise________
questions.answer: A person who sleeps early gets complete rest, so he wakes up fresh, with a clear mind and a strong body. Rising early gives him quiet hours for study, prayer or exercise before the noise of the day begins, and this habit makes him punctual and hard-working. Punctuality and steady effort bring success in studies and later in earning a living. Thus the proverb rightly connects good health, prosperity and wisdom with a simple, disciplined daily routine.
questions.explanation: Open-ended writing task; the model explains each of the three claims of the proverb (health, wealth, wisdom) and links them to a routine.

questions.question: Exercise 1: Write at least two sentences about each of the following topics in your notebook. Then, exchange your notebooks with your classmates to proofread. After you have completed, exchange your notebook with any of your class mates. Read each other's work and give feedback. Make changes in your work if needed. (Write what you say about……) 5. Never, never, never give up________
questions.answer: Failure is not the end of a journey; it is only a lesson that tells us what to change. A student who gives up after one bad result loses every chance to improve, whereas one who tries again with a better method usually succeeds. Persistence, patience and a little self-correction can turn defeat into achievement. So we should keep trying until the goal is reached, remembering that most victories come to those who refuse to quit.
questions.explanation: Open-ended writing task requiring at least two sentences; the answer interprets the maxim and supports it with a student's example.

questions.question:
Exercise 2: Work individually and proofread the following letter by following the key tips provided above. After you have completed, compare your proofreading work with your partner.
"with the invention of the personal computer and the Internet, a new age in communications begins. now people could communicate fastest and more easily than ever before. Writing, editing, and storing information became quick and easy. It was no longest necessary to write draft after draft when changes could be made so easily using a word Processor program. Messages, could now be sended in no time to anywhere in the world, without addressing envelopes or licking stamps. Century most early, around the year 1450 a similar revolution in communications had occurred in the Germany. This happened when johannes gutenberg invented the printing press. he was not the first person to use printing to copy a peace of writing. printing was already being invented in the China, where they used clay to print oriental characters. Small items, such as posters and flyers, were already being printed in Europe too, using the woodblock method of printing. Books and other largest works were still being copied by hand. At this time, books were usually produced only in latin, and only the most educated people read them. Gutenbergs printing press was about to change all of this."
questions.answer:
Corrected passage:
With the invention of the personal computer and the Internet, a new age in communications began. Now people could communicate faster and more easily than ever before. Writing, editing, and storing information became quick and easy. It was no longer necessary to write draft after draft when changes could be made so easily using a word processor program. Messages could now be sent in no time to anywhere in the world, without addressing envelopes or licking stamps. Centuries earlier, around the year 1450, a similar revolution in communications had occurred in Germany. This happened when Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press. He was not the first person to use printing to copy a piece of writing. Printing had already been invented in China, where they used clay to print oriental characters. Small items, such as posters and flyers, were already being printed in Europe too, using the woodblock method of printing. Books and other large works were still being copied by hand. At this time, books were usually produced only in Latin, and only the most educated people read them. Gutenberg's printing press was about to change all of this.

Corrections made:
1. "with" → "With" — the first word of a passage must begin with a capital letter.
2. "begins" → "began" — the narrative is in the past tense, so the verb must agree.
3. "now" → "Now" — a new sentence begins after a full stop.
4. "fastest" → "faster" — the comparative is needed with "more easily than ever before".
5. "no longest" → "no longer" — the correct adverbial phrase is "no longer".
6. "word Processor" → "word processor" — a common noun is not capitalised.
7. "Messages, could" → "Messages could" — the comma wrongly separates the subject from its verb.
8. "sended" → "sent" — "send" has the irregular past participle "sent".
9. "Century most early" → "Centuries earlier" — faulty word order; 1450 is centuries before the computer age.
10. "in the Germany" → "in Germany" — no article is used before the name of a country.
11. "johannes gutenberg" → "Johannes Gutenberg" — proper nouns take capital letters.
12. "he" → "He" — capital letter at the beginning of a sentence.
13. "peace of writing" → "piece of writing" — "piece" means a portion; "peace" means calm.
14. "printing was already being invented" → "printing had already been invented" — the past perfect is needed for the earlier event, and "invent" is not used in the progressive.
15. "in the China" → "in China" — no article before a country name.
16. "other largest works" → "other large works" — no comparison is being made, so the positive degree is required.
17. "latin" → "Latin" — names of languages are capitalised.
18. "Gutenbergs" → "Gutenberg's" — the possessive needs an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: The printed task calls the passage a letter, although it has neither salutation nor closing; it has therefore been proofread as a paragraph. The errors are the ones a Class XI student is expected to catch: capitalisation, tense, spelling, articles, word forms and punctuation.

questions.question:
Exercise 1: Look at the following sets of conversations and identify active listener and the one who responds properly.
Set A — Ahmed: "I'm just really stressed about work at the moment." Kinza: "Me too, you wouldn't believe what one of my co-workers did yesterday." Ahmed: "And it's hard for me to pay enough attention to the kids when I have this much on my plate and just want to relax when I get home." Kinza: "Seriously, what she did was ridiculous." Ahmed: "What did she do?"
Set B — Ahmed: "I'm just really stressed about work at the moment." Kinza: "Why is it more stressful than usual right now?" Ahmed: "Well, one of the people in my team is on holiday for a couple of weeks and I keep getting landed with their usual responsibilities." Kinza: "Have you spoken to your boss about that? You shouldn't be doing someone else's job as well as your own."
questions.answer:
Set B shows the active listener and the person who responds properly, and that person is Kinza.
In Set B Kinza pays attention to Ahmed's words, asks a clarifying question ("Why is it more stressful than usual right now?"), lets him finish his explanation, gives feedback that shows she has understood ("you shouldn't be doing someone else's job as well as your own") and offers a practical, respectful suggestion about speaking to his boss.
In Set A Kinza is not an active listener: she turns the talk to her own co-worker ("Me too, you wouldn't believe..."), ignores Ahmed's remark about his children, gives no feedback on his feelings, and finally Ahmed has to ask "What did she do?" — so he ends up listening to her instead. Set A therefore illustrates a failure of attentive listening, while Set B shows the tips in action: pay attention, show that you are listening, provide feedback, defer judgement and respond appropriately.
questions.explanation: The judgement follows the tips table on the same page: Set B uses questioning, feedback and respectful response; Set A hijacks the conversation and gives no feedback to the speaker.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Now, work in groups of two and discuss the following topics keeping above tips in the mind. Turn by turn, each student should make a simple statement about the following. One of the others should respond accurately to each other. 1. Two students discussing each other on pros and cons of the social media.
questions.answer:
Model dialogue (Student A and Student B):
A: I think social media has made our generation the most connected one in history — I can ask a class fellow a question at midnight and get an answer in a minute. But I also lose two hours a day just scrolling, and I often compare my life with other people's edited pictures.
B: I agree with both points. For me the biggest advantage is learning: I follow two teachers who explain physics better than any book, and I found my scholarship announcement on a Facebook group. What worries me is fake news; last month a wrong health tip was forwarded to my family and my grandmother believed it.
A: That is a serious disadvantage — misinformation spreads faster than corrections. And then there is the effect on our privacy: we share our location and photographs without thinking who may see them.
B: So would you say the pros are bigger than the cons?
A: I would say the tool is neutral and the user decides — if we limit our screen time, check facts before forwarding and keep our accounts private, social media is more useful than harmful.
B: That sounds fair, and it matches my own experience.
questions.explanation: Open-ended speaking task. The model shows the required turn-taking, simple statements, accurate responses, a clarifying question and respectful disagreement, following the listening/responding tips of section 10.3.

questions.question: Exercise 2: Now, work in groups of two and discuss the following topics keeping above tips in the mind. Turn by turn, each student should make a simple statement about the following. One of the others should respond accurately to each other. 2. Two friends asking each other's opinion about equality of all before law.
questions.answer:
Model dialogue (Friend A and Friend B):
A: I believe equality before law is the first condition of justice — a minister and a labourer should be judged by the same rule, or else the law loses the respect of ordinary people.
B: I agree in principle, but in practice money and influence change the result. A poor man waits years for a hearing while a rich man's lawyer delays the case until the poor man gives up.
A: That is why I think free legal aid and speedy trials matter as much as the principle itself. Equality on paper means nothing if a poor man cannot afford a lawyer.
B: True. Do you think the law should treat a child and an adult equally?
A: No — equality before law means equal protection, not identical treatment. A child, a sick person or a first offender may need different handling, but that difference must be written in the law and applied to everyone alike.
B: Then we agree: equal protection, no privilege, and special rules only when the law openly provides them.
questions.explanation: Open-ended speaking task; the model dialogue keeps turn-taking, offers opinions with reasons, asks and answers a follow-up question and closes with agreement, as required by the tips in the section.

questions.question:
Exercise 1: Given below is a sample of brief synopsis of a research report. It is written in active voice. Work in pairs and change the following from active voice into passive voice. After you have completed, share your work with your partner.
"In this research, I administered a research survey. I created a compelling sample of 100 scientists. I invited them to participate in the survey by sending them an invite through emails. I received e-mail addresses from different research centres of the country."
questions.answer:
Passive version:
"In this research, a research survey was administered by me. A compelling sample of 100 scientists was created by me. They were invited by me to participate in the survey by being sent an invitation through emails. E-mail addresses were received by me from different research centres of the country."

Notes: (i) the object of each active sentence becomes the subject; (ii) the subject 'I' becomes 'me' after 'by'; (iii) simple past 'administered/created/invited/received' becomes 'was/were + past participle'; (iv) in the third sentence the gerund phrase 'by sending them an invite' is also made passive ('by being sent an invitation'), because the researchers, not the scientists, were doing the sending.
questions.explanation: The conversion applies the rules in the printed table: past simple → was/were + past participle, and the pronoun I → me after 'by'.

questions.question:
Exercise 2: Given below is a sample of newspaper report. It is written in passive voice. Work individually and change the following from passive voice into active voice. Then, write the same in your notebook.
"A bus has been stolen from outside the school. The thief was seen by some children. The bus is being searched by the police now. Children's descriptions will be used by them to catch the thief."
questions.answer:
Active version:
"Someone has stolen a bus from outside the school. Some children saw the thief. The police are searching the bus now. They will use the children's descriptions to catch the thief."

Notes: (i) 'has been stolen' → present perfect active 'has stolen', with the unknown doer supplied as 'someone'; (ii) 'was seen by some children' → past simple active 'saw', with 'some children' as subject; (iii) 'is being searched by the police' → present continuous active 'are searching' (police takes a plural verb); (iv) 'will be used by them' → future active 'will use', the pronoun 'them' becoming 'they'.
questions.explanation: Each passive verb is converted to the matching active tense and the agent in the 'by'-phrase is made the subject; where no agent is given, an indefinite subject such as 'someone' is supplied.

questions.question:
Exercise 3: Work in pairs and change the voice of the following sentences. Rewrite the sentences in your notebook and share your work with your partner.
1. Don't touch the naked wire. 2. There is nothing to say. 3. He has to purchase a car. 4. One should listen to one's conscience. 5. I like the people to respect me. 6. Turn him out. 7. Someone killed the criminal. 8. It is time to switch off T.V. 9. I am to take tea. 10. Please bring me a glass of water. 11. Let her write a poem. 12. Did you tell a lie? 13. Why did you help her? 14. The judge enquired in to the case. 15. She made me sing.
questions.answer:
1. Don't touch the naked wire. → Let the naked wire not be touched. (negative imperative: Let + object + not be + V3)
2. There is nothing to say. → There is nothing to be said. (infinitive after 'nothing' becomes passive)
3. He has to purchase a car. → A car has to be purchased by him. ('has to' + passive infinitive)
4. One should listen to one's conscience. → One's conscience should be listened to. (the object becomes subject; the preposition 'to' is retained)
5. I like the people to respect me. → I like to be respected by the people. ('to respect me' → 'to be respected by the people')
6. Turn him out. → Let him be turned out. (imperative → 'Let ... be + V3')
7. Someone killed the criminal. → The criminal was killed. (the indefinite agent 'someone' is dropped)
8. It is time to switch off T.V. → It is time for the T.V. to be switched off. (passive infinitive with 'for + object')
9. I am to take tea. → Tea is to be taken by me. ('am to' + passive infinitive; I → me)
10. Please bring me a glass of water. → You are requested to bring me a glass of water. (polite request in passive; also acceptable: Let a glass of water be brought to me.)
11. Let her write a poem. → Let a poem be written by her. ('Let' is kept; the infinitive becomes passive)
12. Did you tell a lie? → Was a lie told by you? (past interrogative passive)
13. Why did you help her? → Why was she helped by you? (the question word stays first; 'did + V1' → 'was/were + V3')
14. The judge enquired in to the case. → The case was enquired into by the judge. (prepositional verb keeps its preposition)
15. She made me sing. → I was made to sing by her. (after 'make' in the passive, 'to' is restored before the infinitive)
questions.explanation: Each sentence is converted according to its structure (imperative, interrogative, infinitive, prepositional verb or causative); the reason is given in brackets so the rule applied is visible.

questions.question:
Exercise 4: Work in pairs and use words given below to complete the following text. After you have completed, share your work with your partner. Words: resembles, wilderness, purpose, findings, valley, strangest, construction, political, pending, inhabitants, mystery, unclear, archaeologists, believed, vastness, located.
"The historic Rani Kot Fort is a______. It was built on mountains of the Khirthar Ranges of Sindh. It is ______about 28 kilometres from the Sann Gate from Jamshed. It is ______to be the largest fort in the world having walls nearly 35 kilometres long. The age of the fort is______, however, ______predict that the magnificent structure was built sometime in the 9th-century. Visually, its walls are truly a roller coaster ride, sometimes going as high as three thousand feet above sea level while other times instantly sliding down towards the ground. Archaeologists want to ensure Rani Kot Fort gets the recognition it deserves. Its ______resembles the Great Wall of China which is why it is often referred to as 'The Great Wall of Sindh.' Since 1993, it is has been on the tentative list to be designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its status is still______. Many agree that it is the most fascinating place in Sindh. The surrounding walls of Rani Kot Fort are made from gypsum and lime cut sandstone. To give you an idea of the ______of Rani Kot Fort, it is so large that there is enough space in it for building hundreds of other forts. It has been determined that Rani Kot Fort was built for the ______of defence and to house many______. The rulers of different times lived here and it was the center of ______activities where many ancient leaders of Sindh gathered. Artefacts uncovered at Rani Kot tell a fascinating story of its inhabitants and a rich history that spans thousands of years. Some of the ______include archaic coins, terracotta of the Indus Civilization, an engraved sign of a swastika, a leaf of the papal tree (sacred fig); evidence of a peacock, sunflower, and lotus flower; remains of Zoroastrians and Buddhists, and arrows of different kinds. The entire fort is surrounded by hills that form a small ______through which a stream passes. Its name is taken from this stream; 'Rani' meaning Stream. The Rani Kot Fort ______no other fort in the world. Its unusual size, lost history, strategically useless position, uninhabited area, and unexplored features make the fort one of the ______places in the world. One would require a time machine to solve its mystery. Its unusual size and location in the absolute ______doesn't make sense, at least in the present times."
questions.answer:
Completed text:
"The historic Rani Kot Fort is a mystery. It was built on mountains of the Khirthar Ranges of Sindh. It is located about 28 kilometres from the Sann Gate from Jamshed. It is believed to be the largest fort in the world having walls nearly 35 kilometres long. The age of the fort is unclear, however, archaeologists predict that the magnificent structure was built sometime in the 9th-century. Visually, its walls are truly a roller coaster ride, sometimes going as high as three thousand feet above sea level while other times instantly sliding down towards the ground. Archaeologists want to ensure Rani Kot Fort gets the recognition it deserves. Its construction resembles the Great Wall of China which is why it is often referred to as 'The Great Wall of Sindh.' Since 1993, it is has been on the tentative list to be designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its status is still pending. Many agree that it is the most fascinating place in Sindh. The surrounding walls of Rani Kot Fort are made from gypsum and lime cut sandstone. To give you an idea of the vastness of Rani Kot Fort, it is so large that there is enough space in it for building hundreds of other forts. It has been determined that Rani Kot Fort was built for the purpose of defence and to house many inhabitants. The rulers of different times lived here and it was the center of political activities where many ancient leaders of Sindh gathered. Artefacts uncovered at Rani Kot tell a fascinating story of its inhabitants and a rich history that spans thousands of years. Some of the findings include archaic coins, terracotta of the Indus Civilization, an engraved sign of a swastika, a leaf of the papal tree (sacred fig); evidence of a peacock, sunflower, and lotus flower; remains of Zoroastrians and Buddhists, and arrows of different kinds. The entire fort is surrounded by hills that form a small valley through which a stream passes. Its name is taken from this stream; 'Rani' meaning Stream. The Rani Kot Fort resembles no other fort in the world. Its unusual size, lost history, strategically useless position, uninhabited area, and unexplored features make the fort one of the strangest places in the world. One would require a time machine to solve its mystery. Its unusual size and location in the absolute wilderness doesn't make sense, at least in the present times."

7 | Its status is still ______ | pending
8 | an idea of the ______ of Rani Kot Fort | vastness
9 | built for the ______ of defence | purpose
10 | to house many ______ | inhabitants
11 | the center of ______ activities | political
12 | Some of the ______ include | findings
13 | a small ______ through which a stream passes | valley

questions.explanation: All sixteen words from the word bank are used exactly once; each choice is fixed by grammar and collocation (e.g. 'is believed to be', 'status is still pending', 'absolute wilderness').

questions.question: Recite any of your favourite poems in Sindhi, Urdu or English.
questions.answer: I would recite Allama Iqbal's well-known Urdu poem 'Lab pe aati hai dua ban ke tamanna meri'. I choose it because it is short, its rhymes fall easily on the tongue ('tamanna meri' / 'zindagi shama ki surat ho khudaya meri'), and its prayer for a life of light and service says in eight lines what the whole of Section B says about living well. My recitation would follow the poem's own movement: the first two lines softly, as a child speaking to God; the middle lines, which ask for love of the country and for strength against evil, a little louder and slower, with a pause after 'dua'; and the last line, 'zindagi shama ki surat ho khudaya meri', almost a whisper, so that the closing wish stays in the room.
