This is a poem meant to be remembered by people who are tired, so simplicity is a strategy, not a limitation.

2. Theme: Perseverance. The poem argues that failure is usually temporary and that most people fail by stopping too soon; success is redefined as 'failure turned inside out'.

3. Structure: Four six-line stanzas, each rhyming aabbcc (will/uphill, high/sigh, bit/quit), with lines built on four stresses and a short closing line. Each stanza is a complete movement - trouble, reversal, nearness of the goal, redefinition - and the first and last stanzas close with the same command, so the poem ends where it began, only with more force.

4. Language: The language is direct, using the second person ('you'), contractions, imperatives ('Rest', 'Don't give up', 'stick') and anaphora ('When ... When ...'). Rhyme and alliteration give it a marching rhythm; the tone is encouraging, brotherly and slightly sentimental, which suits its purpose.

5. Message: Do not surrender in the middle of the fight. Rest if you must, but return; you cannot see how near the goal is, and the effort that seems futile may be the one that wins.
questions.explanation: All five printed aspects are covered in order, with the stanza rhyme pattern checked (will/uphill/high/sigh/bit/quit) and the refrain noted as structural frame.

questions.question: Explain the following stanza: Stanza 1 - 'When things go wrong ........... but don't you quit.'
questions.answer: The opening stanza sets the scene of ordinary hardship and gives the poem's first command. 'When things go wrong, as they sometimes will' - the parenthesis is important, because it tells us that trouble is not exceptional but the common weather of life. 'When the road you're trudging seems all uphill' - 'trudging' is the slow, heavy walk of a tired man, and an uphill road gives no view and no rest. 'When the funds are low and debts are high' states the trouble in its plainest, most modern form: money. 'And you want to smile but have to sigh' turns to the feelings behind the money, the gap between the face one wants to show and the breath one actually draws. 'When care is pressing you down a bit' adds the weight of worry, and the modest 'a bit' makes the line believable. Then comes the answer: 'Rest, if you must, but don't you quit.' The poet allows rest because bodies and minds tire, but he separates resting from surrendering - you may stop for a while, you may not stop for good.
questions.explanation: Lines 1-6 explained in sequence, with attention to 'trudging', 'as they sometimes will' and the crucial distinction between rest and surrender.

questions.question: Explain the following stanza: Stanza 2 - 'Life is queer .... with another blow.'
questions.answer: The second stanza explains why quitting is a mistake. 'Life is queer with its twists and turns' - life is strange, full of bends that no one can foresee; 'As every one of us sometimes learns' adds that this is not theory but the common experience of everybody. 'And many a failure turns about, / When he might have won had he stuck it out' - here 'failure' means a man who has failed, and 'turns about' means he reverses his fortune. The couplet makes the central claim of the poem: the difference between the man who wins and the man who loses is often nothing but the decision to hold on a little longer. 'Don't give up though the pace seems slow - / You might succeed with another blow.' 'Pace' is speed: progress may look slow without being absent, and 'another blow' is another stroke of effort. The stanza therefore moves from observation (life is unpredictable) to advice (do not give up) to hope (one more effort may succeed).
questions.explanation: Lines 7-12 explained, with 'queer' glossed as strange, 'turns about' as reverses his fortune, and 'blow' as a stroke of effort.

questions.question: Explain the following stanza: Stanza 3 - 'Often the goal ....... to the golden crown.'
questions.answer: The third stanza is the emotional centre of the poem. 'Often the goal is nearer than, / It seems to a faint and faltering man' - the goal does not move, but the tired man's judgement does: 'faint' means weak and discouraged, 'faltering' means stumbling, and such a man always overestimates the distance left. 'Often the struggler has given up, / When he might have captured the victor's cup' - the tragedy is stated plainly: the prize was within reach at the very moment of surrender. 'And he learned too late when the night slipped down, / How close he was to the golden crown.' The image of night slipping down is the finest in the poem: failure comes quietly, like darkness, and only afterwards, in the dark, does the man measure how near he had come. 'The golden crown' and 'the victor's cup' are metaphors for victory, taken from the race and the contest. The stanza does not scold the struggler; it mourns him, and in mourning him it warns the reader.
questions.explanation: Lines 13-18 explained, with 'faint and faltering' glossed and the two victory metaphors identified.

questions.question: Explain the following stanza: Stanza 4 - 'Success is failure ..... that you mustn't quit.'
questions.answer: The last stanza redefines success and closes with the poem's command. 'Success is failure turned inside out' - a startling metaphor: success is not the opposite of failure but the same cloth reversed, so that what looked like defeat becomes achievement when it is turned round by persistence. 'The silver tint of clouds of doubt' continues the image with the proverb of the silver lining: doubt is a cloud, and its edge is already bright. 'And you never can tell how close you are, / It may be near when it seems so far' gives the reasoning behind hope - our sense of distance is unreliable, so despair is never justified by appearances. 'So stick to the fight when you're hardest hit - / It's when things seem worst that you mustn't quit.' The two closing lines use the imperative and a dash to make the advice sound like a command shouted to a soldier. The stanza thus ends the poem on its strongest note: precisely when everything looks worst, the one thing forbidden is surrender.
questions.explanation: Lines 19-24 explained, with the central metaphor unpacked and the closing imperative noted.

questions.question: Work in groups of three. Compose your own poem on the theme of 'Don't Give Up', using elements of poetry based on three stanzas. Each member of the group should compose 1 stanza. After your group has composed the poem, exchange it with other groups.
questions.answer:
Don't Give Up

I
When the first plan breaks and the road turns steep,
And the friends you counted have gone to sleep,
When the marks are low and the days are long,
Remember the seed that the winter made strong.

II
The digger who stops at the hardest stone
Will never uncover the vein of gold;
The runner who quits when he runs alone
Will never have such a story told.

III
So take the blow and steady your feet,
The darkest hour is before the light;
The gate you are sure you will never meet
Is standing open, just out of sight.

(Group note: the three stanzas rhyme aabb in the first and abab in the second and third, like Guest's mixture of couplets and alternating rhyme. Stanza I uses a metaphor - the seed strengthened by winter - and alliteration in 'first plan' and 'days are long'. Stanza II uses two parallel examples, the digger and the runner, the second of which echoes Guest's 'victor's cup'. Stanza III uses personification of the 'darkest hour' and ends with the image of a gate standing open, a symbol of the success that is nearer than it looks.)
questions.explanation: Creative task; a complete three-stanza poem is supplied with a note naming the elements of poetry used, as the exercise requires.

questions.question: Read the following quote and guess the theme of the poem: "Graveyards are full of the people who thought themselves indispensable"
questions.answer: The quote suggests that no one is indispensable: the people who believed the world could not go on without them are lying in graveyards like everybody else, and the world has gone on. From this I guess that the poem will be about the vanity of human pride and the shortness of power and fame. The theme is likely to be that greatness, wealth and authority are temporary, that monuments cannot preserve a name, and that time and nature finally level every human boast. The poem is 'Ozymandias', and the title itself is the name of a king who thought his works would outlast everything.
questions.explanation: Pre-reading prediction; the guess is drawn from the quote's argument and confirmed by the poem's own subject, a ruined statue of a boastful king.

questions.question: Column A has words from the poem; underline these words in the poem. Column B has the contextual meanings of these words, but they are jumbled up. Work in pairs. Try and match the appropriate meaning of each word, and write your answer in column C. Share your work with your partner after you have completed.
questions.answer:
No. | Column A | Column C (correct meaning)
1 | frown | d - a displeasing or concentrating face. 'whose frown' — the carved lines of displeasure on the visage.
2 | visage | g - a human or animal face. 'a shattered visage lies'.
3 | sculptor | b - an artist who makes sculpture. 'Tell that its sculptor well those passions read'.
4 | mock | e - make fun of. 'The hand that mocked them' — the sculptor's hand imitated and mocked the king's passions.
5 | pedestal | f - the base of sculpture. 'And on the pedestal, these words appear'.
6 | colossal | c - huge. 'Of that Colossal Wreck'.
7 | remains | a - the parts left over. 'Nothing beside remains'.
questions.explanation: Each match is confirmed by the poem's context: the frown is a carved expression, the visage is the broken face, the sculptor is the artist, 'mocked' is the mocking imitation of the passions, the pedestal is the statue's base, 'colossal' describes the size of the wreck, and 'remains' means what is left.

questions.question: 'Ozymandias' is a poem depicting that the life is________.
questions.answer: (b) transient - the poem shows that life, power and glory pass away: 'Nothing beside remains.'
questions.explanation: The ruined statue in an empty desert is the poem's argument that everything human is short-lived; beauty, attraction and allurement are not its subject at all.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) beautiful   (b) transient   (c) attractive   (d) alluring

questions.question: The poet met a traveller from________.
questions.answer: (a) an ancient land - 'I met a traveller from an antique land'.
questions.explanation: The opening line is quoted almost verbatim; 'antique' means ancient, and the land is Egypt, though the poem does not name it.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) an ancient land   (b) aboard   (c) a neighbouring country   (d) a desert

questions.question: The traveller told the poet that he had seen________ in the desert.
questions.answer: (a) a statue - two vast trunkless legs of stone and a shattered visage lying in the sand.
questions.explanation: The traveller describes the remains of a colossal statue; the sculptor is mentioned only as its maker, and no oasis or snake appears in the poem.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) a statue   (b) a sculptor   (c) an oasis   (d) a snake

questions.question: The words on the base of statue tell us that the king Ozymandias was a________ king.
questions.answer: (c) proud - 'My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!'
questions.explanation: 'King of Kings' and the challenge to the Mighty to despair are the language of pride. The 'sneer of cold command' suggests cruelty as well, but the inscription itself is a boast, so pride is the answer the question asks for.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) kind   (b) humble   (c) proud   (d) cruel

questions.question: The message of the poem for all powerful authority and glory is________.
questions.answer: (c) 'nothing remains' - 'Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that Colossal Wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away.'
questions.explanation: The phrase states the poem's moral directly: of all the king's works nothing is left but a broken statue. The other quoted phrases describe the statue or the desert, not the message.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 'sands stretch far away'   (b) 'frown and wrinkled lips'   (c) 'nothing remains'   (d) 'stamped on these lifeless things'

questions.question: In the poem 'Ozymandias', the condition of the statue is________.
questions.answer: (b) bad - only 'Two vast and trunkless legs of stone' stand, and the face lies 'Half sunk, a shattered visage' in the sand.
questions.explanation: The statue has lost its body and its head, and the head itself is broken; the poem calls it 'that Colossal Wreck'.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) good   (b) bad   (c) excellent   (d) marvellous

questions.question: 'My name is Ozymandias - King of Kings;' is ________ literary device.
questions.answer: (b) Irony - the boast 'King of Kings' is carved on a broken statue in an empty desert, so the words mean the opposite of what they claim.
questions.explanation: Irony is the device the whole poem turns on: the king who commands the Mighty to look at his works has left nothing to look at. Note that the title itself can also be read as hyperbole or as a metaphor of absolute power; the printed key may vary, but the contextual device is irony.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Simile   (b) Irony   (c) Personification   (d) Metaphor

questions.question: One of the following lines does NOT make use of alliteration in the poem.
questions.answer: (b) 'I met a traveller from an antique land' - no consonant is repeated at the beginning of stressed words.
questions.explanation: Option (a) repeats 'l' (lone, level), (d) repeats 's' (sunk, shattered) and (c) carries the 'r' of 'remains' and 'Round' (a weaker instance, which is why it is not the answer). Line (b) has no such repetition, so it is the line without alliteration.

options.text: The lone and level sands stretch far away
I met a traveller from an antique land
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown

questions.optionsRaw: (a) The lone and level sands stretch far away   (b) I met a traveller from an antique land   (c) Nothing beside remains. Round the decay   (d) Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown
questions.correctAnswer: (b) I met a traveller from an antique land

questions.question: Work in pairs and read the above poem again. Comprehend it thoroughly and paraphrase it in simple words. After you have completed, share it with your partner.
questions.answer:
Paraphrase in simple words:

I met a traveller who came from an ancient country. He told me that two huge legs of stone, with no body left, stand in the desert. Near them, half buried in the sand, lies a broken face. Its frown, its wrinkled lip and its sneer of cold command show that the sculptor understood the king's feelings very well, and those feelings still live, stamped on these lifeless stones - the hand that copied them and the heart that fed them.

On the base of the statue these words are carved: 'My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings. Look at my works, you Mighty ones, and despair!' Nothing else is left. Around the ruins of that enormous wreck, boundless and bare, the lonely, level sands stretch far away.

In one sentence: a traveller describes a broken statue in the desert, whose proud inscription is contradicted by the endless empty sand around it.
questions.explanation: A close paraphrase of the whole fourteen lines in modern, simple English, keeping the order and details of the original.

questions.question: What did the traveller see in the desert and whom he told about it?
questions.answer: The traveller saw the remains of a huge statue in the desert: 'Two vast and trunkless legs of stone' standing on the sand, and near them, half sunk and shattered, a great face with a frown, a wrinkled lip and 'a sneer of cold command'. On the pedestal of the statue an inscription was carved. He told all this to the poet, the speaker of the poem, who reports it in the opening line: 'I met a traveller from an antique land, / Who said -'. Nothing in the poem tells us whether the traveller was an explorer, a merchant or a wondering tourist; his importance is that he is a witness, so the story reaches us at second hand, like a report from a far country.
questions.explanation: The answer follows lines 1-10 and notes the framing device - the poet repeats what the traveller said rather than seeing the statue himself.

questions.question: How can you say that the sculptor was a great artist?
questions.answer: Because he could read a man's character and reproduce it in stone so exactly that it survives after the man and the empire are gone. The poem says the frown, the 'wrinkled lip' and the 'sneer of cold command' on the broken face 'Tell that its sculptor well those passions read / Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things'. The passions outlived both the king and the sculptor, and they did so only because the sculptor's hand had 'mocked' them - copied them with such skill that the stone still sneers. A great artist is not only a craftsman of stone but a reader of the heart, and here the sculptor understood the pride and cruelty of the tyrant he was paid to flatter, and even mocked it while carving it. His art, not the king's power, is what survived.
questions.explanation: Lines 5-8 supply the evidence: the expression on the shattered face and the words 'well those passions read' and 'The hand that mocked them'.

questions.question: What was written on the pedestal of the statue of Ozymandias?
questions.answer: These words were carved on the pedestal: 'My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' The inscription gives the king's name, claims for him the highest title on earth, and challenges every other powerful ruler to look at what he has built and despair of equalling it. The irony is that the 'Works' the traveller can see are two broken legs and a shattered head, and the only thing the Mighty would despair of is finding anything at all. The boast is therefore the strongest proof of the poem's message: the inscription survives, but the works it advertises have vanished into sand.
questions.explanation: Lines 9-11 are quoted exactly, and the contrast with lines 12-14 supplies the irony the question expects.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the phrase in the poem "the heart that fed"?
questions.answer: It means the king's own heart, which fed and nourished the passions carved on his face. The full sentence runs: the frown, the wrinkled lip and the sneer 'Tell that its sculptor well those passions read, / Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things / The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed'. Grammatically the phrase belongs with 'those passions': the passions were fed by the heart of Ozymandias and mocked by the hand of the sculptor. The heart is called a 'heart that fed' because pride, contempt and the lust for command are not passing moods but appetites that a man keeps feeding until they become his whole character. The phrase therefore blames the living man, not the stone: the statue is only a copy of what the heart had already made.
questions.explanation: The phrase is read in the syntax of lines 6-8, where 'the hand that mocked them' and 'the heart that fed' are parallel: the sculptor's hand copied the passions, the king's heart fed them.

questions.question: What is ironic about the fate of Ozymandias?
questions.answer: The irony is complete and double. First, the king who called himself 'King of Kings' and ordered the Mighty to look at his works and despair now has no works to show: only 'Two vast and trunkless legs of stone' and a 'shattered visage' half sunk in the sand, with 'Nothing beside remains'. Second, the boast itself has been preserved by the very art he meant only to advertise - the sculptor's mocking hand outlived the empire, so that the words 'look on my Works' now point at ruin. A third layer is that the 'Mighty' whom he addressed have also vanished, and the only thing that stretches 'far away' is 'The lone and level sands'. The statue that was built to make his name eternal has become the monument of his insignificance.
questions.explanation: The irony is between the inscription (lines 10-11) and the scene around it (lines 12-14), reinforced by the sculptor's survival in lines 6-8.

questions.question: What is the message of the poem?
questions.answer: The message is that human power, pride and glory are temporary, and that time destroys every monument and every empire. Ozymandias ruled as 'King of Kings', yet his statue is a wreck in an empty desert and his 'Works' have disappeared; the only thing that has lasted is the sculptor's art and the desert sand. Shelley is warning the powerful - and the reader - against the illusion of permanence: to build monuments to oneself is to build for the sand. At the same time the poem quietly praises art, since the sculptor's mocking hand preserved both the king's arrogance and its refutation. The message, in the words of the inscription turned against itself, is 'Nothing beside remains'; and the proper human response is humility rather than despair.
questions.explanation: The message is gathered from the inscription, the description of the wreck and the closing image of the 'lone and level sands'; the secondary point about art is drawn from lines 6-8.

questions.question: How does this poem relate to your life?
questions.answer: The poem relates to my life in three ways. First, it is a cure for boasting: I have sometimes wanted to be praised for a good result or a prize, and Ozymandias shows where the desire to be admired ends - a name carved on a broken stone. Second, it teaches proportion: the things I am anxious about, a mark in a test or an argument I must win, look very small beside 'the lone and level sands'. Third, it gives a better ambition: since power and possessions do not last, what is worth building is what the sculptor built - skill, honesty and work done well, which outlived the king who paid for it. I would rather be the artist whose hand told the truth than the king whose inscription was proved false by the desert.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the answer draws three specific lessons (humility, proportion, value of art and honest work) from the poem.

questions.question: The proud Ozymandias lies forgotten in the desert. Comment.
questions.answer: The line is a fair summary of the poem's judgement. Ozymandias built a colossal statue of himself and carved on it the command 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!'; what is left is a pair of 'trunkless legs' and a face 'Half sunk, a shattered visage' in the sand. The frown and the 'sneer of cold command' still tell us what kind of man he was, but nothing tells us what he did; even his name is known only because a traveller repeated an inscription. He is 'forgotten' in the precise sense that no city, no law and no living memory of his rule remains, and the desert has taken his works. Shelley's point is not that Ozymandias was unusual but that he is typical: every proud ruler ends as a ruin in somebody's desert. The comment is therefore ironic rather than cruel - the poem does not gloat, it simply lets time do the arguing.
questions.explanation: The comment is supported by the description of the wreck, the inscription and the closing image of the sands; 'forgotten' is interpreted as the loss of everything but a name on a stone.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the poem based on the following aspects. Compare your work with your partner after you have done it. 1. Poetic Diction  2. Theme  3. Structure  4. Language  5. Message
questions.answer:
1. Poetic Diction: The diction is formal, archaic and monumental - 'antique land', 'trunkless legs', 'shattered visage', 'sneer of cold command', 'ye Mighty', 'Colossal Wreck'. Words such as 'visage', 'pedestal' and 'colossal' belong to the world of monuments and inscriptions, so the vocabulary itself sounds like stone. The one modern, plain phrase, 'Nothing beside remains', hits hard precisely because it is plain.

2. Theme: The vanity of human power and the transience of glory; time and nature outlast tyrants, while art survives to mock them.

3. Structure: A Petrarchan sonnet of fourteen lines, rhymed ababacdcedefef, in which the octave reports what the traveller saw and the sestet reports the inscription and its setting. The poem is framed in reported speech ('I met a traveller ... Who said'), so the reader hears the story at second hand, as history reaches us. The turn comes at line 9 with 'And on the pedestal'.

4. Language: Shelley uses irony as the organising principle: the boast is placed in the middle of the ruin, so that statement and setting contradict each other. Alliteration ('lone and level', 'sunk, a shattered'), imagery of size and emptiness ('boundless and bare'), and the powerful antithesis between 'King of Kings' and 'Nothing beside remains' do the rest. The tone is detached and grimly amused rather than angry.

5. Message: No earthly power is permanent. Pride builds monuments that become ruins, and the only immortality worth having belongs to the truth told about power, not to power itself.
questions.explanation: All five printed aspects are answered, with the rhyme scheme, the framing device and the central irony identified.

questions.question: 'Every rise has a fall.' Work in pairs and discuss it in the light of the poem.
questions.answer: The proverb says that no height is permanent, and 'Ozymandias' is its illustration in stone. Ozymandias 'rose' to be King of Kings, the ruler of an empire great enough to raise a colossal statue of himself in the desert; the statue's pedestal still carries his challenge to the Mighty. His fall is not recorded as an event - no battle, no rebellion is mentioned - because Shelley is not interested in how empires collapse, only in the fact that they do. The fall is visible in the legs without a body, the face in the sand and the words 'Nothing beside remains'. In the light of the poem, then, the proverb is not a threat but a law of nature, like gravity: whatever is raised by human power will be brought down by time. The poem adds a warning that the proverb does not: the higher the rise, the more absurd the fall, because the proud man has built his monument to himself. And it adds a consolation: the sculptor's art, which served no ambition, has outlived the king's power.
questions.explanation: Discussion task; the answer applies the proverb to the poem's evidence (the rise implied by the title 'King of Kings', the fall shown by the wreck) and adds the poem's own qualification about pride and art.

questions.question: Explain the following lines: Line No. 1-8 - 'I met a traveller ......... and the heart that fed;'
questions.answer: The octave reports what a traveller saw. 'I met a traveller from an antique land' establishes the frame: the poet has not seen the statue himself, and the story comes from a distant, ancient country, which gives it the authority of report and the distance of legend. The traveller speaks in his own voice: 'Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert.' 'Vast' gives the size and 'trunkless' the mutilation - the body is gone, only the legs remain, standing for nothing. 'Near them, on the sand / Half sunk, a shattered visage lies' gives us the head, face down and broken, half swallowed by the desert. Then the face is read like a document: 'whose frown, / And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command' - three details that rebuild the tyrant's character in stone. 'Tell that its sculptor well those passions read' praises the artist's insight, and 'Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things' makes the crucial point that the passions outlived the man. The closing phrases, 'The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed', set artist against king: the hand that copied and mocked, the heart that fed the passions it could not master.
questions.explanation: Lines 1-8 are explained in sequence, with attention to the framed narration, the irony of 'trunkless', the three facial details and the contrast between hand and heart.

questions.question: Explain the following lines: Line No. 9-14 - 'And on the pedestal ..... stretch far away.'
questions.answer: The sestet turns from the broken statue to the words carved on it. 'And on the pedestal, these words appear' - the inscription is quoted as if it were still speaking: 'My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' The voice is the voice of absolute power: it names itself, claims the highest title on earth, and commands all other rulers to look and be humbled. The next line destroys the boast with four words: 'Nothing beside remains.' The colon of the inscription leads straight into emptiness. 'Round the decay / Of that Colossal Wreck, boundless and bare' describes what is left - a wreck so large that its ruin is itself impressive, surrounded by a desert without limit or feature. The last line, 'The lone and level sands stretch far away', is the poem's true reply to the inscription: 'lone' and 'level' answer 'King of Kings', and 'stretch far away' answers 'my Works'. The rhyme of 'despair' with 'bare' quietly turns the king's command against himself.
questions.explanation: Lines 9-14 explained, with the inscription's imperatives contrasted word by word with the adjectives 'lone', 'level', 'boundless' and 'bare'.

questions.question: Work in groups of three. Compose your own poem on the theme of 'all power is temporary, no matter how proud a person is'. Make sure that you are using the elements of poetry. Each member of group should compose 1 stanza. After your group has composed the poem, exchange it with other groups.
questions.answer:
The Broken Throne

I
The king who carved his name in stone
And bade the nations bow,
Now sits upon a broken throne
With sand upon his brow.

II
The tower that his masons piled
Is level with the dust;
The wind has taken back the wild
Bright banners of his trust.

III
So walk, O prince, with quiet tread,
And hold your crown in hand;
The proudest empire of the dead
Is nothing but the sand.

(Group note: each member wrote one stanza. Stanza I uses irony - the king 'sits upon a broken throne' - and alliteration in 'bade the nations bow' and 'sand upon his brow'. Stanza II uses the metaphor of the tower 'level with the dust' and personification of the wind that 'has taken back' the banners. Stanza III addresses a prince directly (apostrophe), uses the symbol of the crown held in the hand for power surrendered willingly, and closes on the same image of sand that ends Shelley's sonnet. The rhyme is abcb throughout, and the last line of each stanza is short, like the sound of something falling.)
questions.explanation: Creative task; a complete three-stanza poem with a note naming the devices used, in the manner the exercise requires.

questions.question: "The stronger the wind, the stronger the tree". Read the line and guess the theme of the poem.
questions.answer: The line says that resistance makes strength: a tree that has to stand against a strong wind grows tough roots and a hard trunk, while a sheltered tree stays weak. From this I guess that the poem will be about hardship as a teacher - that difficulties, storms and struggle do not destroy a person but develop him, and that comfort and ease produce softness. The title 'Good Timber' supports the guess, because timber means wood used for building, and good timber is exactly the wood that has grown slowly in wind and cold. I expect the poem to compare trees and men and to conclude that the same law governs both.
questions.explanation: Pre-reading prediction; the guess is drawn from the line's logic and from the title's word 'timber', and it matches the poem's actual argument.

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner.
questions.answer:
No. | Word | Contextual meaning
1 | timber | Wood suitable for building; in the poem it means a person of strong, tested character - 'In trees and men good timbers grow'. Not the wood itself but the quality of being sound and useful.
2 | scrubby | Stunted, thin and poor in growth; the 'scrubby thing' is the sheltered tree that never grew to full size, and by implication a small, undeveloped person.
3 | toil | Hard, continuous labour; 'The man who never had to toil / To gain and farm his patch of soil' - to work the soil with effort and patience.
4 | patriarchs | The oldest and most respected heads of a family or tribe; here the tallest, oldest trees of the forest, and the strong, experienced men compared with them.
5 | counsel | Advice, consultation; 'they hold counsel with the stars' means the old trees and old men seem to take counsel - to talk and plan - with the sky above them.
6 | scars | Marks left on the skin by a healed wound; here the broken branches of the old trees, which are the visible marks of the storms and struggles they have survived.
questions.explanation: Each entry gives the dictionary sense and then the sense the line requires, as the exercise asks; note that 'timber' shifts from material to character and 'counsel' is used figuratively.

questions.question: The poem explains to us that good qualities always develop in________.
questions.answer: (a) hardships - 'Good timber does not grow with ease, / The stronger wind, the stronger trees.'
questions.explanation: The whole poem argues that wind, storm, cold and struggle produce strength; ease produces only 'a scrubby thing'.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) hardships   (b) ease   (c) idleness   (d) illness

questions.question: "Never became a forest king" means never________.
questions.answer: (b) acquired a prominent position - the sheltered tree never rose to be the tallest and most honoured tree of the forest.
questions.explanation: 'Forest king' is a metaphor for the tree that dominates the forest; applied to men, it means a person of standing and achievement, not a literal lion or king.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) became a lion   (b) acquired a prominent position   (c) possessed courage to fight   (d) enjoyed life

questions.question: "But lived and died as he began" points out towards ________ human being.
questions.answer: (b) an effortless human being - one who never struggled, so he ended exactly as he started, with nothing gained.
questions.explanation: The stanza is about 'the man who never had to toil'; because nothing was ever demanded of him, nothing was ever added to him. 'Effortless' describes such a life of ease.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) a courageous   (b) an effortless   (c) a wealthy   (d) a successful

questions.question: In the poem 'Good Timber', the poet discusses themes of________.
questions.answer: (c) nature, struggle and fulfilment - the poem reads human growth in the forest, treats struggle as the condition of growth and ends in the fulfilment of 'good timbers' and 'the common law of life'.
questions.explanation: The three terms match the poem's structure: the tree and forest imagery, the storms and toil, and the mature 'patriarchs' who have reached their full height.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) nature, wealth and defeat   (b) power, relationship and hope   (c) nature, struggle and fulfilment   (d) nature, nurture and chaos

questions.question: The poem teaches us that the people reach their true potential by overcoming________.
questions.answer: (d) adversities - 'The more the storm, the more the strength' and 'By sun and cold, by rain and snow / In trees and men good timbers grow'.
questions.explanation: The obstacles the poem names are wind, storm, cold, rain and snow - hardships of circumstance, not feelings, enemies or desires.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) feelings   (b) enemies   (c) desires   (d) adversities

questions.question: "But lived and died a scrubby thing" means lived a/an________ life.
questions.answer: (a) unimportant - 'scrubby' means stunted and poor, so the sheltered tree lived and died a small, insignificant thing.
questions.explanation: The contrast is with 'a forest king'; the scrubby tree is the opposite of prominent, so its life is unimportant rather than comfortable or useful.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) unimportant   (b) high status   (c) useful   (d) comfortable

questions.question: 'By sun and cold, by rain and snow' is________ literary device.
questions.answer: (c) Alliteration - 'sun' and 'snow' repeat the 's' sound at the start of stressed syllables.
questions.explanation: The line repeats initial consonants ('sun ... snow', and 'rain ... snow' in the same breath) and contains no comparison at all, so metaphor and simile are ruled out; an oxymoron would need contradictory words, which sun and cold are not.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Metaphor   (b) Oxymoron   (c) Alliteration   (d) Simile

questions.question: "Broken branches" in last stanza is the example of________.
questions.answer: (b) metaphor - the broken branches 'show the scars / Of many winds and much of strife', so the branches stand for the wounds that a life of struggle leaves behind.
questions.explanation: Literally the branches are broken wood; the poem calls them 'scars', the marks of healed wounds, and so makes them a metaphor of endurance. There is no 'like' or 'as', so it is not a simile.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) simile   (b) metaphor   (c) hyperbole   (d) none of them

questions.question: What is the significance of the title of the poem?
questions.answer: 'Timber' means wood that is fit for building - sound, straight, strong wood that has grown slowly and hardened. The title therefore works in two directions at once. Literally, it points to the forest: the poem is about trees, and 'good timber' is the tree that has fought for sun and stood against wind and snow. Figuratively, it points to people: 'In trees and men good timbers grow', so good timber means a person of tested character, useful to others and able to bear weight. The adjective 'good' matters too, because the poem distinguishes good timber from the 'scrubby thing' that grew in the shelter of the plain. The title is thus a compressed statement of the theme - strength is grown, not given - and it prepares the reader for a poem that is a parable rather than a description of forestry.
questions.explanation: The title is interpreted through the poem's key line 'In trees and men good timbers grow' and through the contrast between good timber and the 'scrubby thing'.

questions.question: What happens to the people who work hard?
questions.answer: They grow into their full size, become useful and are honoured. The poem's third stanza states the law: 'Good timber does not grow with ease, / The stronger wind, the stronger trees'; and its fourth stanza shows the result - in the thickest part of the forest grow the 'patriarchs', the oldest and tallest trees, whose 'broken branches show the scars / Of many winds and much of strife'. Applied to men, this means that those who toil, face storms and keep standing become 'manly' men, capable of bearing responsibility, respected by others, and able to 'hold counsel with the stars' - that is, to have wisdom and a wide view of life. Their scars are not a disfigurement but a record of survival. So hard work does not merely produce results; it produces the person who can carry them.
questions.explanation: The answer follows the poem's argument from stanza 3 (the law) to stanza 4 (the patriarchs and their scars).

questions.question: How can one achieve one's true potential in life according to the poem?
questions.answer: According to the poem, one achieves one's true potential by accepting struggle instead of avoiding it. The tree that 'never had to fight / For sun and sky and air and light' but 'always got its share of rain' becomes a 'scrubby thing'; the man who 'never had to toil' remains exactly as he began. Growth comes from the opposite conditions: 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees, / The further sky, the greater length, / The more the storm, the more the strength.' In practical terms this means seeking the difficult task rather than the easy one, competing for one's share of 'sun and sky and light and air' instead of waiting to be given it, and enduring cold, rain and snow without withdrawing. The poem's metaphor of roots and branches suggests patience as well: potential is realised slowly, over years, and the scars one collects on the way are the proof that the growth has taken place.
questions.explanation: The answer draws on stanzas 1-3, where the negative examples of the sheltered tree and effortless man are set against the law of growth through storm.

questions.question: Why does the poet suggest people to be like good timber?
questions.answer: Because good timber is wood that can be used - it bears weight, holds up a roof and does not break - and the poet wants people to be like that: strong, sound and useful rather than ornamental. In the poem good timber is the product of a hard life, not of a sheltered one: it has fought for light, stood in wind and snow, and carries the scars of many storms. Its strength is therefore tested strength, which is the only kind that can be trusted when a load is placed on it. A person of that kind can be relied on by a family, a village or a country; a 'scrubby thing' cannot, however comfortable its life has been. The poet also values the timber's usefulness to others: wood is good not because it is admired but because it serves. The comparison therefore asks the reader to measure himself by what he can bear and give, not by what he can avoid.
questions.explanation: The comparison is explained through the properties of timber (strength, usefulness, tested by weather) and through the poem's contrast with the sheltered, 'scrubby' tree.

questions.question: Which poetic devices are used in the poem?
questions.answer:
1. Metaphor - the tree is a man and the man is a tree: 'In trees and men good timbers grow'; 'Never became a forest king'; 'they hold counsel with the stars'. The whole poem is an extended metaphor.
2. Personification - 'they hold counsel with the stars' gives the old trees the human act of taking counsel; the tree that 'never had to fight' is also given a human struggle.
3. Alliteration - 'The tree that never had to fight' (t); 'For sun and sky and air and light' (s); 'lived and died' (l, d); 'Good timber does not grow with ease' (g); 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees' (s, w); 'the more the storm, the more the strength' (m, s); 'sun and cold ... rain and snow' (s).
4. Anaphora and parallelism - 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees, / The further sky, the greater length, / The more the storm, the more the strength' repeats one grammatical pattern three times.
5. Antithesis - the sheltered tree against the forest king; 'lived and died' against 'grow'; the plain against the thickest forest.
6. Symbol - the tree, the storm, the broken branches and the scars stand for human hardship and endurance.
7. Imagery - 'stood out in the open plain', 'Where thickest lies the forest growth', 'broken branches show the scars' give clear pictures.
8. Repetition - 'good timber' and 'trees and men' recur, keeping the comparison before the reader.
questions.explanation: Each device is quoted from the poem; the extended tree-man metaphor and the anaphora of stanza 3 are the poem's two governing devices.

questions.question: Write central idea of the poem.
questions.answer: The central idea is that strength of character, like good timber, is produced by hardship and not by comfort. Malloch makes the point twice, once for trees and once for men: the tree that never had to fight for light and always got its share of rain 'lived and died a scrubby thing', and the man who never had to toil 'lived and died as he began'. The third stanza states the law that governs both - 'Good timber does not grow with ease, / The stronger wind, the stronger trees' - and the fourth shows its result: the oldest and greatest trees stand where the growth is thickest and carry the scars of 'many winds and much of strife'. The poem's closing line, 'This is the common law of life', extends the law to all living things. The idea is therefore both a consolation and a challenge: hardship is not a misfortune to be escaped but the condition of growth.
questions.explanation: The idea is stated and then traced through the two parallel examples, the law in stanza 3 and the conclusion in stanza 4.

questions.question: How does this poem relate to your life?
questions.answer: It relates to my life as a student in a very direct way. I have often wished for the easy path - a teacher who gives notes instead of questions, a syllabus with no difficult chapters, a test that asks only what I already know. The poem tells me that this is exactly the 'open plain' where nothing grows. The subjects I found hardest, and the teachers who demanded most, are the ones that changed me; the easy months left no mark. It also helps me interpret failure: a bad result is a storm, and the tree that survives it grows a thicker trunk. And it warns me against comparing myself with someone who is sheltered: his ease is not an advantage but a stunting. What I take from the poem is a rule for the years ahead - choose the difficult thing while I am young enough to be shaped by it, and expect the scars to be part of the growth.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the answer applies the poem's law to study, difficulty and failure in a student's own experience.

questions.question: Work individually and identify the poetic devices in the poem. Make a list of them and use them in your sentences. Share your work with your class fellows once you have completed.
questions.answer:
Devices found in 'Good Timber':

1. Metaphor - 'Never became a forest king'; 'In trees and men good timbers grow'; 'they hold counsel with the stars'. The tree stands for a man throughout. My sentence: 'My grandfather was an old banyan: shade for everyone and roots no storm could move.'

2. Personification - 'The tree that never had to fight'; 'they hold counsel with the stars'. My sentence: 'The old gate complained every time we opened it.'

3. Alliteration - 'The tree that never had to fight'; 'For sun and sky and air and light'; 'lived and died'; 'Good timber does not grow with ease'; 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees'. My sentence: 'Slow streams shape smooth stones.'

4. Anaphora / parallelism - 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees, / The further sky, the greater length, / The more the storm, the more the strength'. My sentence: 'The harder the question, the sharper the mind; the longer the climb, the wider the view.'

5. Antithesis - 'lived and died a scrubby thing' against 'became a forest king'; the sheltered plain against 'Where thickest lies the forest growth'. My sentence: 'The easy road is short and the hard road is long, but only one of them arrives.'

6. Symbol - the storm, the broken branches and the scars stand for hardship and endurance. My sentence: 'The crack in the wall is a symbol of the earthquake we all survived.'

7. Imagery - 'stood out in the open plain', 'broken branches show the scars', 'hold counsel with the stars'. My sentence: 'The bare branches cut black lines across the winter sky.'

8. Repetition - 'good timber' and 'trees and men' return in each stanza. My sentence: 'Practice, practice, practice - that is the whole secret.'
questions.explanation: Each device is quoted from the poem, explained and used in an original sentence; the extended tree-man metaphor is identified as the poem's governing device.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the poem based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. 1. Poetic Diction  2. Theme  3. Structure  4. Language  5. Message
questions.answer:
1. Poetic Diction: The diction is plain, homely and agricultural - 'timber', 'scrubby', 'toil', 'patch of soil', 'patriarchs', 'scars'. These are the words of a farmer or a forester rather than of a philosopher, and they give the poem its solid, workaday feel. The diction also carries the parable: because the words describe trees literally, they can describe men figuratively without strain.

2. Theme: Character is formed by hardship. Comfort produces weakness ('a scrubby thing'), struggle produces strength ('good timber'), and this is 'the common law of life' for trees and men alike.

3. Structure: Four six-line stanzas, each rhyming aabbcc in iambic tetrameter. The stanzas move in a clear sequence: the sheltered tree (1), the sheltered man (2), the law of growth (3), the mature patriarchs and the conclusion (4). The first two stanzas are parallel, the third states the principle and the fourth provides the proof, so the poem has the shape of an argument.

4. Language: Malloch relies on the extended metaphor of the tree and on parallelism - 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees, / The further sky, the greater length' - which gives the lines a proverbial, hammering force. Alliteration ('sun and sky', 'lived and died'), personification ('hold counsel with the stars') and antithesis (scrubby thing against forest king) fill out the style. The tone is calm, assured and slightly old-fashioned in its moral confidence.

5. Message: Do not run from difficulty. The wind that bends the tree makes it strong, and the man who never struggles never grows. Accept the storm, keep your roots down, and let your scars be the record of your strength.
questions.explanation: All five printed aspects are answered, with the stanza form (four sixains, aabbcc) and the argumentative structure identified.

questions.question: Work in groups of three. Compose your own poem on the theme of 'When life gives you lemons, make lemonade', using elements of poetry based on three stanzas. Each member of group should compose 1 stanza. Once your group has composed the poem, exchange it with other groups.
questions.answer:
Lemonade

I
Life gave me lemons, sharp and sour,
I ate them raw in a bitter hour;
Then someone taught me to add the sweet
Of patience, water and steady heat.

II
The blacksmith's iron is beaten cold,
The diamond is cut by the grit it fears,
The story that makes the heart grow bold
Is the story written in patient years.

III
So pour the water, and stir the glass,
And sweeten the sorrow that you were given;
The worst of the seasons is sure to pass,
And the lemon will taste like a gift from heaven.

(Group note: the first stanza is a metaphor in which 'lemons' stand for troubles and 'lemonade' for what we make of them; the second uses two comparisons, the beaten iron and the cut diamond, as images of growth through pressure; the third turns to direct address with imperatives - 'pour', 'stir', 'sweeten' - and ends on personification of the season that 'is sure to pass'. The rhyme is aabb in the first stanza and abab in the second and third, and each stanza has four lines, so the poem has a regular beat like Malloch's.)
questions.explanation: Creative task; the model supplies a complete three-stanza poem with a note naming the elements of poetry used.

questions.question: 'Life grows when a person comes out of comfort zone.' Elaborate this statement in the light of the poem 'The Good Timber'. Note down your points in the notebook and share it with your class fellows.
questions.answer:
The poem is an argument for exactly this statement. Its first stanza describes a tree that stayed in its comfort zone: it 'never had to fight / For sun and sky and air and light', it 'stood out in the open plain' where nothing challenged it, and it 'always got its share of rain' without asking. The result was not peace but stuntedness - it 'Never became a forest king / But lived and died a scrubby thing'. The second stanza repeats the pattern for a man who 'never had to toil', and his life also ends where it began. Growth, in the poem, happens only where there is resistance: 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees, / The further sky, the greater length, / The more the storm, the more the strength.' The fourth stanza shows what a life outside the comfort zone looks like at the end - the 'patriarchs' of the forest, tall, old, consulted by the stars, and marked by scars that prove they endured 'many winds and much of strife'. The poem then universalises the point: 'This is the common law of life.'

My points for the notebook: (1) comfort removes the need to try, and effort is what develops ability; (2) difficulty tests and therefore strengthens character; (3) scars are evidence of growth, not of damage; (4) the person who never risks anything remains exactly as he began; (5) leaving the comfort zone should be a habit begun young, because growth is slow.
questions.explanation: Elaboration task; each point is tied to a specific stanza or line of the poem, and the notebook list is given as the exercise asks.

questions.question: Explain the following lines: Line No. 1-6 - 'The tree that ...........a scrubby thing.'
questions.answer: The opening stanza gives the negative example. 'The tree that never had to fight / For sun and sky and air and light' - note that the tree is given a human activity, fighting, and that what it would have fought for is the ordinary food of any plant: light and air. 'But stood out in the open plain / And always got its share of rain' describes a life without competition: the plain is open, the rain comes without asking, nothing is denied it. The consequence is stated bluntly: 'Never became a forest king / But lived and died a scrubby thing.' 'Forest king' is a metaphor for the tallest, most dominant tree; 'scrubby' means stunted and poor. The stanza's irony is that the tree's advantages - space, rain, safety - are exactly what kept it small. Malloch is preparing the comparison with men, and he chooses the plainest possible words so that the moral will be unmistakable.
questions.explanation: Lines 1-6 explained, with 'forest king' identified as a metaphor and the irony of the sheltered life pointed out.

questions.question: Explain the following lines: Line No. 7-12 - 'The man who ....died as he began.'
questions.answer: The second stanza repeats the first with a human subject. 'The man who never had to toil / To gain and farm his patch of soil' - 'toil' is hard, continuous labour, and the phrase 'gain and farm' suggests that even the land had to be earned before it could be worked. 'Who never had to win his share / Of sun and sky and light and air' uses the language of the first stanza deliberately: a man, like a tree, must compete for his share of what sustains him, and the word 'win' implies effort and the possibility of loss. The result is stated in the same flat rhythm as before: 'Never became a manly man / But lived and died as he began.' 'Manly' here does not mean aggressive; it means fully developed, mature, able to bear weight. 'Lived and died as he began' is the saddest line in the poem, because it describes a life in which nothing was added. The stanza's parallelism with the first makes the comparison explicit before the next stanza states the law.
questions.explanation: Lines 7-12 explained with attention to the deliberate echo of stanza 1 ('win his share' answering 'got its share') and to the meaning of 'manly'.

questions.question: Explain the following lines: Line No. 13-18 - 'Good timber does not....... good timbers grow.'
questions.answer: The third stanza states the law that the first two stanzas have illustrated. 'Good timber does not grow with ease' - the sentence is almost a proverb, and 'ease' is the enemy named in the previous stanzas. The next three lines pile up parallel clauses to show how the opposite of ease works: 'The stronger wind, the stronger trees, / The further sky, the greater length, / The more the storm, the more the strength.' This is anaphora and parallelism at once: each clause has the same shape ('the more ... the more'), and the repetition makes the law sound inevitable rather than arguable. 'The further sky, the greater length' adds the idea of striving upward for room, and 'the more the storm, the more the strength' compresses the whole poem into six words. The stanza closes by joining the two worlds: 'By sun and cold, by rain and snow / In trees and men good timbers grow.' The alliteration of 'sun' and 'snow' and the balanced pairs make the line feel like a conclusion, and 'good timbers' carries the title into the human comparison.
questions.explanation: Lines 13-18 explained, with the parallel 'the more ... the more' construction named as anaphora and the final line linked to the title.

questions.question: Explain the following lines: Line No. 19-24 - 'Where thickest lies.........common law of life.'
questions.answer: The last stanza shows the finished product of the law. 'Where thickest lies the forest growth / We find the patriarchs of both' - in the dense part of the forest, where competition for light is hardest, stand the oldest and greatest trees; 'of both' means patriarchs of trees and of men. 'Patriarchs' is a word for the respected elders of a tribe, so the trees are given the dignity of age and authority. 'And they hold counsel with the stars' is the poem's finest image: the tops of the old trees seem to converse with the sky, and the phrase suggests wisdom, wide vision and calm. Then comes the cost: 'Whose broken branches show the scars, / Of many winds and much of strife.' The old trees are not unmarked; their scars are the record of everything they survived, and the scars are worn as proof rather than as shame. The final line, 'This is the common law of life', closes the poem by extending the law from forest to humankind - and to all living things.
questions.explanation: Lines 19-24 explained, with 'patriarchs', 'hold counsel with the stars' and the meaning of the scars discussed, and the closing line read as the poem's universal conclusion.

questions.question: Look at the picture and express what you observe in it.
questions.answer: The picture shows a winter scene on a lonely moor. Snow covers the open ground, a bare hawthorn hedge and a low stone wall run across the slope, and a small wooden bridge crosses a stream in the distance. In the foreground a little girl in a cloak is walking away from a small cottage, holding a lantern in her hand; her footprints are the only marks on the white snow. The sky is heavy and grey, and the whole scene feels quiet, cold and rather sad. Looking at it, one feels that the child is alone in a wide, unfriendly landscape and that something is about to go wrong.
questions.explanation: Open-ended observation task. No illustration is reproduced on the printed page in this edition, so the answer describes the winter-moor scene that the ballad itself creates (lantern, snow, hedge, stone-wall, wooden bridge, solitary child).

questions.question: How can you describe an obedient child?
questions.answer: An obedient child is one who listens to his parents and does what he is asked, but obedience is more than simply saying yes. Such a child answers respectfully, does the errand promptly and cheerfully rather than sulking, and can be trusted with small responsibilities. He also understands why a rule exists, so he does not need to be watched all the time. At the same time, an obedient child is not a frightened child: he feels free to ask questions, to point out a difficulty and to say when something seems unsafe. Lucy Gray in the poem is exactly this kind of child - she answers her father, "That, Father! will I gladly do" - and that is what makes her story so painful.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question, answered with a definition and linked to Lucy's reply in lines 17-20.

questions.question: How much are your parents attached to you?
questions.answer: My parents are attached to me in ways I often take for granted. My mother knows from my face whether the day has gone well, and my father, who says little, will still wait up until I reach home. They remember what I like to eat, worry about my exams more than I do, and sacrifice their own comfort for my schooling. Sometimes their attachment feels like pressure, because they want me to do well and I do not always agree with their plans. But when I am ill or disappointed, there is no doubt in my mind that I am the centre of their world. The poem shows the same bond in the parents who shout for Lucy all night and weep when they find her footprints.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the closing sentence connects the answer to the parents' search in lines 33-44.

questions.question: Does anyone among you know any story related to a child?
questions.answer: Yes, I know a story that my grandmother tells about a child in our village. One winter evening a boy of seven was sent to the next street to return a borrowed kettle. He took a shortcut through the fields, the fog came down, and he lost his way. His family searched all night with torches, and at dawn they found him asleep in a haystack, cold but safe, with the kettle still in his arms. The village laughed about it for years, but my grandmother always ends the story seriously: a small errand can turn into a great danger when the weather changes. That is almost exactly the situation of Lucy Gray, who was sent on an errand in the snow and never came back.
questions.explanation: Open-ended question inviting a personal anecdote; the model supplies one and links it to the poem's situation.

questions.question: What do you know about William Wordsworth?
questions.answer: William Wordsworth (1770-1850) was the greatest of the English Romantic poets of nature. He was born in Cockermouth in the Lake District, was orphaned early, and grew up among mountains and lakes which remained the subject of his poetry all his life. With Samuel Taylor Coleridge he published 'Lyrical Ballads' in 1798; its preface, added in 1800, argued that poetry should be written in the real language of ordinary people and about ordinary rural life. His long autobiographical poem 'The Prelude' describes the growth of a poet's mind. He believed that nature is a living presence that teaches and heals, and that childhood is a time of special vision. 'Lucy Gray', like the 'Lucy' poems, shows his interest in a simple country child, in nature, and in the mystery of early death.
questions.explanation: Biographical background question; the facts about Wordsworth's life and beliefs prepare students for the ballad's plain diction and nature setting.

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 1: solitary]
questions.answer: "Solitary" means alone, single, without companions. In the poem it describes Lucy as the speaker first sees her: "The solitary child" (line 4), a girl who had "No mate, no comrade" (line 5) and lived on a wide moor. The word carries both facts - she is physically alone - and mood: it makes her seem small, exposed and vulnerable in the wide landscape, and it prepares us for the loneliness of her death.
questions.explanation: Contextual support: line 4, "The solitary child", reinforced by "No mate, no comrade Lucy knew" in line 5.

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 2: wretched]
questions.answer: "Wretched" means very unhappy, miserable, pitiable. In the poem it describes the parents on the night Lucy is lost: "The wretched parents all that night / Went shouting far and wide" (lines 33-34). Here the word does not mean 'wicked' or 'worthless' as it can in older English; it expresses the depth of their grief and helplessness as they search the snow for their child.
questions.explanation: Contextual support: lines 33-36, where the parents shout all night with "neither sound nor sight / To serve them for a guide".

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 3: comrade]
questions.answer: "Comrade" means a companion, friend or mate, especially one who shares one's work or way of life. In the poem the word is used negatively: "No mate, no comrade Lucy knew" (line 5). The pair "mate" and "comrade" stresses that Lucy had no playmate at all on the moor; her only company was nature, which makes her childhood unusually silent and makes her disappearance in the snow even more pitiable.
questions.explanation: Contextual support: line 5. The negation is important - the word measures her isolation.

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 4: wanton]
questions.answer: "Wanton" here means playful, lively, free and unrestrained - not 'cruel' or 'immoral' as in some modern uses. The poet says Lucy's feet "disperse the powdery snow" with "many a wanton stroke" (lines 26-27). The word catches the carefree energy of a child running through fresh snow, and it contrasts sharply with the deadly storm that follows a few lines later.
questions.explanation: Contextual support: lines 25-28, where Lucy is compared to a mountain roe and her steps make the snow rise "like smoke".

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 5: tripping]
questions.answer: "Tripping" means moving lightly and quickly with small, dainty steps. In the last stanza the villagers say that Lucy "trips along" over "rough and smooth" (lines 61-62). The word suggests a light, dancing, almost ghostly movement, and because she "never looks behind" it adds to the supernatural atmosphere of the legend with which the ballad ends.
questions.explanation: Contextual support: lines 61-64, the closing legend of Lucy singing "a solitary song / That whistles in the wind".

questions.question: Read the poem again and encircle the correct option. 1. The poet chanced to see Lucy________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (a) at the break of day.
questions.explanation: Supported by line 3: "I chanced to see at break of day / The solitary child."
questions.optionsRaw: (a) at the break of day   (b) in the evening   (c) in the afternoon   (d) at night

questions.question: 2. Lucy's father asked Lucy to go to the town with a lantern to bring her________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (d) mother.
questions.explanation: Lines 13-16: "You to the town must go; / And take a lantern, Child, to light / Your mother through the snow."
questions.optionsRaw: (a) aunt   (b) sister   (c) brother   (d) mother

questions.question: 3. Lucy replied to her father that she would________ go to the town to take back her mother.
questions.answer: The correct option is (a) gladly.
questions.explanation: Line 17: "That, Father! will I gladly do".
questions.optionsRaw: (a) gladly   (b) sadly   (c) unwillingly   (d) probably

questions.question: 4. Lucy couldn't reach the town because________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (d) she lost her way in storm.
questions.explanation: Lines 29-32: the storm "came on before its time", she "wandered up and down" and "never reached the town".

options.text: she lost her way in storm

questions.optionsRaw: (a) it was late   (b) she didn't get any conveyance   (c) her mother reached home   (d) she lost her way in storm
questions.correctAnswer: (d) she lost her way in storm

questions.question: 5. The wooden bridge was at distance of________ from Lucy's home.
questions.answer: The correct option is (b) a furlong.
questions.explanation: Lines 39-40: "the bridge of wood, / A furlong from their door" - a furlong is about 200 metres.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) a mile   (b) a furlong   (c) a kilometre   (d) a few feet

questions.question: 6. Lucy's parents became certain of her death when they saw ________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (a) her foot prints.
questions.explanation: Lines 43-44: "the mother spied / The print of Lucy's feet", and the trail ends in the middle of the bridge (lines 55-56).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) her foot prints   (b) her body   (c) her lantern   (d) her shoes

questions.question: 7. Some people still believe that Lucy can be seen ________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (a) in mountains.
questions.explanation: Lines 57-60: "Yet some maintain that to this day / She is a living child; / That you may see sweet Lucy Gray / Upon the lonesome wild." The 'lonesome wild' is the open moorland, so among the printed options 'in mountains' is the nearest.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) in mountains   (b) in wind   (c) in town   (d) on bridge

questions.question: 8. People believe Lucy can be seen doing these activities except ________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (d) talking to people.
questions.explanation: Lines 61-64 say she "trips along", "never looks behind" and "sings a solitary song"; talking to people is not mentioned. The options 'looking straight' and 'moving rapidly' paraphrase "never looks behind" and "trips along".
questions.optionsRaw: (a) looking straight   (b) singing songs   (c) moving rapidly   (d) talking to people

questions.question: Read the poem again and answer the following questions. 1. Where did Lucy live and what kind of child she was?
questions.answer: Lucy lived with her parents in a cottage "beside a human door" on a wide, lonely moor (lines 5-8). She was an only child with "no mate, no comrade": her playmates were the fawn and the hare, and the whole moor was her world. The poet calls her "the sweetest thing that ever grew" and "the solitary child", so she was gentle, lovely and innocent. Her reply to her father - "That, Father! will I gladly do" - shows that she was also cheerful, trusting and obedient, and the comparison with a mountain roe shows how light-footed and full of life she was.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 4-8 (her home and solitude), line 17 (her obedience), lines 25-28 (her lightness).

questions.question: 2. Where did Lucy's father send her and why?
questions.answer: Her father sent her to the town, across the moor, on a stormy winter night. Her mother was in the town and had to come home through the falling snow, so Lucy was to carry a lantern and walk ahead of her to light the way. The father says: "To-night will be a stormy night - / You to the town must go; / And take a lantern, Child, to light / Your mother through the snow" (lines 13-16). The errand was meant to be a short, helpful one, but it took the child into the storm that killed her.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 13-16; the purpose of the lantern is stated in line 15.

questions.question: 3. What did Lucy mean when she said 'yonder is the moon'?
questions.answer: Lucy was answering her father's warning about the dark and the storm. She meant that it was still early - "'Tis scarcely afternoon" - and that the moon was already visible over the moor ("yonder" means 'over there'). In her innocence she thought she had plenty of light: the afternoon sun, then the moon, and the lantern in her hand. Her words show her eagerness to go and her complete trust that nothing could go wrong. They are also painfully ironic, because the storm came "before its time" and neither moon nor lantern could save her.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 17-20. The dramatic irony is completed in lines 29-32.

questions.question: 4. Why did Lucy take lantern with her?
questions.answer: Lucy took the lantern because her father told her to: it was to "light / Your mother through the snow" (lines 15-16). Her mother had to walk home from the town in the dark, and a lantern would show her the path over the rough moor and past the wooden bridge. For Lucy herself the lantern was also a comfort, since it made her feel that the way was safe. In the event it became the saddest detail of the story: the child who carried light for her mother was lost in the snow, and the lantern was never found.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 13-16 and line 24, "and Lucy took / The lantern in her hand".

questions.question: 5. Do you think that the tragedy would have been prevented if Lucy's father himself had gone down the town?
questions.answer: Yes, most probably. If the father had gone himself, Lucy would have stayed in the cottage and the storm could not have harmed her; an adult could also have judged the weather better and turned back. The poem makes this clear by showing that the storm "came on before its time" (line 29) - a danger no child could foresee. But it is also fair to say that the father's decision was an ordinary one: the town was only a furlong away, the errand was small, and he did not know the storm would break early. The tragedy is not caused by cruelty but by a small, human miscalculation, which is what makes the ballad so disturbing.
questions.explanation: Open-ended judgement question. The answer weighs both sides and supports each with lines 29-32 and lines 39-40.

questions.question: 6. What happened to Lucy while she was going to the town?
questions.answer: While Lucy was crossing the moor the storm broke earlier than anyone expected: "The storm came on before its time" (line 29). The whirling snow hid the path, and she "wandered up and down" and climbed "many a hill" but "never reached the town" (lines 30-32). Overcome by cold and exhaustion, she died in the snow. Her footprints later led her parents down the hill, through the hawthorn hedge and the stone wall, across a field and on to the wooden bridge, where they stopped in the middle of the plank - the only trace left of her.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 29-32 and the trail of footprints in lines 45-56.

questions.question: 7. What efforts did Lucy's parents make in finding her?
questions.answer: They searched all night. "The wretched parents all that night / Went shouting far and wide" (lines 33-34), but there was "neither sound nor sight / To serve them for a guide". At daybreak they climbed a hill that overlooked the moor and from there saw the wooden bridge a furlong from their door (lines 37-40). Then the mother caught sight of Lucy's footprints in the snow, and they followed them "one by one" - down the steep hill, through the broken hawthorn hedge, along the long stone wall, across an open field, and at last on to the bridge, where the marks ended.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 33-56 describe the night search and the tracking of the footprints.

questions.question: 8. What led the Lucy's parents to the bridge?
questions.answer: The footprints in the snow led them. When the mother "spied / The print of Lucy's feet" (lines 43-44), the parents followed the small marks "downwards from the steep hill's edge", through the "broken hawthorn hedge" and "by the long stone-wall" (lines 45-48). They crossed an open field, where "the marks were still the same", tracked them "nor ever lost", and so "to the bridge they came" (lines 49-52). Finally they followed the prints "into the middle of the plank" (line 55), and there they stopped.
questions.explanation: Textual support: the tracking sequence runs from line 45 to line 56.

questions.question: 9. What do people still maintain about Lucy Gray and why?
questions.answer: Some people still maintain that Lucy is not dead but "a living child", and that she may be seen "upon the lonesome wild" - tripping over rough and smooth, never looking behind, singing "a solitary song / That whistles in the wind" (lines 57-64). They believe this because her body was never found: the footprints ended in the middle of the bridge, and no further trace was ever discovered. Out of that mystery the country people made a legend, and the ballad keeps it alive. The ending is deliberately ambiguous: the reader may accept the ghostly story or the plain fact of a child lost in the snow.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 57-64. The legend grows out of the unexplained ending of the footprints at line 56.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the poem based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [1. Poetic Diction]
questions.answer: Wordsworth uses the plain, bare diction of the old ballad rather than the ornate language of Augustan poetry. Most of the words are monosyllables - "snow", "moor", "hook", "lantern", "bridge", "wall" - and the few longer words ("solitary", "comrade", "wretched") are simple and familiar. Archaic ballad forms such as "Oft", "yonder" and "'Tis" give the poem the sound of an old country song, while the dialogue ("That, Father! will I gladly do") uses the actual speech of a child and a cottager. Concrete nouns and verbs do the work that adjectives might do elsewhere: we see the faggot-band, the hawthorn hedge and the stone wall, and we hear the parents shouting. The effect is honesty and pathos - the story seems reported rather than invented, which makes it more moving.
questions.explanation: Diction is discussed with examples of monosyllables, archaisms and the child's direct speech.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the poem based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [2. Theme]
questions.answer: The central theme is the loss of an innocent child and the grief that follows. Around it cluster several related themes. One is the fragility of childhood: Lucy is "the sweetest thing that ever grew", yet a single winter night destroys her. Another is obedience and parental trust: Lucy goes "gladly" on the errand, and her father trusts her with it, so the disaster grows out of love rather than cruelty. A third is the power and indifference of nature: the storm comes "before its time" and does not spare the child, even though the same nature is beautiful enough to be compared to a fawn or a roe. Finally there is memory and legend: the footprints end mid-bridge, the body is never found, and the villagers keep Lucy alive as a figure on the moor. The poem thus moves from fact to folklore, suggesting that the dead survive in the stories we tell.
questions.explanation: Theme is supported by lines 7-8 (innocence), 17 (obedience), 29 (nature's power) and 57-64 (legend).

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the poem based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [3. Structure]
questions.answer: The poem is a ballad of sixteen four-line stanzas, sixty-four lines in all. It is written in the ballad stanza: the first and third lines are longer (usually iambic tetrameter) and the second and fourth shorter (iambic trimeter), rhyming abab - for example "Gray/day" and "wild/child" in stanza 1.
