In the poem the sense is the first: the Khahoris' movement looks like rambling to the world, but it is in fact a disciplined search, so the word carries an irony - what seems aimless is the most purposeful journey of all.
questions.explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; its meaning contrasts the world's view of the Khahoris with the poem's view.

questions.question: Work in pairs and find out the meaning of the following words by using dictionary. Read the poem carefully and write the contextual meaning against each word. After completing, share your work with your partner. [No. 8: flicker]
questions.answer: "Flicker" means to burn or shine unsteadily, with a light that brightens and dims; as a noun it is such a wavering light. In the poem's imagery the fire lit in the wilderness flickers, and so does the lamp of faith in the seeker's heart - small and unsteady, yet enough to guide him through the dark.
questions.explanation: The word is not in the printed excerpt; the fire imagery is supplied by lines 10-11.

questions.question: Read the poem again and encircle the correct option. 1. Khahoris trouble their bodies to attain their________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (a) goal.
questions.explanation: Line 6: "Giving much trouble to their bodies, they sought their goal." The poem's word is 'goal', meaning the spiritual aim of their search.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) goal   (b) class   (c) earnings   (d) destination

questions.question: 2. Khahoris face severe________ while achieving their goals.
questions.answer: The correct option is (c) hardships.
questions.explanation: Lines 4-9 describe bodily hardship: searching in the rocks, being "reduced to bones", dry faces and "slippers old and torn". They are not shown facing criticism, so 'all of them' is too wide; 'hardships' is the accurate summary.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) criticism   (b) conditions   (c) hardships   (d) all of them

questions.question: 3. Khahoris never take their________ when they have goals.
questions.answer: The correct option is (a) property.
questions.explanation: The poem says the Khahoris give up "both the worlds" (line 14) and travel with nothing; they do not carry property with them when they set out towards their goal. (The printed sentence is awkward; if it is read as 'never take care of themselves', option (b) could also be argued, but 'property' fits the poem's theme of renunciation best.)
questions.optionsRaw: (a) property   (b) care   (c) followers   (d) none

questions.question: 4. "Khahoris' faces are dry, on their feet are slippers old and torn" shows the________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (c) hardships.
questions.explanation: The line (line 7) is a list of physical signs of hardship - dry faces and worn-out slippers. 'Struggle' is close in meaning, but 'hardships' is the exact word for the conditions described, and it matches the wording of question 2.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) struggle   (b) emotion   (c) hardships   (d) pleasure

questions.question: 5. Khahoris recognition is like ________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (b) raft in ocean.
questions.explanation: Line 3: "Their recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world." The world is the ocean and the recognition of the Godly is the raft that keeps the seeker from drowning.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) caravan in desert   (b) raft in ocean   (c) guide in mountains   (d) safety in jingle

questions.question: 6. Khahoris can be found even where there is no trace of:
questions.answer: The correct option is (c) birds.
questions.explanation: Line 10: "Where not a trace of birds is seen, fire is lit". The place is so desolate that not even a bird is to be seen, yet the ascetics are there.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) human beings   (b) animals   (c) birds   (d) cattle

questions.question: 7. In fourth stanza, the word 'save' is used in sense of ________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (d) except.
questions.explanation: Line 11: "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" Here 'save' is a preposition meaning 'except': who except a group of ascetics can light that fire? It does not mean 'rescue' or 'preserve'.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) safety   (b) preservation   (c) together   (d) except

questions.question: 8. True seekers can only be known to those who are for ________.
questions.answer: The correct option is (d) spiritual realm.
questions.explanation: Lines 15-17: "True seekers still exist, / Known only to those who are for spiritual realms". The phrase is repeated from the poem, so 'spiritual realm' is the answer.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) jungle dwelling   (b) deserted abodes   (c) mountain peaks   (d) spiritual realm

questions.question: Work in pairs and read the above selection again. Comprehend it thoroughly and paraphrase it in simple words. After you have completed, share it with your partner.
questions.answer:
Paraphrase:

Mother, I have seen those people who have had a vision of the Beloved. To understand them one must spend at least one night in the company of those who live with God. The recognition of such people becomes a raft that carries one across the ocean of this world.

The Khahoris set out early on their journey. They search among the rocks and are reduced to mere bones; they give their bodies a great deal of trouble in order to reach their goal. Their faces are dry and their slippers old and torn. They have crossed a land in which even the wisest lose their way, and their secret ones speak of the secrets of that distant land.

In a place where not even a bird can be seen, a fire is lit. Who but a group of ascetics could kindle it? Those who went into the jungle were not led astray; those who took the highway were ambushed; but those who gave up both this world and the next were saved from ignorance.

True seekers still exist. They are known only to those who belong to the spiritual world, and having found that world they have built their nests close to it.
questions.explanation: Open-ended paraphrase task; the model follows the six stanzas line by line in plain modern prose.

questions.question: Read the selection again and answer the following questions. 1. How is Khahori's character depicted by the poet?
questions.answer: The Khahori is depicted as a wandering ascetic who has given up both worlds. He sets out early, searches among rocks, reduces his body "to bones", and wears slippers that are "old and torn"; his face is "dry" from hardship. He is patient, disciplined and fearless, travelling through a land "where even the knowing ones are lost". He is also secretive and inward - "Their secretive ones, talk secrets of that far off land" - and utterly devoted, since he troubles his body only to reach his "goal". The poet admires him: his "recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world", and he is one of the "true seekers" whose nests are built close to the spiritual realm.
questions.explanation: Character sketch supported by lines 3-9 and 15-17.

questions.question: 2. How do the Khahoris experience sleep?
questions.answer: The poem does not describe a comfortable night's rest, because the Khahoris have renounced comfort. They spend their nights in the open or in caves, on rock and hard ground, after long hours of prayer and meditation; their bodies are "reduced to bones" and they give themselves "much trouble", so sleep is brief and austere rather than refreshing. The opening lines suggest the right way to know them: "One must stay a night with those who with God have been" (line 2) - a night in their company is itself a spiritual lesson. Their sleep, in short, is a form of discipline: little of it, taken in a hard place, and offered up as part of their search.
questions.explanation: Inference question: the printed selection mentions the night spent with the Godly (line 2) and the mortification of the body (lines 5-7), but does not describe sleep directly.

questions.question: 3. Where and why do Khahoris spend their days and nights?
questions.answer: They spend their days and nights in wild, lonely places: among the rocks, on the highland ridges, in the jungle and in "that far off land" where even the knowing lose their way, where "not a trace of birds is seen". They go there because their goal is spiritual, not worldly. Solitude removes the distractions of the marketplace, family and reputation, and hardship trains the body to obey the soul. The poem also suggests that the way is dangerous - some who took the highway "were way-laid" - so the desert is safer for the seeker than the crowded road. They are not running away from life; they are looking for its reality.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 4-14 (the places and the dangers) and line 6 (the goal).

questions.question: 4. What does the poet want to say when he says "Where not a trace of birds is seen, fire is lit"?
questions.answer: He means that in the most desolate place imaginable - so empty that not even a bird passes over it - the ascetics still light their fire. The fire is both literal, the small fire of wanderers in the cold, and symbolic: it is the fire of divine love, of remembrance and of spiritual vision. The line therefore says that God is found where the world is absent, and that the inner light burns brightest where there is nothing else to see. The rhetorical question that follows, "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?", adds that only those who have renounced everything are capable of such devotion.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 10-11, where the literal fire carries a symbolic meaning.

questions.question: 5. What reward does a Khahori get after his hard work?
questions.answer: His reward is spiritual, not material. The poem says that the recognition of the Godly "becomes a raft in this ocean of the world" (line 3): it carries the seeker safely across the troubles of worldly existence. The true seekers "have found" the spiritual realm and "have built their nests close to them" (line 17), which suggests peace, belonging and nearness to God. They are also "known" to those who belong to that realm - the reward of being recognised by the spiritually wise. In Sufi terms, the Khahori's hard work ends in union with, or closeness to, the Beloved.
questions.explanation: Textual support: lines 1-3 and 15-17.

questions.question: 6. Sur Khahori is the narration of Khahoris' struggle. Elaborate.
questions.answer: Yes, the selection is a record of struggle from beginning to end. It begins with the effort of understanding: one must stay a night with the Godly to recognise them. It then shows the physical struggle - the Khahoris set out early, search in rocks, reduce their bodies to bones, and walk until their faces are dry and their slippers old and torn. Next comes the struggle with the country itself: they cross a land where even the knowing are lost, a place without a trace of birds. The poem then names the dangers of different paths - the jungle did not mislead, the highway ambushed - and ends with the hardest struggle of all, giving up "both the worlds". The final lines show the result: the true seekers survive and build their nests near the spiritual realm. The whole poem is thus a narrative of trial, endurance and arrival.
questions.explanation: Open-ended elaboration; the answer traces the stages of struggle through all six stanzas.

questions.question: 7. Which poetic devices have been used in this poetry? Write with the examples.
questions.answer: The selection uses several devices. Metaphor: "Their recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world" - the world is an ocean and spiritual recognition a raft. Symbolism: fire stands for divine love (line 10), the nest for the soul's settled home (line 17), and the ocean for worldly life. Rhetorical question: "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11). Apostrophe: the poem opens by addressing "Mother!" (line 1). Alliteration: "Searching in the rocks, reduced to bones" (line 5) and "slippers old and torn" (line 7). Contrast: the jungle and the highway, and "gave up both the worlds" (line 14). Repetition and anaphora: "Those who went... Those on... Those who gave up" (lines 12-14), and the echo of "known" in lines 15-16. Imagery: visual details such as dry faces, torn slippers and bones; and hyperbole in "reduced to bones". The verse is unrhymed free verse with lines of uneven length, which suits its meditative, translated style.
questions.explanation: Devices are quoted from the printed lines, with line numbers.

questions.question: 8. How do you express your emotions on the struggle of your friend or a family member?
questions.answer: When someone close to me is struggling, I try to do three things. First, I listen without hurrying to give advice; often the person needs to say the difficulty aloud more than he needs a solution. Second, I offer concrete help rather than vague sympathy - sharing the housework when my mother is unwell, sitting with a friend the night before his exam, or going with him to the doctor. Third, I remind him of what he has already survived, because a person in the middle of a struggle forgets his own strength. I also pray for him and, if he allows it, pray with him. What I try not to do is compare his struggle with mine or tell him that it will pass. The Khahoris' journey teaches me that struggle is easier when someone stays a night with you, which is exactly what line 2 of the poem recommends.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response question; the model answer connects the answer to line 2 of the poem.

questions.question: Work in groups of three. Compose your own poem on the theme of Search of Reality, using elements of poetry based on three stanzas. Each member of group should compose 1 stanza. Once your group has composed the poem, exchange it with other groups.
questions.answer:
A model group poem (three stanzas, one by each member):

I left the market and the noise,
the counted coin, the guarded door;
I walked into the hills alone
to look for something more.

The rocks were sharp, the night was long,
my shoes were torn, my lamp burned low;
but something in the darkness sang
the way that I should go.

I did not find a throne of gold,
I found a fire that would not die -
and all the world I left behind
was smaller than the sky.

How the elements were used: the three quatrains rhyme abcb (door/more, low/go, die/sky) and keep a steady ballad rhythm. The "market" and the "guarded door" are symbols of worldly life, the hills and rocks are the hardships of the search, the lamp is faith and the fire is the divine presence; "something in the darkness sang" is personification, and "smaller than the sky" is a comparison that measures the world against spiritual reality. The stanzas follow the same three stages as Sur Khahori: leaving the world, enduring the way, and finding a reality that is not gold.
questions.explanation: Open-ended creative task. The model supplies a complete poem and an explanation of its devices, images and structure.

questions.question: Work individually and write the central idea of the lines of Sur Khahori in your notebook. Once you have completed, exchange your work with your class fellows.
questions.answer: The central idea of this selection is that the search for spiritual reality demands total renunciation and patient endurance, and that such a search is rewarded by nearness to God. The Khahoris give up home, comfort and even the good opinion of the world; they cross rocks and deserts until their bodies are worn out, because their goal is not wealth but vision. The poem presents the world as a dangerous ocean through which the recognition of the Godly is the only raft, and it insists that the real seeker cannot be recognised by ordinary people: "True seekers still exist, / Known only to those who are for spiritual realms". In the end the seeker finds a place near the spiritual world and builds his "nest" there. The message for the reader is that reality is not found in the marketplace but in discipline, humility and the company of those who live with God.
questions.explanation: Central idea supported by lines 1-3 (the raft), 4-9 (hardship), 12-14 (renunciation) and 15-17 (the reward).

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [1. Poetic Diction]
questions.answer: The diction is simple, grave and intensely devotional. The translator has avoided ornate English and kept the plain vocabulary of Sufi poetry: "Beloved", "recognition", "ascetics", "spiritual realms", "seeker". Concrete words - rocks, bones, slippers, fire, nest - carry the abstract meaning, so that a spiritual idea is always attached to something the reader can see. The opening apostrophe "Mother!" gives the verse the intimacy of a family conversation, while phrases such as "that far off land" and "their secretive ones" preserve the mystery of the original Sindhi. Repetition of "those who" and "known" creates a liturgical, chant-like effect, appropriate to poetry meant to be sung in the company of devotees. The diction therefore serves the subject: it is humble in vocabulary and elevated in feeling.
questions.explanation: Diction analysed through concrete nouns, devotional vocabulary and repetition.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [2. Theme]
questions.answer: The theme is the search for Reality - for God - through renunciation and endurance. Everything in the selection serves it: the Beloved seen by the few, the night spent with the Godly, the raft of recognition, the Khahoris' early departure, their broken bodies, the birdless waste where the fire is lit, the dangers of jungle and highway, the giving up of "both the worlds", and the final nest built near the spiritual realm. A related theme is the hiddenness of true wisdom: the real seekers are not advertised, and they are "known only to those who are for spiritual realms". A third is the contrast between the world's idea of a wasted life and the poem's idea of a life well spent: what looks like wandering is in fact the most purposeful journey a human being can make.
questions.explanation: Theme traced through the six stanzas, with the contrast between worldly and spiritual values.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [3. Structure]
questions.answer: The selection is a short free-verse poem of seventeen lines arranged in six stanzas of uneven length: three lines, three, three, two, three and three. There is no regular rhyme or metre, as is usual in translated Sindhi verse, but there is a clear structure of thought. Stanza 1 (lines 1-3) states the vision and the raft; stanzas 2-3 (lines 4-9) describe the Khahoris and their journey; stanza 4 (lines 10-11) presents the fire in the wilderness and the rhetorical question; stanza 5 (lines 12-14) draws the contrast between the three kinds of travellers; and stanza 6 (lines 15-17) concludes with the true seekers and their reward. The movement is thus from statement to description to paradox to conclusion, and the short fourth stanza, with its single question, acts as the turning point of the poem.
questions.explanation: Structure described by stanza lengths and the progression of ideas.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [4. Language]
questions.answer: The language is metaphorical, symbolic and quietly musical. The controlling metaphor is that of the world as an ocean and spiritual recognition as a raft (line 3). Fire, nest, rocks, slippers and bones are symbols as well as objects. The poet uses a rhetorical question - "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11) - to make the reader answer for himself, and repetition with variation - "Those who went... Those on... Those who gave up" (lines 12-14) - to give the lines a chant-like force. Alliteration ("Searching in the rocks, reduced to bones") and long vowel sounds slow the verse down, matching the slow, hard journey described. The tone is reverent and compassionate rather than excited; the poet speaks of the Khahoris with admiration and of the reader with gentle instruction.
questions.explanation: Language analysed through the central metaphor, symbolism, rhetoric, repetition and sound.

questions.question: Work in pairs and give a critical appreciation of the lines based on the following aspects. Once you have written, compare your work with your partner. [5. Message]
questions.answer: The message is that spiritual reality is found only by those who are willing to give up everything else, and that such a search, however hard, is worth making. The Khahoris endure hunger, cold, rocky paths and torn slippers, and they surrender "both the worlds", yet the poem does not present them as pitiable: their recognition is a raft, their struggle ends in nearness to God. To the ordinary reader the message is a challenge - to ask what he is living for, and whether he is brave enough to travel light. At the same time the poem teaches tolerance and humility: true seekers may be hidden among the poor and the unimpressive, and only those who are themselves spiritual can recognise them. The poem thus combines devotion with a quiet warning against judging by appearances.
questions.explanation: Message drawn from the Khahoris' renunciation, their reward, and the hiddenness of true seekers.

questions.question: Work individually and identify the poetic devices in the selection. Make a list of them and use them in your sentences. Share your work with your class fellows after you have completed.
questions.answer:
List of devices, with the poem's example and a sentence of my own:

1. Metaphor - "Their recognition becomes a raft in this ocean of the world" (line 3). My sentence: In the examination hall, my elder brother's advice was a raft in the ocean of questions.

2. Symbolism - the fire (line 10), the nest (line 17), the ocean (line 3) and the rocks (line 5). My sentence: The little lamp on our table is a symbol of the hope that keeps our family together.

3. Rhetorical question - "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?" (line 11). My sentence: Who but a mother can understand a child's silence?

4. Apostrophe - "Mother!" (line 1), where the poet addresses his mother directly. My sentence: O Pakistan, how patiently your people have waited for justice!

5. Alliteration - "Searching in the rocks, reduced to bones" (line 5); "slippers old and torn" (line 7). My sentence: The sad, silent seekers sat among the stones.

6. Contrast - the jungle that did not mislead and the highway that ambushed travellers (lines 12-13); "gave up both the worlds" (line 14). My sentence: The rich man slept uneasily while the poor labourer slept in peace.

7. Repetition / anaphora - "Those who went... Those on... Those who gave up" (lines 12-14). My sentence: Those who work, those who wait and those who pray are all serving the country.

8. Imagery - dry faces, torn slippers, bones, a fire in a birdless waste. My sentence: After the flood we saw cracked walls, broken cots and a single smoking fire.

9. Hyperbole - "reduced to bones" (line 5). My sentence: I have told you a thousand times to carry an umbrella.

10. Enjambment and free verse - the sense runs on from line to line without a fixed rhyme, as in lines 1-3. My sentence (a short free-verse couplet): The road kept climbing / and the sky came closer.
questions.explanation: Open-ended device-hunting task; every device is quoted from the printed lines and used in an original sentence.

questions.question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 1-3: Mother! I saw those, ... raft in this ocean of the world.]
questions.answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: These are the opening lines of the selection. The poet turns to his mother and tells her what he has seen and understood about the people who have known God.

Explanation: The exclamation "Mother!" gives the lines the intimacy of a son confiding in the person closest to him. The poet says he has seen those who have "Beloved seen" - the mystics who have had a vision of God. To understand such people, one must "stay a night" with those "who with God have been": their holiness is not learnt from books but absorbed by living in their company. Their "recognition" - the knowledge of God that they possess - "becomes a raft in this ocean of the world", carrying the seeker across the dangerous sea of worldly life. The metaphor makes the world vast and drowning, and makes spiritual knowledge the one thing that keeps a person afloat.
questions.explanation: The opening stanza states the value of the company of the Godly and introduces the raft metaphor.

questions.question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 4-6: Khahoris prepared ... they sought their goal.]
questions.answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: Having spoken of those who have seen God, the poet now describes the Khahoris - the wandering ascetics who set out in search of Him.

Explanation: The Khahoris "prepared early to depart", which shows both discipline and eagerness: they do not delay once they have chosen the path. They are "searching in the rocks" and are "reduced to bones", so their bodies have been worn thin by fasting, walking and exposure. They give "much trouble to their bodies" - they treat the body as a servant of the soul, not its master - and all this is done because "they sought their goal". The stanza makes the search physical as well as spiritual: the reader sees the rocks, the thin bodies and the effort, and understands that the spiritual life described in the first stanza has a price.
questions.explanation: The stanza describes the Khahoris' early departure and bodily hardship in pursuit of their goal.

questions.question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 7-9: Their faces are dry ... secrets of that far off land.]
questions.answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: The poet continues his description of the Khahoris on their journey.

Explanation: "Their faces are dry" suggests sun, wind and fasting, and "slippers old and torn" shows how far they have walked and how little they own. They have "traversed that land, where even the knowing ones are lost" - a country so trackless that even the wise cannot find their way - and yet the Khahoris pass through it. Their "secretive ones" speak "secrets of that far off land", that is, the mysteries of the spiritual world they have reached. The phrase "far off" keeps that world distant and mysterious for the ordinary listener, while the torn slippers keep the journey firmly on the ground.
questions.explanation: The stanza combines physical hardship with the mystery of the spiritual country the Khahoris know.

questions.question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 10-11: Where not a trace ... ascetics can kindle it?]
questions.answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: The description of the desolate country reaches its height in these two lines.

Explanation: The place is so empty that "not a trace of birds is seen" - no living thing crosses it - and yet "fire is lit" there. The fire is literal, the small fire of wanderers in the cold, and symbolic, the fire of divine love and remembrance. The rhetorical question, "Who save a group of ascetics can kindle it?", answers itself: only those who have renounced the world have the purity and courage to light such a fire in such a place. Here "save" means 'except'. The couplet is the spiritual centre of the poem: where the world is completely absent, the presence of God becomes visible.
questions.explanation: The couplet uses a rhetorical question and the symbol of fire to show that only renouncers can reach the divine.

questions.question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 12-14: Those who went to jungle ... ignorance saved.]
questions.answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: The poet compares different kinds of travellers and their fates.

Explanation: "Those who went to jungle were not misled" - those who chose the hard, lonely way were kept on the right path. "Those on high way were way-laid" - those who chose the easy, crowded road were ambushed, whether by robbers or by worldly temptations. The third line gives the reason: "Those who gave up both the worlds, were from ignorance saved." The "two worlds" are this life and the next; the seeker who clings to neither is freed from ignorance. The three parallel clauses form a contrast: the difficult road saves, the easy road endangers, and total renunciation brings true knowledge. The paradox is deliberate - what the world calls loss is here called salvation.
questions.explanation: The stanza contrasts the jungle, the highway and total renunciation, and states the paradox of salvation through loss.

questions.question: Work individually and explain the following lines. Write down your work in the notebook and share it with your class fellows once you have completed. [Line No. 15-17: True seekers still ... nests close to them.]
questions.answer:
Poem and poet: 'Selection from Sur Khahori' by Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai, translated by Professor Amina Khamisani.

Context: These are the closing lines of the selection, after the account of the Khahoris' hardships.

Explanation: The poet ends on a note of reassurance: "True seekers still exist." The Khahoris are not only figures of the past. But they are "known only to those who are for spiritual realms" - the worldly cannot recognize them, because recognition itself requires a spiritual eye. Having found the spiritual realm, "they have built their nests close to them": the image of the nest suggests rest after wandering, belonging, and a settled home in God. The closing lines thus complete the movement of the poem from the raft on the ocean, through the hard journey, to the nest at the end - and they invite the reader to become one of those who can recognize the true seekers.
questions.explanation: The closing stanza affirms that true seekers still exist and describes their reward as a nest near the spiritual realm.

chapters.title: Section C: Play — A Visit to a Small Planet

questions.question: Work in pairs and scan the text to write the synonym of the following words contextually. Use them in sentences. After completing, share your work with your partner. (Table columns: No, Word, Contextual meaning, Sentence. Words: 1. impromptu, 2. lunatic, 3. blazing, 4. giddy, 5. reconnoitring, 6. disposition, 7. primitive, 8. seethe, 9. unctuous, 10. fidgets, 11. sordid, 12. resonant)
questions.answer:
No. 1 | impromptu | unplanned, done on the spur of the moment | Kreton admits that 'this visit was all rather impromptu' - he had made no plan to land in the Speldings' garden.
No. 2 | lunatic | mad, insane, wildly foolish (person) | Spelding tells the nation that the 'spaceship' is only the fancy of 'certain lunatic elements'.
No. 3 | blazing | burning fiercely, extremely hot | Ellen argues that the object cannot be a meteor, because 'meteors are blazing hot', while this one is cold.
No. 4 | giddy | dizzy, light-headed | Kreton says the rush of human thoughts makes him 'a bit giddy' and that his head is 'vibrating like a drum'.
No. 5 | reconnoitring | making a preliminary survey of the ground, spying out an area before an attack | General Powers suspects that Kreton has been sent 'for the express purpose of reconnoitring prior to invasion'.
No. 6 | disposition | final settlement or handling of a matter | Powers waits for word from Washington about 'the final disposition of this problem'.
No. 7 | primitive | belonging to an early, simple stage of development; uncivilised | Kreton calls Earth a 'primitive society' and speaks of the 'wonderful rawness' of primitive minds.
No. 8 | seethe | to boil; to be full of turbulent, suppressed emotion | Kreton says that human beings 'simply seethe with unlikely emotions'.
No. 9 | unctuous | oily, smooth, insincerely earnest or flattering | The stage direction describes Spelding as 'middle-aged, unctuous, and resonant' - the very voice of a false television manner.
No. 10 | fidgets | moves restlessly with small nervous movements | The stage direction says that Ellen 'fidgets as she listens' to her father's broadcast.
No. 11 | sordid | dirty, base, ignoble | Ellen says 'I've never felt so sordid' after Kreton reveals that he can hear every thought of theirs.
No. 12 | resonant | deep, full and echoing; sonorous | Spelding's 'resonant' broadcast voice is part of his professional mask, which drops the moment the microphone is switched off.
questions.explanation: Contextual meanings are taken from the exact uses in the play (book pages 226-242): the stage directions supply unctuous, fidgets and resonant; the dialogue supplies the rest.

questions.question: The play takes place in a small suburb in__________.
questions.answer: (a) Maryland. The action takes place in the Speldings' house in Silver Glen, Maryland: Spelding ends his broadcast 'from my old homestead in Silver Glen, Maryland', and later tells Kreton, 'This is a house in the State of Maryland, U.S.A.'
questions.explanation: The play text names Maryland twice. Note the inconsistency: the Introduction (book page 226) says Kreton lands 'nearly a century later in Manassas, Virginia', so option (c) can be defended from the Introduction even though the dialogue says Maryland.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Maryland   (b) Washington   (c) Virginia   (d) Indiana

questions.question: Spelding________ flying object in space.
questions.answer: (b) denies. In his broadcast Spelding says the flying object is 'not, as many believe, a secret weapon of this country. Nor is it a spaceship as certain lunatic elements have suggested', and he later calls it a mere meteor or weather balloon.
questions.explanation: Textual support: Spelding's opening broadcast, book page 227, and his repeated 'I'm sure it's a meteor' on page 229.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) accepts   (b) denies   (c) doubts   (d) confirms

questions.question: Spelding criticizes John for growing________.
questions.answer: (d) peanuts. Spelding sneers that Ellen should not marry 'a boy who plans to sit on a farm all his life, growing peanuts'. Ellen immediately corrects him: 'But, Daddy, John grows walnuts...'
questions.explanation: Book page 228. The joke is that Spelding is too contemptuous to remember what John actually grows; the printed key is peanuts, i.e. what Spelding says, not what John grows.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) cabbage   (b) walnuts   (c) corn   (d) peanuts

questions.question: Kreton appears to be in his ______.
questions.answer: (c) forties. The stage direction reads: 'The visitor is in his forties, a mild, pleasant-looking man with side-whiskers and dressed in the fashion of 1860.'
questions.explanation: Direct textual evidence in the stage direction at the end of Scene I, book page 230.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) twenties   (b) thirties   (c) forties   (d) fifties

questions.question: The impression of Kreton on seeing the inside of the house was__________.
questions.answer: (b) delighted. Kreton looks around 'delightedly' and says, 'Oh, it's better than I'd hoped!' and 'To think this is really the 20th Century. I must sit down a moment and collect myself. The real thing!'
questions.explanation: Book page 231, Scene I. The stage direction '(Looks around delightedly)' gives the answer directly.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) disgusted   (b) delighted   (c) callous   (d) sorrowful

questions.question: The spaceship landed in Mrs. Spelding's__________.
questions.answer: (a) rose garden. Mrs. Spelding cries, 'Right in my rose garden!' and repeats, 'Roger, it's landed right in my rose garden.' Kreton later asks Spelding to move 'that thing off my rose bed'.
questions.explanation: Book page 229. Mrs. Spelding's repeated worry about the roses becomes a running joke about suburban priorities.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) rose garden   (b) petunia bed   (c) greenhouse   (d) vegetable garden

questions.question: Kreton said that the earthmen were his__________.
questions.answer: (a) hobby. Kreton tells Ellen and John, 'I've been studying it for years. In fact, one might say, you people are my hobby', and later tells Spelding, 'You are my hobby. I love you. And that's all there is to it.'
questions.explanation: Book pages 232 and 241. The word recurs, so it is clearly the intended answer.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) hobby   (b) ruination   (c) hope   (d) models

questions.question: Kreton mistakenly thought that he had come to earth in the__________.
questions.answer: (b) 19th century. Kreton wanted to see the Civil War of 1861 and arrives dressed 'in the fashion of 1860'; he says, 'I'd hoped to be in the costume of the period. As you see I am about a hundred years too late.'
questions.explanation: Book page 230-232. 1860 falls in the nineteenth century, and 'a hundred years too late' points to the same answer.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 18th century   (b) 19th century   (c) 20th century   (d) 21st century

questions.question: The first person who arrived to investigate the spaceship was
questions.answer: (a) Powers. General Powers arrives with troops and his Aide, surrounds the house and sends the Aide down to inspect the ship: 'The place is surrounded by troops. Where is the monster?' John reaches the ship first but he is a member of the household, not an investigator.
questions.explanation: Book page 232. 'Laurent' is not a character in this abridged text (the character list on page 226 names only Kreton, Roger Spelding, Ellen, Mrs. Spelding, John Randolph, General Powers and Aide), so option (b) cannot be supported from the printed play.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Powers   (b) Laurent   (c) President of the United States   (d) neighbour

questions.question: Kreton said people on his planet did not________.
questions.answer: (c) did not die. When Powers threatens that he will die if he proves hostile, Kreton answers, 'Poor fragile butterflies, such brief little moments in the sun ... You see we don't die.'
questions.explanation: Book page 233. The printed options repeat 'did not', which is a printing slip in the stem; the intended meaning is 'people on his planet did not ...'.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) did not fight   (b) did not speak   (c) did not die   (d) did not love

questions.question: Kreton's space ship was of__________ shape.
questions.answer: (a) elliptical. The Aide reports: 'Well, it's elliptical, with a fourteen foot diameter. And it's made of an unknown metal which shines and inside there isn't anything.'
questions.explanation: Book page 234. The word is used by the Aide in his report to General Powers.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) elliptical   (b) oval   (c) circular   (d) triangular

questions.question: John could not use the telephone because ________.
questions.answer: (c) Powers declared martial law. The Aide blocks John: 'I'm sorry, sir, but you can't use the phone... This house is a military reservation until the crisis is over: Order General Powers.'
questions.explanation: Book page 235. The house is under martial law, with 'no telephone calls, no communication with the outside' (page 240).
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Kreton had cut communication   (b) Speldings did not have any   (c) Powers declared martial law   (d) Spelding wouldn't give him permission

questions.question: General Powers was thinking about__________.
questions.answer: (a) his promotion. Kreton sees the General's sketch of 'Three silver stars' on a shoulder and says, 'You're making a picture. Three silver stars. You're pinning them on your shoulder, instead of the two stars you now wear', and Powers admits, 'I was thinking of my promotion.'
questions.explanation: Book page 237. The joke is that the man who talks only of national security is privately dreaming of rank.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) his promotion   (b) security of the country   (c) arrest of Kreton   (d) murder of the visitor

questions.question: According to Kareton, civilization is just__________.
questions.answer: (b) at the beginning. Reciting Earth's geography like a school lesson, Kreton concludes, 'Civilization is only just beginning', and when Spelding protests he adds, 'You are only in the initial stages, the most fascinating stages as far as I'm concerned.'
questions.explanation: Book page 232. The stem misprints the name as 'Kareton' for Kreton; it is kept verbatim.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) at the ending   (b) at the beginning   (c) full bloom   (d) creeping

questions.question: The elements of science fiction in this passage are most pronounced in__________.
questions.answer: (a) Kreton's supernatural abilities. The science-fiction core of the play is Kreton himself: he reads minds ('I don't really read it. I hear it'), raises an invisible wall and a force field round his ship, cannot be touched, does not die, and travels in a ship with no instruments.
questions.explanation: Book pages 233-241. Options (b) and (d) are comedy and character, not science fiction; (c) is never claimed in the text.

options.text: Kreton belongs to another breed of human

questions.optionsRaw: (a) Kreton's supernatural abilities   (b) reactions to Kreton   (c) Kreton belongs to another breed of human   (d) hobbies of Kreton

questions.question: Kreton placed an invisible wall around his spaceship because__________.
questions.answer: (b) the army was going to take it apart. Powers says, 'we're going to take your ship apart'; Kreton pleads, 'Oh, I wish you wouldn't', and when Powers insists that 'Security demands it', he replies, 'In that case my security demands you leave it alone', and the Aide then reports the invisible wall.
questions.explanation: Book pages 238 and 242. The ship is his only way home, so he protects it.

options.text: the army was going to take it apart.
the earth's atmosphere was damaging it.
his own people had suggested it.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) the army told him to.   (b) the army was going to take it apart.   (c) the earth's atmosphere was damaging it.   (d) his own people had suggested it.
questions.correctAnswer: (b) the army was going to take it apart.

questions.question: Powers accused Kreton of coming to earth__________.
questions.answer: (d) to reconnoitre before an invasion. Powers says, 'it is my view that you have been sent here by another civilization for the express purpose of reconnoitring prior to invasion', and earlier calls him 'a spy, sent here by an alien race to study us, preparatory to invasion'.
questions.explanation: Book pages 236 and 241. This is the central Cold War joke of the play.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) 100 years too soon   (b) to spread a mysterious disease   (c) to discover some natural resources   (d) to reconnoitre before an invasion

questions.question: Kreton said John's thoughts about Ellen were__________.
questions.answer: (c) purple. Kreton tells Spelding, 'No, no. You must go right on thinking about Ellen. Such wonderfully purple thoughts!'
questions.explanation: Book page 240. John's embarrassed response - 'From now on I'm going to think about agriculture' - completes the joke.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) black   (b) red   (c) purple   (d) yellow

questions.question: Kreton considers human civilization__________.
questions.answer: (b) primitive. Kreton speaks of 'a primitive society', of 'primitive minds' and of 'your exciting primitive lives', and he calls human pride 'one of your most endearing primitive traits'.
questions.explanation: Book pages 232, 240 and 241, where 'primitive' is used of human society, minds and lives.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) modern   (b) primitive   (c) conservative   (d) rational

questions.question: Kreton intends to take charge of__________.
questions.answer: (d) world. When Powers asks 'Of the United States?', Kreton answers, 'No, of the whole world. I'm sure you'll be much happier and it will be great fun for me.'
questions.explanation: Book page 242, the climax of Scene III.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) rose garden   (b) Spelding's house   (c) USA   (d) world

questions.question: Work in pairs. Skim through the text. First, write the name of respective character who said the following dialogues in Column B, and write the context of the dialogues in which character had said that particular dialogue in Column C. First one has been done as an example. After completing, share your work with your partner. (Table: Column A Dialogue; Column B Character; Column C In the Context of)
questions.answer:
No. 1 | 'Fair enough. All right, I'll stay on for a while.' | Kreton | This statement is said to Spelding when Spelding instructed him to stay because of General Powers' interview. (Example given in the book.)
No. 2 | 'He has no get-up-and-go.' | Spelding | Said to Ellen in the living room while the family discusses John. Ellen has just defended John as a hard worker, and her father answers that John has 'every virtue except the most important one'.
No. 3 | 'I am a hobbyist. I love to gad about.' | Kreton | Said to General Powers in the study when Powers asks why he is here. Kreton explains that his people no longer travel because they see everything through monitors and re-creators, but that he himself loves to roam about out of curiosity.
No. 4 | 'But I prefer the ones made of metal, the ones you used to wear, you know: with the feathers on top.' | Kreton | Said to General Powers in the living room after Powers asks, 'What are you dressed up for, a fancy-dress party?' Kreton is admiring the General's uniform and comparing it with the plumed armour of five hundred years earlier.
No. 5 | 'Poor fragile butterflies, such brief little moments in the sun ...' | Kreton | Said to General Powers during the first interrogation, just after telling him 'You see we don't die'. Kreton is pitying human mortality and the shortness of human life.
No. 6 | 'I like his whiskers. They're so very ... comforting.' | Mrs. Spelding | Said to her husband and family in the living room after asking whether Kreton is spending the night. She compares his whiskers to Grandfather Spelding's, showing that she has accepted the visitor without a trace of fear.
questions.explanation: Contexts are drawn from Scene I (book pages 228-235) and Scene II (pages 236-238). Rows 2-6 are the five blank rows; row 1 is the book's worked example.

questions.question: Work individually and make a list of the elements of science fiction you find in the play. After you have done, compare your list with your class fellows.
questions.answer:
1. An alien visitor from another planet in another solar system, who arrives in a flying saucer: 'Not on this planet... In another dimension.'
2. A spacecraft of unknown metal, elliptical, fourteen feet in diameter, with no instruments, no fuel and no food inside: 'there isn't anything.'
3. Interstellar travel that needs no machinery: Kreton does not know how his own ship works - 'these cars are rather common in my world'.
4. Telepathy: Kreton hears thoughts - 'What's inside your mind? ... I don't really read it. I hear it.'
5. Superhuman physical powers: an invisible wall and a force field around the ship, and a body that cannot be touched - 'You can't touch me. That's part of the game.'
6. A race that has conquered death: 'You see we don't die.'
7. A civilisation about two thousand years ahead of Earth, which watches other worlds through 'special monitors and re-creators' and has no need to travel, trade or fight.
8. Time travel in effect: Kreton aims at the Civil War of 1861 and lands in the late twentieth century, 'about a hundred years too late'.
9. The 'first contact' situation, with soldiers, martial law, censorship and a security alert around the landing site.
10. The alien's gentle takeover threat - 'I've come here to take charge... of the whole world' - a standard science-fiction invasion motif turned into comedy.
questions.explanation: Open-ended listing task; every item above is supported by a line or stage direction in the printed text (book pages 230-242).

questions.question: Work in pairs and arrange the scrambled events in the order of their occurrence in the play by giving the number. After you have completed, share your work with your partner. (Table columns: No, Events, Order)
questions.answer:
No. | Event | Order
1 | Kreton arrives on the earth. | 3
2 | General Powers comes with his Aide. | 4
3 | Kreton reads the mind of General Powers. | 7
4 | General Powers orders to grab Kreton. | 10
5 | John spots a spaceship. | 2
6 | Kreton announces to take over the world. | 9
7 | Spelding makes a broadcast and denies any spaceship landing on earth. | 1
8 | Aide stops Spelding from making a call. | 5
9 | Kreton reads the minds of John and Ellen. | 8
10 | General Powers and Kreton have a conversation in the study. | 6
questions.explanation: Sequence: broadcast (Scene I opening) - John sees the saucer - Kreton emerges - Powers and Aide arrive - Aide blocks the telephone while the men move into the study - the study interrogation, in which Kreton reads Powers' mind - Scene III, where he reads John's and Ellen's minds - his takeover speech - the order to grab him - curtains. Events 8 and 10 overlap slightly, since the study conversation begins as the Aide stops the call; the order given follows the printed staging.

questions.question: What is ironic about Spelding's broadcast at the beginning of the play?
questions.answer: Spelding tells the whole nation, on General Powers' authority, that the flying object is 'not... a spaceship as certain lunatic elements have suggested', that it is 'highly doubtful there is any form of life on other planets capable of building a spaceship', and that 'If any travelling is to be done in space, we will do it first.' A few minutes later the 'meteor' lands in his own rose garden, and a visitor from another planet walks out of it and shakes hands with his future son-in-law. The irony is double: the man who denied the spaceship on television is the first householder to receive its passenger, and the boast about American space travel is made in the very house where an alien has just parked his ship. The audience sees the contradiction at once, which is dramatic irony as well as verbal irony.
questions.explanation: Textual support: the broadcast on page 227 and the landing on pages 228-230.

questions.question: Why is Spelding unhappy about the relationship between Ellen and John?
questions.answer: Spelding is a social climber and a snob. He admits that John has 'every virtue except the most important one: he has no get-up-and-go', meaning that John is content to stay on his own farm instead of striving for wealth and position. He wants Ellen to marry 'someone hard-working ambitious, a man who'll make his mark in the world', not 'a boy who plans to sit on a farm all his life, growing peanuts'. He also dislikes Ellen's independence: he calls her 'Miss Know-it-all' when she corrects his quotation from Shakespeare, and he sneers that 'there is nothing wrong with marrying a wealthy man'. His objection is therefore less about John's character than about John's lack of money and ambition, which would not reflect credit on Roger Spelding.
questions.explanation: Textual support: the family quarrel on pages 227-228, including 'He has every virtue except the most important one' and the peanuts/walnuts exchange.

questions.question: Why did Kreton want to visit earth?
questions.answer: Kreton comes as a tourist, not an invader. He is 'a hobbyist' who loves to 'gad about', and Earth is his hobby: 'I've been studying it for years. In fact, one might say, you people are my hobby.' He is especially interested in 'this period of your development', and he had hoped to watch the Civil War of 1861 in period costume, only to arrive 'about a hundred years too late'. What draws him most is the emotional life of human beings, which his own controlled race has lost: he wants 'to intoxicate myself with your primitive minds... with the wonderful rawness of your emotions!' In the end he says simply, 'You are my hobby. I love you.'
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 231-232, 240-241. His motive is curiosity and affection, which makes the invasion panic comic.

questions.question: How is Kreton able to communicate with the people on earth?
questions.answer: Kreton speaks English perfectly, and when Powers asks 'You speak all our languages?' he answers, 'Yes, all of them. But then it's easier than you might think since I can see what's inside.' His real means of communication is telepathy: he hears thoughts rather than reading them - 'I don't really read it. I hear it.' That is why he can answer Powers before the question is finished and why he knows that the General is thinking about his promotion and about blowing up the force field. It also explains his exhaustion: 'Your language is still not familiar to me. I had to learn them all, quite exhausting.' The gift is not merely linguistic but mental, and it is the source of much of the play's comedy and menace.
questions.explanation: Textual support: page 238 ('You speak all our languages?') and page 236 ('I don't really read it. I hear it').

questions.question: Describe the reaction of different characters to Kreton's visit?
questions.answer: Mr. Spelding is at first frightened and then greedy for a scoop: he denies the spaceship on air, panics when it lands, and once Kreton is in the house cares only that 'this story will leak out before I can interview him'. Mrs. Spelding is placid and domestic; she worries about her rose garden and about making up a bed, and decides that 'He looks perfectly nice to me... I like his whiskers.' Ellen is thrilled and romantic: 'I think he's wonderful whoever he is', 'Isn't it exciting!' John is practical and scientific, wishing he had examined the ship and concluding that 'they must be advanced scientifically'. General Powers is suspicious and authoritarian, treating Kreton as a spy and putting the house under martial law, while the Aide simply obeys orders and is visibly disturbed by what he sees. Kreton himself is amused and detached throughout.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 228-235 (Speldings, John), 232-234 (Powers and Aide), 240 (Ellen).

questions.question: Why is General Powers paranoid about Kreton's visit?
questions.answer: Powers is a security official in the middle of the Cold War, and his whole training tells him that a stranger is a spy. He says, 'It is my job to guard the security of this country', and 'For all I know, you are a spy, sent here by an alien race to study us, preparatory to invasion.' The evidence feeds his fear: the ship is made of an unknown metal, has no instruments and nothing inside, and Kreton cannot explain how it travels. Kreton's mind-reading and his invisible wall make him seem even more dangerous. Powers therefore surrounds the house with troops, declares martial law, imposes censorship and treats a polite tourist as an enemy agent - the play's satire on American paranoia of the 1950s.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 233-236, 241; the phrase 'reconnoitring prior to invasion' sums up his fixed idea.

questions.question: What restrictions are imposed on Seldling's family?
questions.answer: The house is declared 'a military reservation until the crisis is over' and placed under martial law. Troops surround the place, and the Aide stands guard at the door. There are 'no telephone calls, no communication with the outside', so John cannot even ring his family to say where he is, and nobody may leave the house without General Powers' permission. Spelding is warned to keep the visitor in sight - 'Don't let him out of your sight' - and his own interview is taken over by the General. Censorship is complete: 'There isn't any story. Complete censorship.' In short, an ordinary family is put under house arrest in its own home for the duration of the 'crisis'.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 234-235 and 240. The stem misprints the name as 'Seldling' for Spelding; it is kept verbatim.

questions.question: What extraordinary powers does Kreton possess, and how does he exhibit these powers?
questions.answer: First, telepathy: he hears thoughts, telling Powers exactly what he is thinking - 'That I am either a lunatic from the earth or a spy from another world' - and then, when Powers tests him, describing his plan 'to blow up my little force field'. Second, a force field and an invisible wall: when the army tries to dismantle his ship, the Aide finds 'some kind of wall all around it, an invisible wall', and the ship cannot be touched. Third, invulnerability: when Powers and the Aide rush at him, they stop 'within a foot of him, stunned', and he says calmly, 'You can't touch me. That's part of the game.' Fourth, he does not die. Fifth, he speaks every human language and can travel between dimensions in a ship with no instruments. Sixth, other people's thoughts make him physically giddy, which shows how sensitive his mind is.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 233, 238-239, 241-242; the force field and the untouchable body are shown on stage, not merely reported.

questions.question: Why does Spelding want Kreton to stay?
questions.answer: Spelding wants the story. As soon as he sees the chance of an exclusive, he whispers to Powers, 'I hope I'll be the one to get the story first, Tom', and later, when Kreton offers to leave, Spelding forgets his fear and begs him to stay: 'Do stay, I mean, we want you to get a good impression of us ...' Kreton sees the real reason at once - 'And of course you still want to be the first journalist to interview me. Fair enough. All right, I'll stay on for a while.' A world exclusive with a visitor from space would make Spelding's career and satisfy his vanity, which matters to him more than the danger to his family or his country.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 234 and 240. His professional greed is part of the play's satire on television journalism.

questions.question: Why did Kreton's friends consider him pervasive?
questions.answer: Kreton's friends think him perverse (the play says 'perverse'; the question's 'pervasive' is evidently a misprint) because he is passionately interested in a 'primitive society' that his own advanced civilisation regards as beneath notice. He admits, 'Of course my friends think me perverse to be interested in a primitive society but there's no accounting for tastes, is there?' His people have no wish to visit Earth at all - 'no one wants to visit you. I can't think, why' - and they see everything through monitors instead of travelling. Kreton, by contrast, wants to 'go native', to soak himself in raw human emotion, and even to take charge of the world 'for fun'. To a race that has outgrown war, death, trade and strong feeling, such enthusiasm looks like a strange and slightly indecent eccentricity.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 240-241. The stem's 'pervasive' is a misprint for 'perverse'; the printed stem is kept unchanged.

questions.question: How does Kreton reveal that he does not have any favourable view of earthlings?
questions.answer: Kreton is polite, but almost every comment is condescending. He recites Earth's geography like a schoolroom lesson and concludes, 'Civilization is only just beginning'; he tells the Speldings that they are 'only in the initial stages' and that their pride is 'one of your most endearing primitive traits'. He calls their minds 'primitive', their thoughts 'savage' - 'Such savage thoughts! My head is vibrating like a drum' - and their lives 'exciting primitive lives'. He pities them as 'poor fragile butterflies, such brief little moments in the sun', addresses them as 'dear, wicked children', and describes Powers' suspicion as 'the wonderfully primitive assumption that all strangers are hostile'. Even his compliments - 'You're almost too good to be true, General' - are ironic. Only their emotions, which his own race has lost, win his genuine admiration.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 232, 233, 240-242. His view is affectionate contempt, not hostility.

questions.question: How does Kreton foil General Power's attempts to confine him?
questions.answer: Kreton never struggles; he simply demonstrates that force is useless against him. When the army is about to take his ship apart, he seals it behind an invisible wall and a force field, so that the Aide can only report that 'we can't get near it'. When Powers draws a weapon and thinks of blowing up the force field, Kreton reads the thought and warns him that he will only 'plough up Mrs. Spelding's garden'. When Powers and the Aide finally rush him, they stop 'within a foot of him, stunned', and he remarks, 'You can't touch me.' He then refuses the General's authority outright - 'I sincerely doubt if you could stop me' - and walks off to bed, promising to be there in the morning. The 'prisoner' is free to leave whenever he chooses, which is the final joke at the General's expense.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 238, 240-242. The stem's 'Power's' is kept verbatim.

questions.question: Who is Aide? What is his role in the play?
questions.answer: The Aide is a young army officer, addressed as 'Captain', who serves as General Powers' assistant. He is a minor character, but he performs several useful functions. He moves the plot by inspecting the saucer and reporting what he finds - an elliptical ship of unknown metal with nothing inside - which convinces the audience of Kreton's otherworldly origin. He enforces the martial law that traps the family, blocking John's telephone call and refusing permission to leave. He supplies comic relief through his bewilderment ('I'm not sure, General') and his mechanical obedience ('Yes, General'). And he sets off Powers' bluster, since the General's authority looks emptier each time the Aide reports another failure. In the final scene he joins Powers in the rush at Kreton and is stopped short like his chief.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 232-235, 238, 242. His name is simply his rank-title; he is listed as 'Aide' among the characters.

questions.question: How did Aide describe Kreton's spaceship?
questions.answer: The Aide describes it reluctantly and precisely: 'Well, it's elliptical, with a fourteen foot diameter. And it's made of an unknown metal which shines and inside there isn't anything.' Pressed by Powers, he adds that there are 'No instruments, no food, nothing' inside, and that he is 'not sure' what the object is. Later he reports the invisible wall around it: 'The door's shut and there's some kind of wall all around it, an invisible wall. We can't get near it.' His flat, factual report is more disturbing than any wild description, because it leaves the military with nothing to analyse: a shining machine of a metal nobody knows, with no engine and no contents.
questions.explanation: Textual support: page 234 for the description and page 238 for the invisible wall.

questions.question: Describe the main comic incidents of the play?
questions.answer: The comedy works through contrast and repetition. Spelding's pompous broadcast denying the spaceship is followed at once by the ship landing in his rose garden, and he keeps offering explanations - meteor, optical illusion, weather balloon - while his family watches the truth. He misquotes Shakespeare ('More thankless than a serpent's tooth') and is corrected by Ellen, then sneers at John for growing 'peanuts' when John grows walnuts. Mrs. Spelding knits through the crisis, worries about her roses and offers the alien a bed because she likes his whiskers. Kreton arrives in 1860 dress, a century late, admires the house, asks whether it is an apartment, and says 'How nice of him!' about the President of the United States. He reads Powers' mind and exposes his dream of a third star, then remarks on John's 'wonderfully purple thoughts' while John resolves to 'think about agriculture'. The climax is pure farce: two armed men rush the visitor and freeze a foot away, and he politely goes to bed.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 227-242. The comedy is verbal (misquotation, irony) and visual (costume, the frozen rush, the knitting).

questions.question: How is media depicted in the play?
questions.answer: The media is depicted as vain, managed and more interested in appearance than truth. Spelding is a television commentator whose broadcast is a performance: he reads General Powers' denial as if it were fact, crosses 'to pose with wife and daughter', signs off as 'Roger Spelding, saying good night to Mother and Father America', and the moment the microphone is off 'his mechanical smile and heartiness' vanish. He cares about being first with the story, not about verifying it, and he is furious at the thought that it may 'leak out' before his own interview. The state, in turn, manages the press: Powers imposes 'complete censorship' and announces that 'there isn't any story'. The play thus shows a closed loop in which television repeats official versions and official versions are shaped for television.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 227 (broadcast and pose), 234 ('Complete censorship'), 240 (the scoop).

questions.question: The play is a satire on American society. Discuss.
questions.answer: The play is a satire because it uses an innocent outsider to expose the follies of 1950s America, and it laughs at them rather than condemning them. Through Spelding it mocks television journalism - the resonant voice, the posed family, the readiness to broadcast a official denial as truth and then chase the exclusive. Through General Powers and his Aide it mocks Cold War paranoia: troops, martial law, censorship and the instant assumption that a visitor must be a spy 'reconnoitring prior to invasion'. Through the Spelding household it mocks suburban materialism and snobbery: the rose garden valued above a visitor from space, the knitting wife who notices only whiskers, the father who wants his daughter to marry money and 'make his mark'. Even the national boast that 'If any travelling is to be done in space, we will do it first' is deflated by a saucer already parked in the garden. Kreton's mild astonishment at human greed, fear and self-importance is the satirist's voice.
questions.explanation: Open-ended discussion task; the answer is built from the play's targets - media, militarism, materialism, national vanity - each supported by a quoted line.

questions.question: How does the playwright expose the inferiority of the present race to that of the future?
questions.answer: Vidal does it by making the future race present in the room and letting it be unimpressed. Kreton comes from a civilisation about two thousand years ahead, where people do not die, do not fight, do not trade, control their thoughts and travel between dimensions in ships with no instruments. Against this, the twentieth century looks childish: its army cannot dent an invisible wall, its general cannot touch the visitor, its guns cannot frighten him, and its newspapers can think only of a scoop. Kreton's verdict is delivered as a compliment - humans are 'primitive', 'only in the initial stages', 'poor fragile butterflies' who 'seethe with unlikely emotions' - and that politeness makes the judgement harder to answer. The play also shows the moral inferiority: the future race is calm and curious, while the present race is fearful, aggressive, status-hungry and ready to imprison a guest on suspicion.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 232-233 (civilisation 'only just beginning', 'we don't die'), 240-242 (the failed arrest, the takeover speech).

questions.question: Describe the arrival of the flying saucer in your own words.
questions.answer: The evening begins quietly. Spelding has just finished his weekly broadcast, denying that the strange object in the sky is a spaceship, when John bursts in breathless: 'Come out! Quick! It's coming this way. It's going to land right here!' The family hurries outside. Something bright is coming down, and Mrs. Spelding is certain it will hit the house; Spelding takes comfort in explanations - a meteor, an optical illusion, mass hysteria, a weather balloon - and then bolts indoors to telephone the police and the Army. Ellen thinks it may be a balloon; John insists it is a spaceship 'and right in your own backyard', and runs towards the light while Ellen calls him back. The object settles 'right in my rose garden'. Its side opens, a man in the dress of 1860 steps out, and John shakes hands with him and brings him up to the house, where the family stares at him 'equally interested'.
questions.explanation: Open-ended retelling task; the sequence follows pages 228-230 exactly, in the student's own words.

questions.question: How much advanced is the civilization of Kreton than of the Earth?
questions.answer: Kreton's civilisation is roughly two thousand years ahead of Earth's. When John mentions relativity, Kreton replies that the truth is 'much more involved than that' and that humans 'won't know about time until... about two thousand years'. The gap shows in every field. Technologically, his people cross dimensions in elliptical ships of unknown metal that need no instruments or fuel, and they watch other worlds through 'special monitors and re-creators' instead of travelling. Biologically, they have conquered death. Socially, they have outgrown war, invasion and even trade, which Kreton calls 'something peculiar only to your social level'. Mentally, they control their thoughts and can hear those of others. Kreton also says he could not explain the ship's drive to Powers 'for another five hundred years', which measures the distance in understanding as well as in years.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 233 ('not for another five hundred years'), 238 ('You won't know about time... about two thousand years'), 241 (no trade, no hostility).

questions.question: Why can the people of earth not compete with people of Kreton?
questions.answer: Because the contest is not between armies but between levels of development. Kreton's race is about two thousand years ahead: it understands time, matter and mind in ways that human science has not reached, and its technology needs no weapons at all. An invisible wall keeps the army away from the ship; a force field absorbs whatever Powers plans; and Kreton's body cannot be touched, so 'You can't touch me' ends the arrest before it begins. Human beings are also divided among themselves - a general guarding his career, a broadcaster guarding his scoop, a family arguing about walnuts - while Kreton acts with complete calm because he has nothing to fear. In Kreton's words, Earth is 'only in the initial stages', and a primitive society cannot compete with a civilisation that has already passed through the stages it is still entering.
questions.explanation: Textual support: pages 238-242. The play makes the point comically rather than tragically: the soldiers are stopped, not killed.

questions.question: What type of life do you foresee in the year 5000?
questions.answer: If the play's logic holds, life in the year 5000 will be much less anxious and much more mental. Technology will be almost invisible: machines will be sealed, silent and self-running, the way Kreton's saucer has no instruments and nothing inside, and travel will be a matter of entering a small craft and naming a destination. Medicine will have advanced far beyond cure into repair, so that the human lifespan will be far longer and disease may be a historical subject. Work will be done by machines, leaving people free for study, art and exploration, and communication may be partly direct, mind to mind, which would make lying and hiding much harder and might make society gentler - or more controlled. I hope that the year 5000 will also have abolished war, poverty and the suspicion of strangers, because those are the things the play shows as primitive. The real risk is that comfort without curiosity would make life dull, which is exactly what Kreton says about outer space.
questions.explanation: Open-ended prediction task; the model answer stays anchored to the play's own future civilisation while adding a personal, reasoned view.

questions.question: What are the literary elements used in 'Visit to a Small Planet,' and how they enhance the story?
questions.answer:
Plot: a comic science-fiction plot with a clear arc - a broadcast denial, a landing, an interrogation, a takeover threat and an escape - which keeps the single evening moving and lets each scene raise the stakes.
Character: types sharply contrasted for satire - the pompous broadcaster, the paranoid general, the dreamy daughter, the practical farmer, the vague housewife and the unflappable alien. Kreton acts as a foil to Powers, and the contrast exposes both.
Dialogue: fast, idiomatic and ironic. Spelding's misquotation and Ellen's correction, Kreton's polite understatements ('Poor fragile butterflies') and Powers' bluster do the work that a narrator would do in fiction.
Setting: one living room and one study, on a single evening, which gives the play the unity of classical drama and makes the ordinary suburban house the stage for a world crisis.
Conflict: human against alien, and individual against the security state; the two run together when Powers tries to arrest Kreton.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows the ship is real while Spelding denies it, and knows that Kreton can hear every thought while Powers boasts of his plans.
Satire and comedy of manners: American television, militarism and suburbia are ridiculed through exaggeration.
Symbolism: the rose garden stands for comfortable, self-absorbed suburban life, which the saucer crushes.
Stage directions: they supply tone and character - Spelding 'unctuous, and resonant', Ellen who 'fidgets', Kreton who 'looks around delightedly' - and they control the comedy of the frozen rush at the end.
questions.explanation: This is a synthesis question; every element listed is illustrated from the printed text, and the notes explain the effect of each rather than merely naming it.

questions.question: Who is your favourite character in this play and why?
questions.answer: My favourite character is Kreton, because he is the only person in the play who is completely honest and completely free. Everyone else is playing a role: Spelding performs for the camera, Powers performs for Washington, Mrs. Spelding hides in her knitting, and even Ellen is half in love with the idea of a visitor from space. Kreton has nothing to gain, so he says exactly what he thinks - that the house is 'better than I'd hoped', that civilization here is 'only just beginning', that the General is 'almost too good to be true'. His manners are perfect and his judgement is devastating, which is the best kind of comic hero. He is also generous: he could take the world by force and instead offers to leave when he sees that his visit is causing trouble. I like him because he shows that curiosity and good humour can be stronger than an army, and because he makes the people around him reveal what they really are.
questions.explanation: Open-ended personal-response task; the answer chooses one character and justifies the choice with events and lines from the play.

questions.question: Suppose an alien visits the Earth from another planet. Work in pairs and prepare a list of your questions that you would ask the alien. Next, prepare the alien's answers. After you have completed, share your work with your class fellows.
questions.answer:
1. Q: Where do you come from, and how long did the journey take? A: From a small planet of a star you cannot see without instruments. The journey took no time at all, because we do not travel through space; we step from one dimension into another.
2. Q: Why did you choose our planet? A: Because you are interesting. My people have stopped being curious, and I have not. You are at the stage we left behind two thousand years ago, and that stage is the most fascinating one.
3. Q: Do your people die? A: No. We stopped dying a long time ago. That is why your griefs seem so urgent to us, and so beautiful.
4. Q: How do you govern yourselves? A: Nobody governs. There is nothing to fight over, so there is nothing to rule. We have no armies and no parties.
5. Q: What do you eat, and what do you do for work? A: We eat very little and work very little, because machines do what needs doing. Most of us spend our time on art, on study and on travel of the kind I am doing now.
6. Q: What do you think of the way we live? A: I think you are brave, noisy and wasteful. You have wonderful emotions and terrible weapons, and you use the weapons more often than the emotions.
7. Q: Will you take me with you? A: Not yet. Your body is not ready for the journey, and your mind would find my world very quiet. Study first; then perhaps we shall meet again.
8. Q: What is the one thing you would change about Earth? A: Your habit of assuming that every stranger is an enemy. It costs you more than any disease.
questions.explanation: Open-ended speaking/writing task. The answers are modelled on Kreton's own attitudes in the play (pages 231-241), so the pair work stays within the text's world.

questions.question: Work individually and sketch the following characters with the help of below given mind map. Once you have completed, share your work with your class fellows. (a) Mr. Spelding
questions.answer:
Personality Traits: Vain, pompous, smooth-tongued and status-hungry; professionally 'unctuous, and resonant'; a snob about money and ambition; cowardly when frightened and ruthless when a story is at stake.
Role: Television commentator and head of the household; Ellen's father; the play's chief satirical portrait of the media.
Actions: Broadcasts a confident denial of the spaceship; poses with his wife and daughter for the cameras; misquotes Shakespeare and is corrected; sneers at John for growing 'peanuts'; telephones the police and the Army; whispers to Powers that he wants the story first; begs Kreton to stay so that he can interview him.
Others' Opinion: Ellen finds him unfair and unkind ('Oh, Daddy, stop it!'); Mrs. Spelding soothes him ('We love your broadcasts, dear'); Kreton calls him 'Poor Mr. Spelding' and sees through his motives at once; Powers treats him as a nuisance to be censored.
